name: Montage XT Cranial Cement (Montage and Permatage settable bone putty family)
company: Abyrx, Inc. (manufacturer of record Orthocon, Inc.)
ownership_history: Orthocon, Inc. is the 510(k) holder and FDA letters are addressed in care of Abyrx, Inc., Stamford, CT; Abyrx markets Montage. A reported transaction created MedEdge Holdings as owner of Abyrx and Kairuku (date and terms unverified). SurgiCor was the announced US distributor from 2014 to 2017.
composition: Two-component settable, resorbable calcium phosphate putty (Montage) and a flowable paste; XT doubles hardening time; Permatage is a non-resorbable variant

regulatory.reference: K221933 (Montage Settable, Resorbable Bone Putty, cranial GXP, 2023-01-13); K231475 (Montage-QS, 2023-10-12); K232771 (Montage Flowable, 2024-02-16); K241027 (Permatage, 2024-09-26); K253854 (Montage XT Cranial Cement, Special 510(k), 2026-01-02); K253732 (Permatage Flowable, 2026-03-13); K261265 (Permatage XT, 2026-06-15); separate MQV bone void filler clearances K222063 and K243526
on_label_indications: Self-setting calcium phosphate cement indicated for use in the repair of neurosurgical burr holes, contiguous craniotomy cuts and other cranial defects with a surface area no larger than 25 cm2; should be used only in skeletally mature individuals (K253854, identical to predicate K221933)
Cardiothoracic (sternotomy) clearance September 2023 for Montage Settable Bone Putty

applications.evidence_summary: No published clinical data found on PubMed as of 2026-10-22; the January 2026 XT cranial clearance was a Special 510(k) (30-day review) resting on the 2023 predicate.
applications.caveats: Cranial flap fixation with Montage Flowable (NCT07103330, n=100, start March 2026) is outside the labeled indication.

applications.evidence_summary: Labeled to 25 cm2 like the legacy cements; no cranioplasty series.
applications.caveats: Eight cranial and bone-void 510(k)s in three years with no clinical publications.

evidence.title: Evaluation of cranial flap fixation with Montage Flowable Settable Bone Paste
evidence.finding: Not yet recruiting as of July 2025 verification; estimated start March 2026, primary completion December 2027; compares flap fixation with paste alone against metallic hardware.

pipeline.expected_milestone: Flap-fixation data 2027 to 2028 if the study enrolls; any flap-fixation claim would need a new 510(k) or De Novo (source: ClinicalTrials.gov record and K253854 labeling).

bd.reimbursement: Bundled; no separate code.
bd.notes: Fastest-moving 510(k) filer in product code GXP (8 clearances 2023 to 2026); distribution historically through SurgiCor and Abyrx's own channels, with Acumed and OsteoMed hosting Montage 510(k) PDFs on their sites, which suggests but does not prove a CMF distribution relationship (unverified).

name: OssiGraft Prime viable bone matrix
ownership_history: Ossium Health (Indianapolis/San Francisco), private; raised a $52 million Series C; core business is organ-donor-derived bone marrow for transplant. OssiGraft distribution agreements with Extremity Medical (US) and Enovis.
composition: Vertebral-body-derived viable bone matrix, about 80% cancellous, from organ donors averaging 35 years; first case was an ankle fusion (July 2024); won a 2024 Orthopedics This Week Spine Technology Award

regulatory.reference: OssiGraft IFU (OHC-IFU-0002 Rev 05, hosted by Enovis): OssiGraft is an HCT/P that meets the 21 CFR 1271.10 criteria for regulation solely under section 361; no 510(k)/PMA/De Novo found
on_label_indications: Bone void filler for voids or gaps not intrinsic to the stability of the bony structure (361 homologous use, presumed)

applications.evidence_summary: No clinical data; marketing rests on younger donor age and vertebral-body sourcing (a 2018 lab study found vertebral-body marrow MSCs at least as osteogenic as iliac crest MSCs, PMID 29795650, unrelated to Ossium).
applications.caveats: Company claims only.

applications.evidence_summary: First case was an ankle surgery (2023); no published outcomes; no trauma data.
applications.caveats: Press releases only.

applications.evidence_summary: No clinical publications found.
applications.caveats: New entrant; evidence gap.

bd.reimbursement: Bundled in fusion MS-DRGs.
bd.notes: Distribution-partner model (Extremity Medical, Enovis); a new entrant competing on donor sourcing rather than clinical data.

pipeline.expected_milestone: None public.

name: Rotium Bioresorbable Wick
company: Atreon Orthopedics (Columbus, OH; 510(k) applicant Nanofiber Solutions, LLC)
ownership_history: Nanofiber Solutions spun out Atreon Orthopedics to commercialize Rotium; clearances K183236 (2019-03-11), K201414 (2020), K231641 (2023), K250021 (2025-02-27, new product code OWW).
composition: Electrospun bioresorbable synthetic nanofiber scaffold placed as an interpositional wick between the tendon and the greater tuberosity footprint during repair.

regulatory.reference: K250021 (Rotium; Nanofiber Solutions, LLC; decision 2025-02-27; 21 CFR 878.3300 surgical mesh, product code OWW, Class II); earlier Rotium Bioresorbable Wick K183236 (2019-03-11), K201414 (2020-06-25), K231641 (2023-07-05; product code MAI)
on_label_indications: Management and protection of tendon injuries without substantial loss of tendon tissue in patients requiring surgical intervention (K250021 Indications for Use; this is not a rotator-cuff-reinforcement or suture-augmentation indication)

applications.evidence_summary: Technique papers only (Beleckas 2023, PMID:36814979; Mousad 2025, PMID:40656718); a planned ultrasound-healing RCT was withdrawn with zero enrollment (NCT04361266).
applications.caveats: No clinical outcome data.

evidence.title: Bioaugmentation of rotator cuff repair with an interpositional nanofiber scaffold
evidence.finding: Surgical technique description; no outcomes.

pipeline.expected_milestone: No registered outcome trial active; next milestone is any comparative clinical series

bd.reimbursement: Packaged into the procedure payment.
bd.notes: Start-up in a category dominated by Smith+Nephew and Arthrex; included as the 'emerging' example in the rotator cuff adjacent note.

challenge: K250021 is a tendon-injury management/protection indication; any rotator-cuff augmentation claim is outside the cleared wording.

name: PearlMatrix P-15 Peptide Enhanced Bone Graft (formerly P-15L / i-FACTOR+ Matrix)
ownership_history: Cerapedics; investigational name P-15L / i-FACTOR+ Matrix during the ASPIRE IDE (2018-2025).
composition: P-15 peptide on anorganic bone mineral in a collagen-based matrix (the lumbar/interbody formulation of the ABM/P-15 technology); Class III drug-device combination product

regulatory.reference: P240001 (PearlMatrix P-15 Peptide Enhanced Bone Graft; FDA decision 2025-06-18; Cerapedics press releases are dated June 23, 2025). S001 approved 2025-12-11 (180-day track) adds ALIF, TLIF, PLIF, OLIF/ATP and LLIF approaches and titanium alloy and PEEK/titanium cages; S002 (2026-04-07) and S003 (2026-09-16) are manufacturing/lab-site notices. Predecessor i-FACTOR is P140019 (2015-11-03).
on_label_indications: PearlMatrix is indicated for intervertebral body fusion in skeletally mature patients: one level, L2-S1, DDD with up to Grade I spondylolisthesis, with a PEEK TLIF fusion device and supplemental internal fixation, after at least six months of nonoperative treatment (P240001, 2025-06-18)
S001 (approved 2025-12-11): additional open or minimally invasive approaches (ALIF, TLIF, PLIF, OLIF/ATP, LLIF) and use with titanium alloy and PEEK/titanium cages

applications.evidence_summary: ASPIRE pivotal RCT (NCT03438747; Harrop 2025, n=290 at 33 US sites, single-blind, ~60% high-risk): composite clinical success 55.5% vs 37.5% local autograft (noninferior and superior, p=0.002); CT fusion 84.3% vs 58.5% at 24 months; time to fusion HR 1.87. Device-related SAEs similar; the January 2026 company release notes a higher rate of secondary surgical interventions with PearlMatrix than autograft.
applications.caveats: Sponsor-funded; control arm fusion (58.5%) is far below typical TLIF literature because of strict CT criteria and high-risk enrollment, which flatters the treatment delta.

applications.evidence_summary: ALIF, PLIF, OLIF and LLIF indications were added by supplement in January 2026 on the strength of the TLIF pivotal plus cage/approach equivalence; no approach-specific RCT.
applications.caveats: Label expansion without new pivotal data for each approach.

applications.evidence_summary: On-label single-level OLIF/LLIF since January 2026 via supplement; evidence extrapolated from ASPIRE TLIF.
applications.caveats: Same as ALIF.

evidence.title: P-15 peptide enhanced bone graft in TLIF: a randomized, controlled IDE study demonstrating improved composite clinical success
evidence.finding: CCS 55.5% vs 37.5%; fusion 84.3% vs 58.5% at 24 months; similar device-related SAEs.

evidence.title: P-15 peptide enhanced bone graft improves time to fusion in TLIF: a randomized, controlled IDE study
evidence.finding: Kaplan-Meier fusion 57.6% vs 26.9% at 6 months and 81.1% vs 54.9% at 24 months; HR 1.87 for time to fusion.

evidence.title: An assessment of P-15L bone graft in TLIF with instrumentation (ASPIRE)
evidence.finding: Active, not recruiting; 72-month follow-up continues to 2028.

evidence.title: ASPIRE pivotal PMA IDE study (company summary in FDA approval release)
evidence.finding: Primary 24-month composite clinical success met with superiority vs autograft; faster fusion at 6 months.

pipeline.expected_milestone: Approved 2025-06-18 (P240001); first US patient July 2025; S001 approach/cage expansion approved 2025-12-11 (company announced January 2026).

bd.reimbursement: Bundled in the level-based spinal fusion MS-DRG family in force since FY2025 (402, 426-430, 447-451, 456-458; 523-525 added FY2027; 471-473 cervical) inpatient; no NTAP or pass-through found in sources reviewed; physician +20930 bundled. Cerapedics publishes a PearlMatrix coding guide (PDF, not text-extractable in this sweep).
bd.notes: Breakthrough Device designation April 2021; approval came 180 days-class on a panel-track PMA. The TLIF label puts PearlMatrix head-to-head with Infuse for the first on-label TLIF biologic, eight months before Medtronic's TLIF approval.

challenge: PMA P240001 approved 2025-06-18 (openFDA, pass 2); supplement S001 label expansion approved 2025-12-11 and announced 2026-01-13. Pass 3 could not reach the FDA PMA search page (bot challenge).

name: Recent US bone void filler clearances relevant to trauma (2024-2026 tracker)
company: Various (Elute, RTI Surgical, Artoss, SDIP Innovations, Stryker, SurGenTec, Anika, Acuitive)
ownership_history: Tracker record, not a single product.
composition: Mixed: synthetic resorbable calcium salts, nanocrystalline HA, citrate-based polymer/ceramic (CITREPORE), hyaluronic-acid-based injectable, moldable allograft

regulatory.reference: K241555 RTI Surgical Moldable Bone Void Filler (2025-02-21, RTI Surgical, Inc.); K250346 Elute BonVie+ (2025-02-26, Elute, Inc.); K250521 NanoBone SBX Putty / NanoBone QD (2025-04-07, applicant Biocomposites, Ltd., which owns Artoss/NanoBone); K252797 JAZBI Resorbable Bone Void Filler (2026-05-26, SDIP Innovations Pty Ltd); K261008 Vitoss BiModal foam strip family (2026-04-24, Stryker Spine); K240450 Citrepore (2024-11-06, Acuitive Technologies); SurGenTec OsteoFlo HydroFiber K242797 (2024-12-23), K243949 (2025-05-28), K251720 (2025-07-02); Anika Tactoset Injectable Bone Substitute K212083 (2021-08-31), K231968 (2023-12-20); Fibergraft BG Putty GPS K253147 (2025-10-22, Prosidyan); openFDA: K241555 (RTI Moldable BVF, 2025-02-21); K250346 (Elute BonVie+, 2025-02-26); K250521 (Biocomposites NanoBone SBX, 2025-04-07); K252797 (SDIP JAZBI, 2026-05-26); K261008 (Stryker Vitoss family, 2026-04-24)
on_label_indications: All are standard MQV 'bone void filler for voids not intrinsic to the stability of the bony structure' clearances; none is antibiotic-eluting; the only new antibiotic-eluting authorization in the window is CERAMENT G's open-fracture 510(k) (K234008, 2024-03-13)

applications.evidence_summary: None of these clearances carried clinical data; they expand the commodity void-filler field. Artoss is running a 200-patient US trauma registry of NanoBone (NCT06256458) and Advanced Medical Solutions a 200-patient RCT of its FDBS filler vs MBCP putty in orthopaedic defects (NCT06326827, start October 2026).
applications.caveats: Bench-only clearances; the list was built from product-code listings and may be incomplete.

evidence.title: Multicenter prospective registry of NanoBone bone graft substitute in acute trauma patients (Artoss)
evidence.finding: Recruiting; primary completion December 2026.

evidence.title: Randomised investigation of FDBS (GraftR3) vs MBCP Putty in filling orthopaedic bone defects (Advanced Medical Solutions)
evidence.finding: Not yet recruiting; start October 2026.

bd.reimbursement: Bundled inpatient MS-DRG / packaged outpatient APC for all.
bd.notes: Signal: FDA cleared at least five MQV fillers in 2025-2026 but no antibiotic-eluting competitor to CERAMENT G; Biocomposites' genex G pivotal (start June 2026) is the first real one.

name: TnR Cranial Implant (formerly TnR CFI)
composition: 3D-printed porous, osteoconductive, resorbable scaffold of polycaprolactone and beta-tricalcium phosphate with interconnected pores, in burr-hole plug, strip and block geometries (15 x 33 to 67 mm strips, 15 x 30 to 50 mm blocks); resorbs over roughly 18 to 24 months per company

regulatory.reference: K251959 (2026-07-30, product code GXP, Traditional 510(k)); predicate Osteopore PCL Scaffold Bone Void Filler K051093
on_label_indications: Repair of neurosurgical burr holes, craniotomy cuts, and other cranial defects; augmentation or restoration of bony contour in the cranial skeleton

applications.evidence_summary: US clearance July 2026 rested on biocompatibility, toxicological risk assessment and GLP animal studies; the company claims more than 20,000 clinical uses in Korea since a 2021 MFDS approval, which is a promotional figure with no published US or peer-reviewed series located.
applications.caveats: No US distributor named as of October 2026; the 510(k) summary carries no size ceiling, unlike the cements.

applications.evidence_summary: Block and strip geometries are labeled for other cranial defects without a cm2 limit, but no clinical data exist for use beyond burr holes and kerfs.
applications.caveats: Label breadth exceeds evidence.

pipeline.expected_milestone: US commercial launch and distributor announcement pending (Korean press, August 2026).

bd.reimbursement: Bundled; no code.
bd.notes: Second 3D-printed PCL-TCP cranial scaffold cleared in the US after Osteopore; T&R Biofab sells PCL craniofacial implants in Korea and Europe.

name: Arthrex Angel cPRP and Bone Marrow Processing System
company: Arthrex (exclusive distributor); manufactured by Cytomedix/Nuo Therapeutics heritage (Angel originally a Sorin/COBE Cardiovascular device)
ownership_history: COBE Cardiovascular cleared the Angel whole-blood separation system in 2004 (K042473); Sorin Group sold Angel to Cytomedix in 2010; Cytomedix (later Nuo Therapeutics) obtained a second 510(k) in November 2012 for processing a mixture of blood and bone marrow aspirate and granted Arthrex exclusive worldwide rights for non-wound-care uses. Current manufacturing/ownership chain not verified for 2025-2026.
composition: Automated, sensor-driven centrifuge and single-use kit that produces platelet-rich plasma or concentrated bone marrow aspirate with adjustable hematocrit/platelet levels.

regulatory.reference: BK110046 (Angel Whole Blood Separation System, Cytomedix; decision 2012-11-07; the clearance that added processing of a blood plus bone marrow aspirate mixture); BK180180 (Arthrex Angel System Kits, Arthrex; decision 2018-07-05); both CBER 510(k)s, product code ORG 'platelet and plasma separator for bone graft handling', 21 CFR 864.9245. Original COBE Angel K042473 (2004-11-19, CDRH, product code JQC).
on_label_indications: Point-of-care preparation of platelet-rich plasma, including PRP concentrate from a mixture of blood and bone marrow aspirate, to be mixed with autograft/allograft bone (FDA product code ORG wording; Arthrex markets it as a 'cPRP and bone marrow processing system')

applications.evidence_summary: Same class evidence as other BMAC systems (Hernigou RCT, Papakostidis meta-analysis); device-specific data are bench comparisons of cell yield published by Arthrex.
applications.caveats: Manufacturer-authored yield comparisons; no clinical outcome trial with this device in the hip.

applications.evidence_summary: Class evidence only (Hernigou 2005).
applications.caveats: Off-label clinical claims.

bd.reimbursement: Same as Harvest: no separate inpatient payment; office/ASC coding via 20939 add-on or 38232 with frequent payer denials.
bd.notes: Arthrex's strength is its sports-medicine and foot-and-ankle rep network, not trauma; in hip osteonecrosis the pull is through arthroplasty and hip-preservation surgeons.

name: Bone marrow aspirate concentrate (BMAC) and percutaneous marrow injection
company: Multiple device makers (Terumo/Harvest SmartPrep, Arthrex Angel, Zimmer Biomet BioCUE, EmCyte, Celling); autologous point-of-care
ownership_history: Terumo Americas agreed to acquire Harvest Technologies on 2011-05-11. Device clearances are for the centrifuge/concentration system, not for a cellular claim.
composition: Autologous iliac crest marrow aspirate concentrated 4-10x at point of care; osteoprogenitor (CFU-F) dose is the biologically relevant variable

regulatory.reference: Concentration systems cleared under 510(k) (e.g., SmartPrep, Angel) for preparing autologous PRP/BMC; same-surgical-procedure exception under 21 CFR 1271.15(b) covers minimal manipulation; any osteoinductive claim is off-label; Device clearances: Harvest SmartPReP2 BMAC K103340 (CDRH, product code JQC, 2010-12-06); CBER 510(k)s under product code ORG 'platelet and plasma separator for bone graft handling' (21 CFR 864.9245): Arthrex/Cytomedix Angel BK110046 (decision 2012-11-07) and Arthrex Angel System Kits BK180180 (2018-07-05), Arthrex ACP Max BK210655 (2022-09-22), Isto/Arteriocyte Precise Cell Concentration System BK200540 (2022-03-17). The ORG labeling is PRP from blood (or a blood and bone-marrow-aspirate mixture) mixed with autograft/allograft to improve handling; no device carries a cell-therapy, fracture-healing or nonunion claim
on_label_indications: Devices: rapid preparation of autologous bone marrow concentrate / platelet concentrate at the point of care; no labeled fracture-healing claim

applications.evidence_summary: Hernigou 2005 injected concentrated marrow into 60 atrophic tibial nonunions and showed union correlated with CFU-F count and concentration (threshold about 1,500 progenitors per mL); a 2024 systematic review of 25 studies found aseptic nonunion success 79-100% (marrow) and 50-100% (BMAC) but extremely heterogeneous designs.
applications.caveats: No US RCT; dose-response data from a single French group; outcomes confounded by concomitant fixation and grafts.
applications.challenge: Ask which centrifuge delivers the Hernigou progenitor dose; most cannot be shown to.

applications.evidence_summary: Hernigou 2020: early percutaneous BMC in 231 Gustilo II-III open fractures (gap under 10 mm) vs 67 no-graft and 76 early ICBG controls, with lower infection and better healing in the BMC group.
applications.caveats: Non-randomized, single-center.

applications.evidence_summary: 2025 network meta-analysis of 15 RCTs (1,286 patients) ranked PRP+BMAC among the best strategies for healing time; diamond-concept series use BMAC with RIA graft.
applications.caveats: Pooled RCTs are small and mostly ex-US.

applications.evidence_summary: Attia 2022 meta-analysis (PMID 35612823) of 718 athlete Jones fractures: union 98.5% with orthobiologic augmentation (mostly BMAC or BMA plus DBM) vs 93.8% with fixation alone; Murawski and Kennedy 2011 (PMID 21212308) 26 athletes with percutaneous screw plus BMAC, mean radiographic healing 5 weeks, one delayed union.
applications.caveats: No comparative trial; selection of high-risk athletes for augmentation; return-to-play unchanged.

applications.evidence_summary: Pinzur 2009 (PMID 19254506): 44 high-risk diabetic Charcot patients (46 feet, 28 with open wounds) corrected with ring fixation plus platelet-rich concentrate and bone marrow aspirate; 42 of 46 feet showed radiographic union, two amputations.
applications.caveats: Single surgeon, no control, PRP and BMA combined.

applications.evidence_summary: Hernigou 2005 (PMID 15995108): percutaneous concentrated marrow injection into 60 atrophic tibial nonunions, union in 53, with union correlating with progenitor count. Tricot 2017 (PMID 28416462): 115 ankle/hindfoot fusions, allograft plus DBM plus BMA vs autograft plus DBM, nonunion 13% vs 18%, infection 4% vs 11%. Anastasio 2025 review (PMID 40680688): moderate-to-high evidence for nonoperative delayed union/nonunion, questionable benefit in arthrodesis.
applications.caveats: Tibial, not foot, data for the strongest series; progenitor yield varies 10-fold between patients and harvest sites; cost and harvest morbidity unjustified by RCT data.

applications.evidence_summary: Routinely layered into bone-block TTC fusions (PMID 34677103: 14 patients, femoral-head allograft plus BMAC plus DBM fibers).
applications.caveats: Never isolated.

applications.evidence_summary: Arthroscopic fixation plus DBM and BMAC injection united 15 of 17 early scaphoid nonunions (Lee 2026, PMID:42098735); a French case report describes concentrated marrow injection in scaphoid nonunion (Maincourt 2025, PMID:39732339). No comparative study.
applications.caveats: Selected nonunions with minimal sclerosis; adds iliac aspiration morbidity and a centrifuge disposable.

applications.evidence_summary: The foundational percutaneous BMAC data are tibial (Hernigou 2005, PMID 15995108: 60 atrophic tibial nonunions, 53 united, failures received fewer progenitors; technique paper PMID 16951103). Humeral nonunions were included in the ORTHO-1 expanded-MSC feasibility trial (28 femur/tibia/humerus nonunions; PMID 29598897).
applications.caveats: Dose-response depends on progenitor count, which most surgeons do not measure; evidence does not separate the humerus.

applications.evidence_summary: Navani 2024 crossover RCT (n=40) found intradiscal BMC improved pain and function vs placebo at 12 months (open-label, crossover).
applications.caveats: See PRP record; same trial.

evidence.title: Percutaneous autologous bone-marrow grafting for nonunions: influence of the number and concentration of progenitor cells
evidence.finding: Concentrated marrow (20 mL) injected into 60 noninfected atrophic tibial nonunions; mineralized callus volume and healing correlated with number and concentration of CFU-F; nonunions that failed received fewer progenitors.

evidence.title: Early injection of autologous bone marrow concentrates decreases infection risk and improves healing of acute severe open tibial fractures
evidence.finding: 231 BMC-treated open tibial fractures vs 67 no-graft and 76 ICBG controls; BMC associated with lower infection and better healing (abstract truncated).

evidence.title: Bone marrow aspirate and BMAC: does the literature support use in long-bone nonunion?
evidence.finding: 25 studies; aseptic nonunion success 79-100% (BM) and 50-100% (BMAC); 18/24 report union over 80%; Level III; needs Level I data.

evidence.title: BMP, PRP and BMAC in delayed union or nonunion: systematic review and network meta-analysis of RCTs
evidence.finding: 15 RCTs; PRP and BMP shortened healing time and raised healing rate vs standard care; PRP+autograft and PRP+BMAC ranked highest by SUCRA.

evidence.title: Surgical management of Jones fractures in athletes: orthobiologic augmentation, a systematic review and meta-analysis of 718 fractures
evidence.finding: Union 98.5% augmented vs 93.8% fixation alone; no difference in return to play.

evidence.title: Percutaneous internal fixation of proximal fifth metatarsal Jones fractures with Charlotte Carolina screw and bone marrow aspirate concentrate
evidence.finding: Mean healing 5 weeks; one delayed union, one refracture.

evidence.title: Use of platelet-rich concentrate and bone marrow aspirate in high-risk patients with Charcot arthropathy of the foot
evidence.finding: 42 of 46 feet united at mean 26 months.

evidence.title: Clinical assessment of 115 cases of hindfoot fusion with two different types of graft: allograft+DBM+bone marrow aspirate versus autograft+DBM
evidence.finding: Nonunion 13% vs 18%, not significant; allograft group had fewer infections.

evidence.title: Concentrated bone marrow aspirate applications in bony fusion for foot and ankle orthopaedic surgery: a review
evidence.finding: Narrative review: supportive for percutaneous nonunion treatment, uncertain for arthrodesis; RCTs needed to justify cost.

evidence.title: Effect of osteogenic progenitor cell concentration on the incidence of foot and ankle fusion
evidence.finding: 97% fusion; no association between colony-forming-unit count and fusion, suggesting a threshold effect.

evidence.title: Arthroscopic osteosynthesis with DBM and BMAC for nonunion of scaphoid in athletes
evidence.finding: 88% union at a mean 15.4 weeks.

evidence.title: ORTHO-1: expanded bone marrow MSCs with biphasic calcium phosphate in tibia, femur and humerus nonunions
evidence.finding: EU multicenter first-in-human feasibility; safe, with healing in most patients; not a marketed product.

evidence.title: Percutaneous autologous bone-marrow grafting for nonunions. Surgical technique (J Bone Joint Surg Am 2006; DOI 10.2106/JBJS.F.00203)
evidence.finding: Technique paper companion to the 2005 series.

evidence.title: Mesenchymal stem cells therapy for the treatment of non-union fractures: a systematic review and meta-analysis (2025; PMC11900535)
evidence.finding: 21 studies; pooled healing 44%/73%/90%/86% at 3/6/9/12 months; authors note lack of high-quality evidence.

evidence.title: Orthobiologic injections for discogenic chronic low back pain: crossover RCT (Pain Physician 2024)
evidence.finding: Intradiscal BMC improved pain and function vs saline trigger-point control; open-label crossover.

bd.reimbursement: Harvest/concentration is bundled into the surgical procedure; CPT 38220/38222 marrow aspiration may be reported by some surgeons; CPT 0232T (PRP injection) is Category III and widely non-covered; no separate payment for BMAC in the facility.
bd.notes: Capital-plus-disposable model (centrifuge placement, per-case kit); device makers cannot make osteogenic claims so the sell is 'autologous, point-of-care, no tissue bank'.

pipeline.expected_milestone: No sponsor seeking a biologic claim; an EU Phase 3 of allogeneic BM-MSCs plus biomaterial in nonunion (OrthoAlloUnion, EUCT 2025-520841-60-00) is the nearest licensed-product attempt and is not US.

name: Harvest SmartPReP 2 BMAC System
company: Terumo BCT (Terumo Blood and Cell Technologies), via Harvest Technologies Corp.
ownership_history: Harvest Technologies (Plymouth, MA) was acquired by Terumo Americas Holding (agreement announced 2011-05-11, $70 million plus milestones). Terumo Blood and Cell Technologies' 2021 release still lists the 'Harvest BMAC Procedure Pack' among its products; no 2025-2026 Terumo product page for the SmartPReP/BMAC system was found, so current catalog status is unconfirmed.
composition: Point-of-care dual-chamber centrifuge and disposable that concentrates nucleated cells and platelets from 60-120 mL of autologous bone marrow aspirate in about 15 minutes.

regulatory.reference: K991430 (SmartPReP Centrifuge System, 1999-05-28); K052925 (SmartPReP2 Centrifuge System, 2006-01-04); K103340 (SmartPReP2 BMAC System and SmartPReP Platelet Concentration System, Special 510(k), decision 2010-12-06); product code JQC (blood-cell centrifuge), applicant Harvest Technologies Corp.
on_label_indications: Clinical laboratory or intraoperative point-of-care preparation of platelet poor plasma and platelet concentrate from a small sample of blood and of a cell concentrate from bone marrow

challenge: The 510(k) clears the centrifuge for making a concentrate, not any clinical claim; any 'stem cell' or healing claim for BMAC is off-label. Hernigou's manually processed marrow evidence does not transfer to this specific device. 2026 catalog status of the Harvest line under Terumo was not confirmed.

applications.evidence_summary: Class evidence: Hernigou's bilateral-hip RCT (125 patients, 25-year follow-up) and Papakostidis 2015 meta-analysis (7 studies, OR 0.2 for collapse) favor BMAC-augmented decompression in pre-collapse disease; post-collapse RCT negative (Hauzeur 2018). None used this device. A 192-patient US RCT (Johns Hopkins, NCT06123481) is recruiting.
applications.caveats: Single-center dominance (Hernigou); device-agnostic evidence; cell dose is rarely measured in practice.

applications.evidence_summary: Hernigou 2005: percutaneous injection of concentrated marrow united 53 of 60 atrophic tibial nonunions, with union correlating with progenitor concentration above ~1,500 CFU-F/mL.
applications.caveats: Tibial data; uncontrolled; concentration achieved by a lab cell separator, not a point-of-care device.

evidence.title: Cell therapy versus simultaneous contralateral decompression in symptomatic corticosteroid osteonecrosis: a thirty year follow-up prospective randomized study of 125 adult patients.
evidence.finding: THA in 24% of marrow-grafted hips versus 76% of decompression-only hips; collapse 28% versus 72%.

evidence.title: The role of cell therapy in osteonecrosis of the femoral head. A systematic review and meta-analysis of 7 studies.
evidence.finding: Odds of collapse reduced (OR 0.2, 95% CI 0.08-0.6) and THA conversion halved (OR 0.6, p=0.06) with marrow cell implantation versus core decompression alone.

evidence.title: Percutaneous autologous bone-marrow grafting for nonunions. Influence of the number and concentration of progenitor cells.
evidence.finding: Union in 53 of 60 atrophic tibial nonunions; non-union cases received significantly fewer progenitors.

evidence.title: Inefficacy of autologous bone marrow concentrate in stage three osteonecrosis: a randomized controlled double-blind trial.
evidence.finding: No difference in THA requirement (15 of 23 hips in each arm) or clinical/radiographic outcomes in post-collapse ARCO III.

bd.reimbursement: No separate payment for BMAC preparation in the inpatient setting; in the office/ASC setting CPT 38232 (bone marrow harvest) or 20939 (bone marrow aspiration for grafting, add-on) may be billed but many payers deny BMAC as investigational; disposable cost is borne by the facility.
bd.notes: Capital-plus-disposable model; Terumo BCT distributes directly and through orthopedic distributors. The orthobiologics BMAC market has shifted toward Arthrex (Angel) and smaller players as Terumo's focus is apheresis.

name: Magellan Autologous Platelet Separator / MAR0Max (BMAC)
company: Isto Biologics (Hopkinton, MA; legal name Arteriocyte Medical Systems, Inc. DBA Isto Biologics; Keensight Capital majority investor since September 2025 per Isto/Levin releases)
ownership_history: Medtronic Vascular cleared the Magellan platelet separator in 2002 (K021902); Arteriocyte Medical Systems (Hopkinton, MA) acquired the Magellan line from Medtronic (circa 2008); ISTO Holdings (Thompson Street Capital Partners) acquired Arteriocyte in October 2016 and formed Isto Biologics, which also sells the CellPoint BMAC kit and InQu/Influx graft materials.
composition: Automated dual-syringe centrifuge system producing PRP or concentrated bone marrow (MAR0Max protocol) at the point of care.

regulatory.reference: K021902 (Magellan Autologous Platelet Separator, Medtronic Vascular, CDRH, decision 2002-08-12); BK030040 (Magellan Autologous Platelet Separation System, Medtronic Sofamor Danek, CBER, decision 2003-09-03, listed as 'syringe, piston'). Current Isto/Arteriocyte clearances: Precise Cell Concentration System BK200540 (2022-03-17, ORG) and a further 510(k) summary dated 2026-01-30 (PRP from blood plus bone marrow aspirate). A clearance specific to the Magellan concentrated-bone-marrow ('MAR0') kits was not located.
on_label_indications: Point-of-care preparation of platelet concentrate (and, per manufacturer, bone marrow concentrate) from autologous blood/marrow

applications.evidence_summary: Class evidence only; no Magellan-specific hip trial found.
applications.caveats: Device-agnostic evidence.

applications.evidence_summary: Class evidence only.
applications.caveats: Off-label clinical claims.

bd.reimbursement: No separate inpatient payment; office/ASC coding as for other BMAC systems.
bd.notes: Private-equity-owned roll-up (Arteriocyte, Progenicare) that pairs a BMAC device with its own graft carriers (InQu); sells mainly through independent orthopedic distributors.

challenge: Ownership and the CBER 510(k) lineage are now sourced, but the clearance covering Magellan's concentrated bone marrow aspirate (MAR0) kits could not be located; Isto's site markets cBMA output while the FDA records found cover PRP and the Precise system.

name: ALLOMATRIX (Injectable Putty, C, DR, Custom)
ownership_history: Wright Medical Technology product (DBM sourced via AlloSource per Osteotech-era filings); Stryker since November 2020; K252085 (September 30, 2025) lists 'Wright Medical Technology, Inc. (Stryker Corporation)' as applicant.
composition: Human demineralized bone matrix in a calcium sulfate (and, in some SKUs, cancellous chip or beta-TCP) carrier; mixed at point of care to a putty.

regulatory.reference: K020895 (2004); K040980, K041168 (2004-08-02), K041663 (2004-09-16); K053319 (2006-03-06); K061939 (2006-07-18); K252085 (Allomatrix Injectable Putty, Allomatrix C and other forms; Wright Medical Technology, Inc.; 2025-09-30)
on_label_indications: Bone void filler for bony voids or gaps that are not intrinsic to the stability of the bony structure, in the extremities, pelvis and spine; as an autograft extender

applications.evidence_summary: Stryker's trauma-tray DBM; class-level evidence only.
applications.caveats: Calcium sulfate carrier resorbs quickly.

applications.evidence_summary: Extender in Masquelet reconstructions.
applications.caveats: Extender only.

applications.evidence_summary: Marketed for nonunion as an injectable DBM with the option of mixing BMAC (IGNITE); series-level evidence only.
applications.caveats: No comparative data located.

applications.evidence_summary: Class-level DBM evidence; Stryker's own efficacy claims rest on a canine proximal-humerus defect model with relevance to humans stated as unknown.
applications.caveats: No AlloMatrix-specific foot/ankle outcome study found.

applications.evidence_summary: The only upper-extremity DBM RCT found: 50 unstable distal radius fractures treated with K-wires, randomized to AlloMatrix or no graft; no difference in function, speed of recovery, union, complications or BMD, longer operating time with graft, and transient extraosseous leakage (D'Agostino 2013, PMID:24151272; NCT00274378).
applications.caveats: Negative trial; investigator-initiated (Louvain).

applications.evidence_summary: Used as an extender in Stryker trauma accounts; no humeral data.
applications.caveats: No evidence.

evidence.title: Demineralized bone matrix in foot and ankle surgery: products, mechanisms, and clinical outcomes
evidence.finding: Lists AlloMatrix among carrier-based DBMs; evidence is level III-IV with no superiority over autograft.

evidence.title: An investigation of the effect of AlloMatrix bone graft in distal radial fracture: a prospective randomised controlled clinical trial
evidence.finding: No beneficial effect of AlloMatrix DBM in K-wire-fixed unstable distal radius fractures; operating time longer with graft.

bd.reimbursement: Bundled in inpatient MS-DRG.
bd.notes: The 2025 510(k) refresh shows Stryker is maintaining the line post-acquisition rather than retiring it.

catalog_status_2026: Stryker's US trauma-and-extremities bone grafting catalog page (read 2026-10-22) lists AlloFiber, AlloMatrix, Augment, BIO4, DBM, FusionFlex, HydroSet XT, Ignite, OsteoSet, Pro-Dense, Pro-Dense LoVisc, Pro-Stim, Tensix, Vitoss, Vitoss BA, Vitoss BA2X and Vitoss BBTrauma as current products.

name: Accell Evo3 / Evo3c DBM (Accell Bone Matrix)
ownership_history: IsoTis OrthoBiologics (Irvine, CA) developed the Accell reverse-phase carrier; Integra LifeSciences acquired IsoTis in 2007 and sold it as Integra Orthobiologics; Integra spun its spine/orthobiologics business out as SeaSpine in 2015; SeaSpine merged into Orthofix (completed 2023-01-05, all-stock, 0.4163 Orthofix shares per SeaSpine share). Orthofix's FY2025 Form 10-K (filed 2026) says Strand Plus, Strand, Evo3, Evo3c, Ballast, Cove and Mozaik 'are all processed internally through IsoTis Orthobiologics, Inc.' and names Accell Bone Matrix as proprietary technology. IsoTis is not Isto Biologics. The FY2025 10-K does not mention 'Progenix'.
composition: Demineralized bone matrix including a dispersed, open-structured 'Accell Bone Matrix' fraction in a reverse-phase medium; Evo3c adds cortical chips

regulatory.reference: K103742 (Accell Evo3, formerly Accell A2i; Integra LifeSciences; decision 2011-03-17, product code MBP); K091193 (Accell Evo3c, IsoTis Orthobiologics, 2009-08-10); K081817 (Accell TBM-R, 2008-09-24); K060306 (Accell Connexus, IsoTis NV, 2006-03-27)
on_label_indications: Bone void filler for voids or gaps not intrinsic to the stability of the bony structure, extremities, spine and pelvis (typical MQV wording; verify)

applications.evidence_summary: Only preclinical comparative data located: athymic rat PLF (Brecevich 2017, n=48) with Accell Evo3 66% and Grafton 100% fusion by palpation at 9 weeks vs 33% for autograft.
applications.caveats: Integra-affiliated author; no human comparative study retrieved.

evidence.title: Efficacy comparison of Accell Evo3 and Grafton DBM putties against autologous bone in a rat posterolateral spine fusion model
evidence.finding: 9-week palpation fusion 66% (Evo3) vs 100% (Grafton) vs 33% (ICBG).

bd.reimbursement: Bundled in fusion MS-DRGs.
bd.notes: Orthofix sells biologics through distributors and sales representatives (10-K); Accell products are Orthofix-owned, unlike the MTF-supplied Trinity line.

challenge: Accell ownership confirmed (Orthofix via IsoTis Orthobiologics, FY2025 10-K). Progenix is not named in the FY2025 10-K, so its current brand status/ownership remains unconfirmed.

name: AlloFuse DBM (Putty, Gel, Plus)
ownership_history: AlloSource (Centennial, CO), non-profit tissue bank; AlloFuse has been marketed since the early 2000s.
composition: Human demineralized bone matrix in a reverse-phase (thermoresponsive) carrier; AlloFuse Plus adds cancellous chips

regulatory.reference: By form: AlloFuse Gel and Putty = 510(k) K071849 (decision 2008-12-04; AlloSource; predicates DynaGraft II, AlloMatrix Putty); AlloFuse Plus Paste/Putty = 510(k) K103036 (decision 2011-01-10; predicates OrthoBlast II, AlloFuse Gel/Putty). AlloFuse Select cellular bone matrix, AlloFuse Fibers/Fiber Boats and AlloFuse Cervical Spacers have no 510(k) in openFDA and are presumed 361 HCT/Ps (AlloSource's Select brochure cites only FDA tissue-testing regulations and AATB standards). GUDID lists AlloFuse gel as an HCT/P.; openFDA: K071849 (AlloFuse Gel and Putty, AlloSource, 2008-12-04); K103036 (AlloFuse Plus, 2011-01-10)
on_label_indications: Bone void filler for voids or gaps not intrinsic to the stability of the bony structure (assumed MQV wording; verify)

applications.evidence_summary: No peer-reviewed spine fusion clinical study retrieved; sold as an extender under the general DBM class.
applications.caveats: Evidence gap.

bd.reimbursement: Bundled in fusion MS-DRGs.
bd.notes: AlloSource sells directly to hospitals and supplies private-label tissue to device companies; specific spine OEM partners not verified.

challenge: Regulatory path depends on the form: DBM paste/putty/gel are 510(k) devices; Select, Fibers and Spacers are presumed 361 (no 510(k) found; AlloSource does not state it on the brochures read).

name: DBX Demineralized Bone Matrix (Putty, Paste, Mix, Strip)
ownership_history: Processed by the Musculoskeletal Transplant Foundation (MTF Biologics, Edison NJ). Marketed by Synthes and, since 2012, DePuy Synthes (J&J MedTech lists DBX Trauma and DBX CMF/Inject as DePuy Synthes products; a DePuy Synthes Spine brochure describes an exclusive MTF partnership of more than 10 years). On 2025-03-13 MTF expanded its agreement with Kolosis BIO, which now also represents and distributes DBX Mix and DBX Putty alongside Kore Fiber and Prime HD, so DBX is no longer sold only through DePuy Synthes; the contract terms and whether DePuy's rights are still exclusive are not public.
composition: Human demineralized bone matrix in a sodium hyaluronate carrier (putty, paste, mix with cancellous chips, and strip forms)

regulatory.reference: MTF 510(k)s verified in openFDA: K040262 (2005-03-17), K040501 (2005-04-29), K042829 (DBX Strip, 2006-01-13), K053218 (2006-12-28), K062205 (DBX Strip, 2007-02-05), K063676 (DBX Mix, 2007-03-05), K080399 (2008-10-10), K091218 (2009-09-28), K091217 (2009-10-02), K103784 and K103795 (2011-04-13); applicant Musculoskeletal Transplant Foundation (product codes MQV/MBP/NUN); openFDA: K063676 (DBX Mix, MTF, 2007-03-05); K080399 (DBX Putty and Paste, 2008-10-10); K091217/K091218 (2009); K103784/K103795 (2011-04-13). Applicant is Musculoskeletal Transplant Foundation, not DePuy Synthes.
on_label_indications: Bone void filler for voids or gaps that are not intrinsic to the stability of the bony structure, in the extremities, spine and pelvis (typical MQV labeling; verify exact DBX wording)

applications.evidence_summary: Intra-patient comparison vs Grafton (Chang 2021, n=19): DBX side fusion 51.9% at 12 months and 66.7% at 24 months, not different from Grafton; DBX Putty is the DBM control in the DePuy Synthes FIBERGRAFT Aeridyan PLF trial (NCT07059065, n=316) and in Kuros's MagnetOs Easypack trial (NCT04679844).
applications.caveats: No sponsor-funded RCT of DBX itself; rat model (Russell 2020) ranked DBX Putty among the lowest fusion performers, which competitors cite.

applications.evidence_summary: Served as the noncellular allograft comparator in a matched ACDF cohort (Zakko 2023, n=68): fusion and PROMs no different from ViviGen.
applications.caveats: Retrospective single-surgeon series.

applications.evidence_summary: The DBM most likely to be in a DePuy Synthes trauma tray; evidence is class-level (DBM as extender), no femoral RCT.
applications.caveats: No product-specific trauma trial.

applications.evidence_summary: Used for metaphyseal void fill mixed with allograft chips; no comparative data.
applications.caveats: Provides no structural support; not suited to load-bearing voids alone.

applications.evidence_summary: Same evidence position as Grafton: extender use in nonunion with no comparative long-bone trials located; one retrospective alveolar-cleft revision series (n=17) found DBX equal to ICBG, which is not transferable.
applications.caveats: No trauma-specific evidence.

applications.evidence_summary: Class-level DBM evidence as for Grafton (PMID 39850040, PMID 35807177); no DBX-specific foot/ankle trial found.
applications.caveats: Brand-agnostic evidence.

applications.evidence_summary: Commonly packed into primary tarsometatarsal arthrodesis; no outcome study isolates it.
applications.caveats: Expert practice only.

applications.evidence_summary: Used as an extender at nonunion revision through the DePuy Synthes trauma channel; no product-specific upper-extremity evidence found.
applications.caveats: Expert-opinion tier.

applications.evidence_summary: Same as above; forearm nonunion series do not separate DBM brands.
applications.caveats: No evidence.

applications.evidence_summary: DBM with resorbable mesh bilaminate for large pediatric calvarial defects: 11 patients, 13 reconstructions in primary cranioplasty (Rogers 2009); the same technique failed in all 7 children used for secondary reconstruction over scarred dura (major revision at mean 2.5 years, Rogers group 2020).
applications.caveats: Brand of DBM not always stated; effective only with intact dural osteogenic potential.

applications.evidence_summary: rhBMP-2 plus DBM in 63 of 93 alveolar grafts at Children's Hospital Los Angeles: failure 14 percent below and 65 percent above a critical cleft volume of 885 mm3 (ICBG: 0 and 71 percent around 810 mm3); a 2023 series used DBX for cleft revision after prior BMP-2 grafting.
applications.caveats: DBM is the carrier, rhBMP-2 the active; off-label in children.

applications.evidence_summary: Six pediatric benign-tumor mandibular defects grafted with DBX, rhBMP-2 and freeze-dried bone chips: no graft failures, 100 percent take in four and about 80 percent in two at six months (2025).
applications.caveats: Case series; non-load-bearing defects with periosteum preserved.

evidence.title: Surgical outcomes of two kinds of DBM putties/local autograft composites in instrumented posterolateral lumbar fusion
evidence.finding: DBX 66.7% vs Grafton 70.4% side fusion at 24 months.

evidence.title: ACDFs supplemented with cellular or noncellular allografts have similar radiographic fusion and clinical outcomes
evidence.finding: No difference in fusion at 3, 6, 12 months between DBM and ViviGen groups.

evidence.title: Efficacy of demineralized bone matrix (DBX) for revision alveolar bone grafting after BMP-2
evidence.finding: DBX and ICBG achieved similar union in a small craniofacial series; cited only to show the evidence base is outside trauma.

evidence.title: Limited evidence to support demineralized bone matrix in foot and ankle surgical procedures: a systematic review
evidence.finding: Class-level DBM union 85.6% in ankle/hindfoot arthrodesis.

evidence.title: Demineralized bone matrix and resorbable mesh bilaminate cranioplasty for large-scale pediatric calvarial defects
evidence.finding: 13 reconstructions in 11 children with large defects reossified using DBM between resorbable mesh layers in primary cranioplasty.

evidence.title: Demineralized bone matrix and resorbable mesh bilaminate cranioplasty is ineffective for secondary reconstruction of large pediatric cranial defects
evidence.finding: All seven children (mean age 4.2) treated for post-craniectomy defects over scarred dura had poor ossification and needed major revision at mean 2.5 years.

evidence.title: Failure rates based on alveolar cleft volume: analysis of the critical-size defect for alveolar bone grafting
evidence.finding: Critical-size cleft volume 810 mm3 for ICBG (failure 0 vs 71 percent) and 885 mm3 for rhBMP-2 plus DBM (14 vs 65 percent).

evidence.title: Successful grafting with allogenic bone following benign pediatric mandibular tumor removal
evidence.finding: DBX plus rhBMP-2 plus freeze-dried bone chips achieved 100 percent take in 4 and about 80 percent in 2 of 6 pediatric mandibular defects at six months.

bd.reimbursement: Bundled in fusion MS-DRGs; no separate payment.
bd.notes: MTF is the processor and OEM supplier; DePuy Synthes sells through its direct spine force. MTF's OEM/private-label model also supplies Orthofix (Trinity, FiberFuse) and others, so the same tissue bank sits behind several competing brands. MTF-Kolosis BIO agreement (2025-03-13) means DBX Mix and Putty also reach surgeons through an independent distributor, so DePuy Synthes exclusivity should not be assumed.

challenge: DePuy Synthes distribution of DBX confirmed from J&J MedTech product pages; MTF added Kolosis BIO as a second distributor (Mix and Putty) in March 2025; indications wording is class-typical (the 510(k) PDFs are scanned images).

name: Grafton DBM / Grafton Plus DBM Paste / Grafton DBF fibers
ownership_history: Developed by Osteotech (Eatontown, NJ); Medtronic completed its acquisition of Osteotech on 2010-11-16 ($6.50 per share, about $123 million). Older 510(k)s (K042707, K043048, K051188, K051195) list Osteotech as sponsor.
composition: Human demineralized bone matrix (particles or fibers) in a glycerol carrier (gel, putty, flex, matrix, paste forms); each lot sourced from a single donor

regulatory.reference: K251193 (Grafton DBM, Grafton Plus DBM Paste, Magnifuse; cleared 2025-06-12; 21 CFR 888.3045, product codes MQV/MBP); earlier Osteotech clearances K042707, K043048, K051188, K051195
on_label_indications: Bone graft extender, bone graft substitute and bone void filler for voids or gaps in the spine, pelvis and extremities that are not intrinsic to the stability of the bony structure (per K251193 summary as described in the FDA listing)

applications.evidence_summary: Prospective intra-patient trial (Cammisa 2004, n=120): Grafton gel/autograft composite fused 52% of sides vs 54% for ICBG at 24 months by blinded plain radiograph (kappa 0.51); Korean intra-patient comparison (Chang 2021, n=19): Grafton 70.4% vs DBX 66.7% side fusion at 24 months.
applications.caveats: Sponsor-funded 2004 study with 30% loss to follow-up; DBM osteoinductivity varies by donor and lot, and a 2020 rat study (SeaSpine-funded) found large between-brand differences.

applications.evidence_summary: Widely used as a local-bone extender in posterior cervical fusion under the general spine void-filler label; no posterior-cervical-specific study retrieved.
applications.caveats: Extrapolated from lumbar data.

applications.evidence_summary: Commonly used as the extender alongside rhBMP-2 in long constructs; no deformity-specific comparative study retrieved.
applications.caveats: Usage inferred from practice patterns, not trial data.

applications.evidence_summary: DBMs are the default autograft extender in nonunion revision; no RCT isolates Grafton's effect in femoral nonunion. Osteoinductivity varies lot to lot and by carrier.
applications.caveats: Donor and processing variability; glycerol carrier historically raised nephrotoxicity questions at high volumes (animal data).

applications.evidence_summary: Used as an extender in Masquelet stage two.
applications.caveats: Extender only; not a stand-alone substitute for critical defects.

applications.evidence_summary: DBM is the default autograft extender in nonunion and Masquelet second stage, but PubMed search found no RCT of any DBM in long-bone nonunion; evidence is case series and lot-to-lot osteoinductivity variability is documented. A 2025 foot-and-ankle systematic review (363 patients) found 'limited evidence'.
applications.caveats: Osteoinductive potency varies by donor and processing; no tibial nonunion comparative data; claims of osteoinduction are product-marketing, not label.
applications.challenge: If asked for the best DBM nonunion study, the honest answer is that there is none at Level I-II.

applications.evidence_summary: Used as a volume extender with RIA/ICBG in the Masquelet second stage in many series; no isolated effect estimate.
applications.caveats: Confounded by autograft.

applications.evidence_summary: Class-level evidence: Hartman 2025 systematic review (PMID 39850040) of 13 DBM foot/ankle studies, 363 patients; union 85.6% for ankle/hindfoot arthrodesis, 100% for fifth-metatarsal and calcaneal fracture cohorts, nonunion 8.8% overall. Schlickewei 2022 (PMID 35807177) found no difference in arthroscopic ankle fusion nonunion with DBM (12.9%) vs without (14.8%).
applications.caveats: Low-level, heterogeneous evidence; no study shows superiority over autograft or over no graft; brand not always specified.

applications.evidence_summary: DBM combined with bone marrow aspirate is the common adjunct in NFL Jones-fracture series (Lareau 2015, PMID 26353796; Hunt and Anderson 2011 revision series, PMID 21632977).
applications.caveats: Case series; DBM never isolated from BMA or fixation.

applications.evidence_summary: Used routinely as a graft extender in Charcot and TTC bone-block series (e.g., PMID 34677103 combined femoral-head allograft, BMAC and DBM fibers in 14 TTC fusions).
applications.caveats: Never studied alone in Charcot.

applications.evidence_summary: DBM is the most common off-the-shelf extender mixed with autograft or cellular allograft at upper-extremity nonunion revision, but no DBM-specific comparative humeral nonunion study was found; the practice rests on surgeon habit and lower-limb/spine data.
applications.caveats: Osteoinductivity varies by donor and lot; DBM products are tested by the manufacturer in athymic rodent assays, not in humans.

applications.evidence_summary: Arthroscopic fixation with DBM plus BMAC injection united 15 of 17 early scaphoid nonunions in athletes at a mean 15.4 weeks (Lee 2026, PMID:42098735).
applications.caveats: Case series; DBM brand not specified; selected mildly sclerotic nonunions.

applications.evidence_summary: Pooled clavicle nonunion series show graft use lowers delayed union but raises complication and reoperation rates; graft type (autograft vs DBM vs allograft) is not separable (Yetter 2023, PMID:36722838).
applications.caveats: Class-level inference only.

applications.evidence_summary: Labeled for sinus lift, socket and ridge augmentation; Medtronic sells Grafton alongside Infuse and Mastergraft into oral surgery; no Grafton-named dental RCT located.
applications.caveats: Osteoinductivity varies by lot and carrier; DBM is rarely used alone in sinus lifts.

applications.evidence_summary: Craniofacial augmentation is on the label; the 2000 rabbit study of Grafton Flex and putty in 15 mm cranial defects showed healing, but pediatric clinical cranial data are DBM-generic.
applications.caveats: Animal and generic data.

evidence.title: Two-year fusion rate equivalency between Grafton DBM gel and autograft in posterolateral spine fusion: side-by-side comparison in the same patient
evidence.finding: Fusion 52% (Grafton/autograft side) vs 54% (autograft side) at 24 months in 81 patients with complete radiographs.

evidence.title: Surgical outcomes of two kinds of DBM putties/local autograft composites in instrumented posterolateral lumbar fusion
evidence.finding: Grafton 70.4% vs DBX 66.7% side fusion at 24 months (ns); no revisions for nonunion.

evidence.title: Performance of seven commercially available DBM fiber and putty products in a rat posterolateral fusion model
evidence.finding: Grafton DBF and Grafton Flex fused at rates not statistically lower than the SeaSpine Strand family; DBX Putty and Optium Putty were significantly lower, suggesting carriers hurt performance.

evidence.title: Limited evidence to support demineralized bone matrix in foot and ankle surgical procedures: a systematic review
evidence.finding: 13 studies; union 85.6% in ankle/hindfoot fusion, 100% in small fracture cohorts; nonunion 8.8% overall; low level and quality of evidence.

evidence.title: Does demineralized bone matrix affect the nonunion rate in arthroscopic ankle arthrodesis?
evidence.finding: Nonunion 12.9% with DBM vs 14.8% without (p=0.83).

evidence.title: Demineralized bone matrix in foot and ankle surgery: products, mechanisms, and clinical outcomes
evidence.finding: Review naming DBX, AlloSync, AlloMatrix, OrthoBlast II and Grafton; strongest DBM evidence is in fracture fixation, with arthrodesis union comparable to but not better than autograft.

evidence.title: Arthroscopic osteosynthesis with DBM and BMAC for nonunion of scaphoid in athletes
evidence.finding: 88% union, 88% return to pre-injury sport or work at 2 years.

evidence.title: Complications and outcomes after surgical intervention in clavicular nonunion: a systematic review
evidence.finding: Bone graft use: delayed union 0.6% vs 3.6% but complications 15% vs 8% and reoperation 29% vs 14%.

bd.reimbursement: Bundled in fusion MS-DRGs; +20930 bundled for Medicare physician payment; no separate HCPCS.
bd.notes: Sold by Medtronic Spine direct reps alongside Infuse and Mastergraft; Grafton is also distributed in Japan. Tissue sourced from US tissue banks (Medtronic processes DBM in its own facilities).

challenge: Grafton launched under 361 tissue rules in 1991; it has carried 510(k)s since the mid-2000s because the glycerol carrier makes it a device. K251193 indications (FDA decision record): bone graft extender, bone graft substitute and bone void filler in the posterolateral spine, intervertebral disc space (excluding Flex or Crunch), pelvis and extremities.

name: Magnifuse Bone Graft (DBM in resorbable mesh)
ownership_history: Medtronic (Osteotech lineage); Magnifuse II is the current generation.
composition: Demineralized cortical bone fibers and chips contained in a resorbable polyglycolic acid mesh bag that holds the graft in the fusion bed and can be hydrated with marrow aspirate

regulatory.reference: K251193 (with Grafton; decision 2025-06-12); K123691 (Magnifuse Bone Graft, cleared under Grafton II eDBM, 2013-01-31); K131673 (Magnifuse / Magnifuse II, 2013-10-03); applicant Medtronic Sofamor Danek
on_label_indications: Bone graft substitute for voids or gaps in the spine, pelvis and extremities not intrinsic to the stability of the bony structure; for interbody use must be combined with an FDA-cleared intervertebral body fusion device labeled for use with a bone void filler

applications.evidence_summary: Marketed for posterolateral gutters and lateral cages; no peer-reviewed comparative clinical study retrieved in this sweep.
applications.caveats: Evidence gap; rests on DBM class data.

applications.evidence_summary: The mesh format is positioned for lateral and OLIF cages; the 2025 clearance explicitly ties interbody use to cages cleared for bone void fillers.
applications.caveats: No clinical data retrieved.

bd.reimbursement: Bundled in fusion MS-DRGs; no separate payment.
bd.notes: Medtronic direct reps; packaged with Medtronic interbody systems.

name: Optium DBM
ownership_history: LifeNet Health (Virginia Beach, VA) product: 510(k) K053098 'Optium DBM Gel and Putty' (human demineralized cortical bone in USP glycerol; applicant 'Lifenet', decision 2005-11-28, no human clinical data in the clearance). LifeNet lists Optium DBM Gel and Putty on its own site (general orthopedics and spine). No DePuy Synthes listing or distribution agreement for Optium was found; DePuy Synthes's DBM is DBX (MTF) and its LifeNet product is ViviGen.
composition: Human DBM in a glycerol-based carrier

regulatory.reference: K053098 (2005-11-28; applicant Lifenet; product code MBP; glycerol carrier); openFDA: K053098 (Optium DBM Gel and Putty, LifeNet, 2005-11-28)
on_label_indications: Bone void filler for bony voids or gaps in the extremities, spine and pelvis that are not intrinsic to the stability of the bony structure (FDA 510(k) summary K053098); remodeled into the patient's skeleton

applications.evidence_summary: No product-specific clinical evidence located.
applications.caveats: Placeholder record pending verification.

applications.evidence_summary: No upper-extremity evidence found.
applications.caveats: Expert-opinion tier.

bd.reimbursement: Bundled inpatient MS-DRG.
bd.notes: LifeNet sells Optium itself (hospital tissue-services contracts); not carried by DePuy Synthes reps. Compare DBX (MTF via DePuy Synthes and Kolosis BIO).

name: Platelet-rich plasma (autologous, point-of-care systems) in fracture and nonunion
company: Multiple (Arthrex ACP/Angel, Zimmer Biomet GPS III, Harvest SmartPReP APC, Stryker/Emcyte, DePuy Synthes Peak PlasmaBlade heritage, others)
composition: Autologous platelet concentrate (2-8x baseline) with or without leukocytes, prepared by centrifugation of 15-60 mL of whole blood; applied as liquid or activated gel at the fracture or nonunion site.

regulatory.reference: Preparation devices cleared under product code JQC (blood separation for PRP); no PRP product has an FDA-cleared indication for fracture healing; Cleared by CBER under product code ORG 'platelet and plasma separator for bone graft handling' (21 CFR 864.9245), e.g., Arthrex ACP Max BK210655 (2022-09-22), Arthrex Angel BK180180 (2018-07-05), Isto Precise BK200540 (2022-03-17), RegenLab RegenKit-THT BK090048 (2010-05-18, product code FMF), and older CDRH centrifuges (JQC); labeling is PRP for mixing with bone graft to improve handling, no fracture-healing indication
on_label_indications: Devices: preparation of platelet-rich plasma from autologous blood at the point of care. No clinical fracture-healing indication is labeled.

challenge: Evidence is weak and the signal is inconsistent: the Cochrane review found a single eligible trial (n=21), and the 2024 umbrella meta-analysis of nonunion/delayed union found a healing-rate benefit only when meta-analyses were pooled, not when individual studies were pooled. A hiring manager will expect the candidate to say PRP in long-bone fracture is not supported, and that its use in hip and femur trauma is negligible.

applications.evidence_summary: Umbrella meta-analysis (Zhu 2024; 5 meta-analyses, 13 studies, 1,362 patients) found PRP shortened healing time by about 1-2 months but did not improve union rate when individual studies were pooled; Cochrane 2012 found insufficient evidence.
applications.caveats: Low-quality, heterogeneous trials, mostly tibia and mixed sites; PRP preparation varies widely.

applications.evidence_summary: A hip-fracture PRP trial was noted as 'underway' in the 2012 Cochrane review; no positive femoral neck RCT located.
applications.caveats: No evidence of benefit.

applications.evidence_summary: Evidence is weak and inconsistent: a 2024 umbrella meta-analysis (5 meta-analyses, 13 studies, 1,362 patients) found PRP improved healing rate only when meta-analyses were pooled, not when individual studies were pooled, and shortened healing time by about 2 weeks with no effect on pain; the 2022 Front Med review (13 studies, 459 patients, 3 RCTs) reached similar tentative conclusions.
applications.caveats: Small, heterogeneous, mostly ex-US trials; PRP formulations are not standardized; Category III CPT with no payment.
applications.challenge: Do not present PRP as a nonunion treatment option; present it as unproven.

applications.evidence_summary: No acute fracture RCT supports PRP; the 2014 and later meta-analyses of acute fracture adjuncts exclude it for lack of data.
applications.caveats: No evidence.

applications.evidence_summary: Weak evidence. Bibbo 2010 (PMID 21056862) reviewed 'only a handful' of basic-science and clinical foot/ankle PRP papers; a prospective Arthrex ACP ankle-arthrodesis study (NCT01131455) was terminated after 10 patients; Bolia 2024 (PMID 38704857) rated the arthrodesis PRP evidence as low quality.
applications.caveats: No RCT shows PRP improves foot/ankle fusion; the only positive high-risk series combined PRP with marrow aspirate (Pinzur 2009).

applications.evidence_summary: Pinzur 2009 (PMID 19254506) used platelet-rich concentrate plus marrow aspirate in 46 Charcot feet with 42 unions; PRP's independent contribution is unknown.
applications.caveats: Confounded single-arm series.

applications.evidence_summary: Weak. A 30-patient trial of intra-articular PRP after pinning of intra-articular distal radius fractures reported better PRWE pain and function at 3 and 6 months (Namazi 2016, PMID:26774901), self-graded level III; a 14-patient scaphoid trial from the same group (PMID:27999456) is uninterpretable. The 2022 PRP-in-fractures meta-analysis has been retracted (PMID:35693268).
applications.caveats: Small single-center trials without blinding; no union endpoint; the only meta-analysis is retracted. The honest position is that PRP has no demonstrated role in upper-extremity fracture or nonunion healing.

applications.evidence_summary: Navani 2024 (Pain Physician) randomized 40 patients to saline trigger-point injection, intradiscal PRP or intradiscal BMC with crossover; both biologics improved pain and function vs placebo at 12 months, but the trial was open-label and all placebo patients crossed over at 3 months.
applications.caveats: Open-label, n=40, authors affiliated with regenerative clinics, crossover design precludes a 12-month placebo comparison.

evidence.title: Platelet-rich plasma in the treatment of delayed union and nonunion fractures: An umbrella meta-analysis.
evidence.finding: Pooling meta-analyses gave RR 1.30 for healing rate, but pooling individual studies showed no effect on healing rate; healing time shortened (MD about -2 months).

evidence.title: Platelet rich therapies for long bone healing in adults (Cochrane review).
evidence.finding: One eligible trial (high tibial osteotomy, n=21); evidence insufficient to support routine use.

evidence.title: Platelet-rich plasma for the treatment of bone defects: from pre-clinical rational to evidence in the clinical practice. A systematic review.
evidence.finding: 64 articles (45 preclinical, 19 clinical): preclinical signal weakens on radiographic/biomechanical endpoints; clinical benefit 'still under debate' with low-quality heterogeneous literature.

evidence.title: Clinical effectiveness of PRP for long-bone delayed union and nonunion: systematic review and meta-analysis
evidence.finding: 13 studies (3 RCTs); PRP associated with higher healing rate and shorter time but low-quality evidence.

evidence.title: Platelet-rich plasma concentrate to augment bone fusion
evidence.finding: Review: only a handful of foot/ankle PRP papers; proposes a risk classification for when to augment.

evidence.title: Autologous concentrated platelet-rich plasma (Arthrex ACP) for local application in ankle arthrodesis
evidence.finding: Terminated after 10 patients; no results posted.

evidence.title: Comparative studies of bone graft and orthobiologics for foot ankle arthrodesis: a critical review
evidence.finding: Critical review of autograft, allograft, DBM, calcium sulfate/phosphate, rhBMP-2, rhPDGF-BB, PRP and BMAC in ankle/hindfoot arthrodesis emphasizing low quality of evidence for most.

evidence.title: Investigating the effect of intra-articular PRP injection on pain and function improvement in patients with distal radius fracture
evidence.finding: Lower PRWE pain and disability scores with PRP at 3 and 6 months.

evidence.title: Efficacy of platelet-rich plasma in the treatment of fractures: a meta-analysis (RETRACTED)
evidence.finding: Retracted publication; must not be cited as support.

evidence.title: Adjunctive platelet-rich plasma in non-union lower extremity fracture management: A systematic review and meta-analysis (Chin J Traumatol 2026; DOI 10.1016/j.cjtee.2026.06.001)
evidence.finding: Pooled tibial/femoral nonunion studies (search to Oct 31, 2025) comparing PRP gel/concentrate/composite graft vs standard care; the abstract frames efficacy as 'still debated' (pooled estimate not extracted).

evidence.title: The Safety and Effectiveness of Orthobiologic Injections for Discogenic Chronic Low Back Pain: A Multicenter Prospective, Crossover, Randomized Controlled Trial with 12 Months Follow-up (Pain Physician 2024)
evidence.finding: Intradiscal PRP and BMC each improved NRS pain and function vs saline trigger-point injection; all placebo patients crossed over; no adverse events, hospitalizations or surgeries at 12 months.

evidence.title: 510(k) summary BK241083, OrthoAscent FG-001 Platelet Rich Plasma Device (prepared Sept 5, 2024)
evidence.finding: Documents the cleared intended use (mix with bone graft to improve handling) and the statement that the PRP has not been evaluated for any clinical indication.

bd.reimbursement: CPT 0232T (PRP injection, any site) is a Category III code that most payers, including Medicare, deny; inpatient use is bundled with no separate payment.
bd.notes: PRP revenue in orthopedics is a sports-medicine and office-injection story; trauma volume is marginal and shrinking as evidence accumulates.

ownership_history: Device-only market; no product owns the biologic.

pipeline.expected_milestone: No sponsor is pursuing an efficacy claim; PRP will remain a device-prepared, off-label-use autologous product.

name: Bioactive glass bone void fillers and wedges (NovaBone 45S5, Bio2 Vitrium, Treace VitaFuse, BonAlive S53P4 and others)
company: Multiple (NovaBone/Isto Biologics, Bio2 Technologies, Treace Medical, BonAlive Biomaterials, Stryker Vitoss BA)
ownership_history: Treace Medical introduced VitaFuse Bioactive Glass Graft in its 2026 AOFAS portfolio update as the newest addition to its biologics line (beside the tissue-based CortiFuse graft). BonAlive S53P4 is CE-marked for osteomyelitis in Europe; its US status for that use was not verified.
composition: Silicate (45S5, S53P4) or borate bioactive glass granules, putties, fiber scaffolds and machined wedges that form a hydroxycarbonate apatite layer and release ions; S53P4 has intrinsic antibacterial activity

regulatory.reference: Per brand: NovaBone putty K240404 (2024-03-05) and K242299 (2024-09-25); Bio2 CLM BG Bioactive Scaffold K142463 (2014-12-18) and K152589 (2016-01-12); Bonalive K231528 (2023-07-11); Vitoss BA K103173/K163621. Treace VitaFuse: no 510(k) found in openFDA under that name or under applicant Treace (searched 2026-10-22) - may be marketed under another clearance or as a different sponsor's device
on_label_indications: Bone void filler for non-structural voids of the extremities, pelvis and posterolateral spine (class-typical); machined wedges for opening-wedge osteotomies

applications.evidence_summary: Shi 2018 (PMID 30316643): 29 high-risk patients, 48 hindfoot joints fused with bioactive glass plus bone marrow aspirate; 25% nonunion overall (16.7% subtalar).
applications.caveats: Retrospective, no comparator, a nonunion rate at the high end for hindfoot fusion.

applications.evidence_summary: Borenstein 2023 republication (PMID 37669405): 17 Cotton osteotomies with bioactive-glass wedges (Bio2), all united, one delayed union; a Bio2 employee is a co-author.
applications.caveats: Industry co-authored, 17 patients, 6.5-month follow-up.

applications.evidence_summary: De Giglio 2020 (PMID 33358382): 44 diabetic foot osteomyelitis patients, 22 with S53P4 bioactive glass after debridement vs 22 debridement alone; osteomyelitis resolution 90% vs 61.9% (p=0.03).
applications.caveats: Italian single-center retrospective; S53P4's antibacterial-use labeling is European; US use for infection is off-label.

applications.evidence_summary: Ma 2021 (PMID 33781640): 31 calcaneal tumor/cyst curettages, 45S5 Bioglass (16) vs allograft (15); faster ingrowth (3.7 vs 4.5 months) and healing with similar AOFAS scores.
applications.caveats: Cysts, not fractures.

evidence.title: Outcomes of hindfoot arthrodesis supplemented with bioactive glass and bone marrow aspirate: a retrospective radiographic study
evidence.finding: 25% nonunion across 48 high-risk joints.

evidence.title: Republication of 'Preliminary experience using bioactive glass wedges for Cotton osteotomy'
evidence.finding: All 17 Cotton osteotomies united with maintained correction.

evidence.title: Efficacy and safety of bioactive glass S53P4 as a treatment for diabetic foot osteomyelitis
evidence.finding: Osteomyelitis resolution 90% with S53P4 vs 61.9% with debridement alone.

evidence.title: Open curettage with bone augmentation for symptomatic tumors and tumor-like lesions of calcaneus: a comparison of bioactive glass versus allogeneic bone
evidence.finding: Faster bone ingrowth and wound drying with 45S5 Bioglass than allograft.

bd.reimbursement: No separate payment; bundled or packaged.
bd.notes: Treace's entry (VitaFuse, 2026) matters because Treace's Lapiplasty rep force is the densest foot-specific sales organization in the US and now carries both a tissue graft and a synthetic; this is the clearest example of a hardware company adding biologics for ASC pull-through.

challenge: VitaFuse clearance number not found; other brands verified.

name: Bonalive granules (S53P4 bioactive glass)
ownership_history: Spun out of Åbo Akademi/Vivoxid; first US 510(k)s 2007-2008 (craniomaxillofacial then extremities); K191274 cleared 2019-08-07; FDA Breakthrough Device designation February 2022 for granules with a proposed claim of protecting against microbial colonization; US distributor is Bonalive Inc (La Jolla, CA), per Bonalive's US page.
composition: S53P4 bioactive glass granules (53% SiO2, 23% Na2O, 20% CaO, 4% P2O5); raises local pH and osmolarity, giving antibacterial activity without antibiotics

regulatory.reference: K071199 (2008, extremities and pelvis, not posterolateral spine, not load-bearing); K191274 (2019-08-07); Breakthrough Device designation 2022 (no new clearance found); Bonalive 510(k)s in openFDA: K070055 and K071199 (2007-2008, applicant Vivoxid), K191274 (2019-08-07), K231528 (Bonalive Orthopedics granules, 2023-07-11, adults and pediatric patients 6 years and older, extremities and pelvis), K253883 (Bonalive Maxillofacial, 2026-05-14)
on_label_indications: Bony voids or gaps not intrinsic to the stability of the bone in the extremities and pelvis; not for load-bearing applications (US labeling carries no antibacterial claim)

applications.evidence_summary: Multinational registry (Lindfors 2017, n=116, 11 centers, mostly tibia) treated chronic osteomyelitis with S53P4 mostly single-stage without local antibiotics; 2025 systematic review (99 studies) rates bone-infection evidence level 1-2 but all ex-US. The antibacterial claim is not on the US label.
applications.caveats: Off-label in the US for infection; no RCT versus antibiotic carriers; CE-marked antibacterial claim only.
applications.challenge: Breakthrough designation (2022) has not produced a cleared infection indication after four years.

applications.evidence_summary: Finnish series used S53P4 for plateau and other metaphyseal fractures; pooled in Alshahrani 2025 plateau meta-analysis as one of the substitute classes.
applications.caveats: Small series.

applications.evidence_summary: Multinational registry of 116 chronic osteomyelitis patients treated with S53P4 as a one-stage dead-space filler without local antibiotics in 85%: cure in 104 of 116 (90%) at median 31 months, sites mainly tibia, femur and calcaneus (Lindfors 2017, PMID:28050878). The antibacterial use is off-label in the US.
applications.caveats: Registry without control; upper-extremity cases rare; US label is void-fill only.

applications.evidence_summary: Bioactive glass was listed among cleared wrist void fillers in 1999 (Ladd 1999, PMID:10504355) but no clinical wrist outcome series was found.
applications.caveats: No data.

applications.evidence_summary: Peltola 2006: 42 patients with chronic frontal sinusitis obliterated with S53P4 granules, accurate obliteration in 39, uneventful outcome in 92 percent, histology at 1, 5 and 10 years showing progressive bony obliteration with no bacterial growth.
applications.caveats: Finnish investigator series, Turku group developed the glass; no randomized comparison to fat or bone.

applications.evidence_summary: Maxillofacial clearance rests on substantial equivalence to the 2007 granules; no US dental trial located.
applications.caveats: Launch of the renamed Maxillofacial product in the US had no press release as of October 2026.

applications.evidence_summary: S53P4 granules and plates have Finnish long-term series in orbital floor and cranial reconstruction (Aitasalo, Peltola group) but no US data.
applications.caveats: Granules need containment; not a load-bearing cranioplasty.

evidence.title: Antibacterial bioactive glass, S53P4, for chronic bone infections: a multinational study
evidence.finding: 11 centers in six countries; tibia most common site; 85% one-stage without local antibiotics; minimum 1-year follow-up with high eradication (abstract truncated).

evidence.title: Clinical use of S53P4 bioactive glass in bone defects and infected bone: systematic review and GRADE assessment
evidence.finding: 99 clinical studies 1990-2024; highest-level evidence in benign tumors, oral/maxillofacial, bone infection, spine and trauma.

evidence.title: Bioactive glass S53P4 as bone graft substitute in treatment of osteomyelitis
evidence.finding: 9 of 11 healed without recurrence; lower extremity and spine.

evidence.title: Bioactive glass S53P4 in frontal sinus obliteration: a long-term clinical experience
evidence.finding: Obliteration achieved in 39 of 42 patients, 92 percent uneventful recovery; biopsies at 1, 5 and 10 years showed bone replacing fibrous tissue around residual granules, with sterile cultures.

evidence.title: Long-term microscopic and tissue analytical findings for two frontal sinus obliteration materials
evidence.finding: Explant analysis after bioactive glass and autologous bone obliteration showing bone formation around glass granules over years.

bd.reimbursement: Bundled inpatient MS-DRG; no product-specific payment.
bd.notes: Positioned as the antibiotic-free alternative in antimicrobial stewardship conversations; US presence small. Prosidyan's FIBERGRAFT Aeridyan (bioactive glass fiber) is in a US open-pilon acute grafting study (NCT07227493).

name: Cortoss Bone Augmentation Material
ownership_history: Orthovita developed Cortoss (CE mark 2001; FDA 510(k) clearance June 2009 after an IDE RCT); Stryker completed its acquisition of Orthovita on 2011-06-28.
composition: Injectable bis-GMA/bis-EMA resin composite reinforced with bioactive glass-ceramic particles (about 70% by weight); self-setting, nonresorbable, lower exotherm and stiffness closer to cortical bone than PMMA. PMMA itself is not a biologic.

regulatory.reference: K080108 (Cortoss Bone Augmentation Material; Orthovita; decision 2009-06-05; product code NDN, vertebroplasty cement). FDA recall Z-2101-2021 (Class 2, 10 cc cartridge, temperature excursion, terminated 2022-04-15) cites K080108 and shows US distribution in 2021.; openFDA: K080108 (Cortoss Bone Augmentation Material, Orthovita, 2009-06-05)
on_label_indications: Augmentation of vertebral compression fractures via vertebroplasty (verify current Stryker IFU wording, including screw augmentation)

applications.evidence_summary: FDA-IDE RCT (Bae 2012, n=256, 2:1 vs PMMA, 21 US sites): noninferior; better pain at 3 months and function at 24 months; serious device-related AEs 4.3% in both arms; subsequent fractures 27.8% vs 31.9% (Gilula 2012).
applications.caveats: Orthovita-funded; modest clinical differences; Cortoss is bioactive but nonresorbable, so it is a 'biologic' only in the sense of surface bioactivity.

evidence.title: A prospective randomized FDA-IDE trial comparing Cortoss with PMMA for vertebroplasty: 24-month follow-up
evidence.finding: Noninferiority met; pain relief at 3 months and function at 24 months favored Cortoss; serious device-related AEs 4.3% each arm.

evidence.title: Subsequent fractures post-vertebral augmentation: analysis of a prospective randomized trial
evidence.finding: New fractures 27.8% Cortoss vs 31.9% PMMA; adjacent fractures 10.3% vs 18.2% in first-fracture subgroup.

bd.reimbursement: Inpatient VCF augmentation bundled in MS-DRGs 518-520 (back and neck procedures except spinal fusion); outpatient kyphoplasty/vertebroplasty paid under APCs with the material packaged; no separate HCPCS for the fill material.
bd.notes: Stryker Interventional Spine; niche vs Stryker's own PMMA products.
