challenge: Cortoss has no dedicated stryker.com product page as of 2026-10-22 and appears only in VCF brochures; treat current US availability as unconfirmed. K number and IFU still not retrieved.
catalog_status_2026: Not on Stryker's bone grafting catalog page; a stryker.com site search for 'Cortoss' (2026-10-22) returns only a 'VCF Solutions Brochure', a '2019 IVS Portfolio Notebook', a VCF competitive comparison guide and an orthobiologics patents page, with no product page (the guessed /spine/products/cortoss.html URL is a 404).

name: FIBERGRAFT (BG Morsels, BG Matrix, Aeridyan Matrix)
company: Prosidyan (promoted in US spine by DePuy Synthes)
ownership_history: Prosidyan Inc. (Warren, NJ), private, holds the FIBERGRAFT trademarks (renewed 2024); DePuy Synthes has had an exclusive US agreement to promote FIBERGRAFT for spine since May 2018. 'Aeridyan' is Prosidyan's trade name for its boron-based bioactive glass, not a company.
composition: 45S5 bioactive glass fibers/granules; Aeridyan Matrix adds boron-containing bioactive glass microspheres and bovine type I collagen

regulatory.reference: K180080 (FIBERGRAFT BG Matrix), K182670 (FIBERGRAFT Aeridyan Matrix), K213803
on_label_indications: Bone graft substitute / void filler for voids or gaps not intrinsic to the stability of the bony structure in the extremities, pelvis and posterolateral spine (verify form-specific wording)

applications.evidence_summary: No published spine clinical data; DePuy Synthes launched a post-market controlled study of FIBERGRAFT Aeridyan Matrix vs DBM in 1-3 level instrumented PLF (NCT07059065, n=316, 10 US sites, started Aug 2025, primary completion 2029).
applications.caveats: Evidence will not exist until 2029; current use rests on bioactive glass class data.

evidence.title: Post-market controlled study of FIBERGRAFT Aeridyan Matrix vs DBM in lumbar posterolateral fusion
evidence.finding: Recruiting; primary endpoint percent levels fused at 12 months.

bd.reimbursement: Bundled in fusion MS-DRGs.
bd.notes: Sold by DePuy Synthes spine reps under a promotion agreement; Prosidyan retains ownership and manufacturing.

name: NovaBone Putty / Morsels (45S5 bioactive glass)
company: NovaBone Products LLC (Isto Biologics since August 2026)
ownership_history: NovaBone Products LLC (Alachua, FL), spun out of USBiomaterials; PerioGlas was the original dental product. Halma plc acquired NovaBone in January 2020 (initial consideration $97 million). Halma completed the sale of NovaBone Products LLC and subsidiaries to Isto Biologics on 2026-08-04 for $60 million on a cash and debt-free basis (Halma RNS; Isto announced the deal the same day). Isto Biologics is itself majority-owned by Keensight Capital since September 2025.
composition: 45S5 calcium-phosphosilicate bioactive glass particulate in a polyethylene glycol/glycerin binder (putty) or as morsels

on_label_indications: Gently packed into bony voids or gaps of the skeletal system (extremities, spine and pelvis) not intrinsic to the stability of the bony structure (K052494)

applications.evidence_summary: No NovaBone-specific spine RCT retrieved; bioactive glass posterolateral fusion literature exists (e.g., Finnish long-term BAG vs autograft studies) but was not retrieved in this sweep.
applications.caveats: Evidence gap for the brand.

applications.evidence_summary: Osteostimulative claims rest on in-vitro ion release; no trauma or nonunion comparative data found for 45S5 putty.
applications.caveats: Evidence gap; most NovaBone clinical data are dental and spine.

applications.evidence_summary: Dental putty and morsels are sold into sinus lift and socket grafting on substantial equivalence; no NovaBone-named RCT in sinus augmentation located on PubMed.
applications.caveats: Commodity synthetic in a xenograft-dominated segment.

applications.evidence_summary: A comparative thesis from Ain Shams University (Egypt) on NovaBone versus Norian in cranioplasty exists in a university repository but is not peer-reviewed.
applications.caveats: No cranial indication on any NovaBone 510(k) (MQV and LYC only).

evidence.title: NovaBone Putty special 510(k) K101860
evidence.finding: Modification clearance; animal resorption data only.

bd.reimbursement: Bundled in fusion MS-DRGs.
bd.notes: Sells direct and through private-label/OEM arrangements with device companies (several spine companies' bioactive glass putties are NovaBone-made; partners not verified here).

name: SIGNAFUSE Bioactive Bone Graft (Putty, Strip)
ownership_history: Bioventus (Durham, NC; spun out of Smith+Nephew's biologics unit in 2012, IPO 2021); SIGNAFUSE was developed internally (510(k) filed through subsidiary MRC-X). Bioventus divested its Advanced Rehabilitation (Bioness) business in 2024 but not its bone graft lines.
composition: Biphasic mineral granules (60% hydroxyapatite / 40% beta-TCP) plus 45S5 bioactive glass suspended in a porous type I collagen matrix; combined with autologous bone marrow aspirate before use

regulatory.reference: K193513 (SIGNAFUSE Bioactive Bone Graft, cleared 2020-06-18, 21 CFR 888.3045, product code MQV); K233490 (SIGNAFUSE Bioactive Strip and Putty, 2023-12-05, expanded indications)
on_label_indications: Verbatim K193513: a bone graft substitute intended for use in bony voids or gaps of the skeletal system not intrinsic to the stability of the bony structure; to be combined with autologous bone marrow aspirate and packed into osseous defects of the extremities, pelvis and posterolateral spine; when used in the posterolateral spine, to be used as an autograft extender

applications.evidence_summary: No peer-reviewed clinical outcome study retrieved; cleared on substantial equivalence to prior ceramic/bioactive glass fillers.
applications.caveats: Evidence gap.

bd.reimbursement: Bundled in fusion MS-DRGs.
bd.notes: Bioventus Surgical Solutions sells through US direct teams plus a complementary indirect (distributor) team (10-K FY2024); the bag also includes OsteoAMP, PUREBONE and Reficio DBM.

name: DirectInject On-Demand HA Cement
composition: Pre-filled two-paste calcium phosphate cement in a double-barrel syringe with mixer cannula; hardens to hydroxyapatite

regulatory.reference: K143661 (2015-09-02, product code GXP)
on_label_indications: Repair of neurosurgical burr holes, contiguous craniotomy cuts and other cranial defects with a surface area of 4 cm2 or less that are not intrinsic to the stability of the bony structure; augmentation or restoration of bony contour in the craniofacial skeleton including the cranial and zygomatic bones; patients whose skeletal growth is complete

applications.evidence_summary: No clinical data in the 510(k) (bench and animal only); no published DirectInject series found on PubMed as of 2026-10-22.
applications.caveats: 4 cm2 ceiling is far smaller than the 25 cm2 on competing cements, so this is a burr-hole and kerf product, not a cranioplasty product.

bd.reimbursement: Bundled; no separate code.
bd.notes: Positioned on ease of use (no mixing) for craniotomy closure; Stryker CMF direct sales force.

name: HydroSet Injectable HA Bone Substitute
ownership_history: Developed and marketed by Stryker (Craniomaxillofacial and Trauma & Extremities divisions). A 2016 'HydroSet XT' 510(k) was filed by Orthovita, Inc., a Stryker subsidiary acquired in 2011.
composition: Self-setting calcium phosphate cement that cures to hydroxyapatite; injectable or moldable, sets in a wet field.

regulatory.reference: K161447 (HydroSet XT, Orthovita, Inc., decision 2016-10-06); earlier Stryker Injectable Cement K060061 (2006-03-01, MQV), K060763 (2006-09-22, product code GXP; cited by FDA recall Z-2054-2013), K060750 (Stryker CMF, 2006-04-19), K051603 (2005-12-30)
on_label_indications: Self-setting calcium phosphate cement to fill bony voids or gaps of the skeletal system (extremities, craniofacial, spine, pelvis) that are not intrinsic to the stability of the bony structure
Cured in situ it can augment provisional hardware (K-wires, plates, screws) to help support bone fragments during the surgical procedure; not intended to provide structural support during healing
regulatory.challenge: The cranial indication sits on the 2006 Stryker Injectable Cement clearance, not on the 2016 HydroSet XT 510(k); a CMF manager will ask which SKU is being sold into neurosurgery and under which labeling. The 25 cm2 ceiling appears on competitors' labels but was not found on the HydroSet pages or K060763 summaries retrieved.

applications.evidence_summary: No HydroSet-specific clinical trial in the femur found; use for metaphyseal void fill rests on class-level CPC data (Norian SRS trochanteric RCTs) and biomechanical work.
applications.caveats: Label says 'not intrinsic to stability' yet the clinical rationale is load-sharing; this gap is the standard hiring-manager challenge for every CPC.

applications.evidence_summary: No HydroSet data in hip fracture augmentation; CPC class evidence (Mattsson 2005, Norian SRS) showed modest early pain benefit only.
applications.caveats: PMMA (Traumacem V+) has displaced CPC for nail augmentation in the proximal femur.

applications.evidence_summary: Class evidence: calcium phosphate cement reduced articular subsidence vs ICBG in a 120-fracture RCT (Russell 2008, using Norian SRS) and a 2008 meta-analysis of CPC RCTs in appendicular fractures; no HydroSet-specific plateau RCT found.
applications.caveats: Evidence is borrowed from a different CPC brand (Norian); HydroSet XT clearance rested on bench testing only. Label explicitly disclaims structural support.

applications.evidence_summary: Used for metaphyseal voids by labeling (extremities, traumatic defects); no pilon-specific outcome data found.
applications.caveats: No clinical evidence located.

applications.evidence_summary: Class-level calcium-phosphate cement evidence: Thordarson 2005 (PMID 15913516) 15 ORIF cases with Norian SRS, no loss of reduction with weight-bearing at 3-6 weeks; Elsner 2005 (PMID 16210159) 18 patients, full weight-bearing at a mean 4 weeks but functional outcome no better than graft; Zeman 2019 (PMID 31941568) no outcome difference with vs without hydroxyapatite cement in 82 Sanders II-III fractures.
applications.caveats: Small series with the predecessor Norian cement (DePuy Synthes), not HydroSet; a Dutch series linked void-filler use to wound complications (PMID 23318101).

applications.evidence_summary: Augmentation of osteoporotic malleolar or pilon metaphyseal fixation; biomechanical data only (e.g., PMID 33189144 in a calcaneal model).
applications.caveats: No clinical ankle-fracture series found.

applications.evidence_summary: Calcium phosphate cement augmentation of locked plating reduced head settling and intra-articular screw penetration vs no augmentation or cancellous chips in a 92-patient retrospective cohort (Egol 2012, PMID:22192764); the cement brand in that series is not HydroSet-specific.
applications.caveats: Single-center retrospective; no HydroSet-specific RCT in the proximal humerus.

applications.evidence_summary: Double-blind RCT of HydroSet vs no graft in volar-plated opening-wedge distal radius osteotomy found no difference in PRWE, QuickDASH, motion or grip at 12 months (Andreasson 2020, PMID:32472263).
applications.caveats: A negative trial for the product: it shows the void can be left empty when cortical contact is maintained.

applications.evidence_summary: Class evidence: calcium phosphate cement plus volar locking plate gave no clinical or radiographic benefit over plate alone in elderly unstable fractures (Kim 2011 RCT, n=50, PMID:21471414).
applications.caveats: Cement brand in Kim 2011 not HydroSet; class-level inference.

applications.evidence_summary: No HydroSet-specific burr hole trial; class evidence for hydroxyapatite plugs versus bone dust (20-patient within-patient comparison) and the pooled HA cement literature.
applications.caveats: Bench and animal data only in the 510(k); the cranial product and the XT product have different labels.

applications.evidence_summary: HA cement for small full-thickness defects: pooled infection or explantation 7.5 percent for large-defect cranioplasty across 35 studies and 1,983 patients; no HydroSet-named comparative study.
applications.caveats: Class-level evidence; cements fail more often above 25 cm2 and in children.

applications.evidence_summary: HA cement cranioplasty after translabyrinthine and retrosigmoid craniectomy lowers CSF leak odds (OR 0.25) and pseudomeningocele versus no cement in an 8-study meta-analysis; single-center series of 369 implants with 3.8 percent adverse events.
applications.caveats: Brand not always reported; HydroSet is one of several HA cements used in the series.

evidence.title: Resorbable cement for the augmentation of internally-fixed unstable trochanteric fractures (Norian SRS, class evidence)
evidence.finding: CPC augmentation gave modest early pain and SF-36 benefits with no difference in radiographic outcome.

evidence.title: Comparison of autogenous bone graft and endothermic calcium phosphate cement for defect augmentation in tibial plateau fractures (Russell & Leighton)
evidence.finding: 120 Schatzker I-VI fractures randomized 2:1 to CPC (82) or ICBG (38); union and time to union equal; articular subsidence at 3-12 months significantly higher with autograft (p=0.009). Level I.

evidence.title: The use of calcium phosphate bone cement in fracture treatment: a meta-analysis of randomized trials
evidence.finding: Pooled RCTs of CPC vs conventional treatment (with or without autograft) in appendicular fractures; CPC associated with less loss of reduction and less pain (abstract truncated in retrieval).

evidence.title: SRS cancellous bone cement augmentation of calcaneal fracture fixation
evidence.finding: No loss of reduction with early weight-bearing; one major wound complication requiring cement removal and free flap.

evidence.title: Augmentation of intraarticular calcaneal fractures with injectable calcium phosphate cement: densitometry, histology, and functional outcome of 18 patients
evidence.finding: Full weight-bearing at mean 4 weeks; cement not fully resorbed at 3 years; outcomes no better than conventional grafting.

evidence.title: Outcomes of treatment of calcaneal fractures using locking compression plate with or without augmentation
evidence.finding: No statistically significant difference in AOFAS outcome or complications with hydroxyapatite cement augmentation of the neutral-triangle defect.

evidence.title: Extended lateral approach for intra-articular calcaneal fractures: an inverse relationship between surgeon experience and wound complications
evidence.finding: Bone-void-filler use was significantly associated with wound complications (p<0.001).

evidence.title: Functional outcome after corrective osteotomy for malunion of the distal radius: a randomised, controlled, double-blind trial
evidence.finding: No difference in PROMs, motion or grip at 3, 6 and 12 months with HydroSet vs empty osteotomy void.

evidence.title: Fracture site augmentation with calcium phosphate cement reduces screw penetration after ORIF of proximal humeral fractures
evidence.finding: Less humeral head settling and significantly less screw penetration with calcium phosphate cement than with no augmentation (P=.02) or cancellous chips (P=.009).

evidence.title: Microstructure and biomechanical characteristics of bone substitutes for trauma and orthopaedic surgery
evidence.finding: Bench comparison of nine cements including HydroSet and Norian SRS; mechanical properties differ widely among products registered for trauma.

evidence.title: Utility of bone cement for cranioplasty following retrosigmoid or translabyrinthine craniectomy: systematic review and meta-analysis
evidence.finding: Across 8 studies (1,044 cement, 1,021 no cement), bone cement after retrosigmoid craniectomy was associated with lower odds of CSF leak (OR 0.25), pseudomeningocele (OR 0.25) and surgical site infection (OR 0.27).

evidence.title: Hydroxyapatite cement cranioplasty following translabyrinthine approach: long-term study of 369 cases
evidence.finding: Seven CSF leaks and seven infections (combined 3.8 percent) in 369 HAC implants with follow-up to 15 years; fewer adverse events than published fat-graft-alone rates.

evidence.title: Outcomes of hydroxyapatite bone cement for craniofacial reconstruction in 1983 patients
evidence.finding: Infection or explantation 7.5 percent for large-defect cranioplasty, 1.5 percent for retrosigmoid cranioplasty and 6.2 percent for secondary contouring after congenital craniofacial surgery; CSF leak 0 to 0.8 percent.

evidence.title: Craniotomy burr hole covers: comparative study of three plug materials
evidence.finding: Autologous bone dust resorbed partially or completely in every burr hole at one year with visible contour irregularity in 60 percent; porous hydroxyapatite plugs kept thickness and cosmesis with no added complications.

bd.reimbursement: Bundled in the inpatient MS-DRG for hip and femur procedures (MS-DRG 480-482) or the relevant trauma DRG; no separate device payment. Outpatient/ASC use is packaged into the procedure APC.
bd.notes: Sold through Stryker Trauma & Extremities reps alongside nails and plates, which is how most trauma void fillers are pulled through; a 2013 Class 2 recall (desiccant leak, 12,719 units) was packaging-related.

challenge: Stryker's catalog page lists the product as 'HydroSet XT' (2026-10-22); use that name.
catalog_status_2026: Stryker's US trauma-and-extremities bone grafting catalog page (read 2026-10-22) lists AlloFiber, AlloMatrix, Augment, BIO4, DBM, FusionFlex, HydroSet XT, Ignite, OsteoSet, Pro-Dense, Pro-Dense LoVisc, Pro-Stim, Tensix, Vitoss, Vitoss BA, Vitoss BA2X and Vitoss BBTrauma as current products.

name: KyphOs FS calcium phosphate bone cement (and other resorbable CPCs for vertebral augmentation)
ownership_history: Kyphon developed KyphOs FS for use with its balloon kyphoplasty system; Medtronic acquired Kyphon in 2007.
composition: Injectable, self-setting magnesium-substituted calcium phosphate cement that converts to a resorbable apatite; fast-setting 'FS' formulation for use after balloon tamp cavity creation

regulatory.reference: No 510(k)/PMA record under 'KyphOs FS' in openFDA (device_name KYPHOS: no matches; Kyphon/Medtronic Kyphon bone-cement 510(k)s are PMMA cements and tamps: K041584, K163032, K171938, K180700, K191148). Australia's TGA lists the Medtronic KyphOs FS calcium phosphate substitute (model C02B) as cancelled.
on_label_indications: Bone void filler for voids or gaps not intrinsic to the stability of the bony structure; use with balloon kyphoplasty to fill the cavity in vertebral compression fractures (verify current labeling)

applications.evidence_summary: RCT of CPC vs PMMA in balloon kyphoplasty (Blattert 2009, n=56 patients/60 fractures): equivalent pain relief, but 9 radiographic losses of correction from cement failure in the CPC arm (burst-type fractures) vs none with PMMA; authors did not recommend routine CPC kyphoplasty. Small Korean series showed better Cobb correction but weaker support with CaP.
applications.caveats: The Blattert RCT tested a CPC (brand not stated in abstract); the mechanical weakness of resorbable cements in burst morphology is the class-level caution. PMMA is not a biologic and remains the standard.

evidence.title: Suitability of a calcium phosphate cement in osteoporotic vertebral body fracture augmentation: RCT of balloon kyphoplasty, CaP vs PMMA
evidence.finding: Pain relief similar; 9/30 CaP vertebrae lost correction (cement failure in burst fractures) vs 0/30 PMMA; 2 PMMA embolisms.

bd.reimbursement: Packaged into kyphoplasty payment (inpatient MS-DRG or outpatient APC); no separate payment for the cement.
bd.notes: Medtronic Interventional Spine; CPC is a small share of augmentation volume, which is dominated by PMMA kyphoplasty (57,646 Medicare kyphoplasties in 2015).

challenge: Could not confirm any US clearance or current availability. Tried openFDA name and applicant searches (Kyphon, Medtronic, 'calcium phosphate'), Medtronic news (2010 US launch was of KYPHON ActivOs 10 hydroxyapatite-PMMA cement, not KyphOs FS) and web search; the only hard record is the TGA cancellation. Treat as ex-US/unverified until Medtronic confirms.

name: Mimix and Mimix QS Bone Replacement (QuickSet Mimix, Mimix MP)
company: Zimmer Biomet (Biomet Microfixation, formerly Walter Lorenz Surgical)
ownership_history: Walter Lorenz Surgical (a Biomet subsidiary) cleared Mimix in 2001 and QuickSet Mimix in 2002; Biomet, Inc. cleared Mimix MP in 2004; Biomet became Zimmer Biomet in 2015 and the CMF line sits in Zimmer Biomet CMF and Thoracic (Jacksonville). GUDID still lists Biomet Microfixation as labeler.
composition: Hydroxyapatite-forming cement of tetracalcium phosphate and alpha-tricalcium phosphate; Mimix QS has finer particles and a roughly 3-minute set

regulatory.reference: K003494 (Mimix Bone Replacement System, LYC, 2001-04-09); K012569 (Injectable Mimix, GXP, 2001-12-21); K023718 (QuickSet Mimix Bone Void Filler, GXP, 2002-12-04); K043280 (Mimix MP, GXP, 2004-12-21)
on_label_indications: Repair of neurosurgical burr holes, craniotomy cuts and other cranial defects, and augmentation or restoration of bony contour in the craniofacial skeleton, for areas no larger than 25 cm2 (K023718)

challenge: Zimmer Biomet's US CMF web page lists Mimix and Mimix QS under neurosurgery and the EU product page is live, but no 2024 to 2026 US brochure or catalog entry was retrieved; confirm active US distribution before presenting as a current competitor.

applications.evidence_summary: No Mimix-specific burr hole study; relies on class evidence.
applications.caveats: Commodity product.

applications.evidence_summary: Included in the 78-child Emory series (Mimix or BoneSource, 6 removals) and an 18-case Korean facial contouring series with no infections at 23 months.
applications.caveats: Small, uncontrolled.

applications.evidence_summary: Secondary malar, forehead, chin and paranasal contouring in 18 patients (mean 16 g) with no infection, seroma or migration at 23 months.
applications.caveats: Contour augmentation, not fracture repair.

evidence.title: Use of rapidly hardening hydroxyapatite cement (Mimix) for facial contouring surgery
evidence.finding: No postoperative infection, seroma or migration over 23 months of follow-up after forehead, malar, chin and paranasal augmentation with a mean 16 g of Mimix.

evidence.title: Use of hydroxyapatite cement in pediatric craniofacial reconstructive surgery
evidence.finding: Seven complications and six removals among 78 children treated with Mimix or BoneSource.

bd.reimbursement: Bundled.
bd.notes: Zimmer Biomet CMF and Thoracic (the former Biomet Microfixation business in Jacksonville, FL); Zimmer Biomet also distributes Osteopore PCL scaffolds in EMEA and APAC since July 2024, which may position PCL over cement in those markets.

name: Norian SRS / Norian XR / Norian Drillable (historical)
company: DePuy Synthes (Johnson & Johnson); originally Norian Corporation, acquired by Synthes in 1999
ownership_history: Norian Corp. (Cupertino, CA) developed the first commercial calcium phosphate cement; Synthes acquired Norian in 1999. In 2009 the US Attorney in Philadelphia charged Synthes, Norian and four executives over unauthorized clinical use of Norian XR in vertebral compression fractures (a labeled contraindication); Norian pleaded guilty in 2010 (about a $23 million fine) and Synthes agreed to divest Norian; executives were sentenced in 2011. J&J acquired Synthes in 2012. Despite the 2010 divestiture agreement, DePuy Synthes (J&J MedTech) still carries the Norian brand in 2026: its Norian Drillable inventory control form is on jnjmedtech.com and a 'Norian Putty / Fast Set Putty Bone Void Filler' patient leaflet (TV-TEC-216396 Rev B, September 2026, sponsor DePuy Synthes (Australia) Pty Ltd) lists 'Norian'. The most recent Norian 510(k) is K102722 (Norian Drillable Inject / Fast Set Putty, 2011-01-27, Synthes USA Products LLC). What the divestiture covered is not clear from public sources.
composition: Carbonated apatite calcium phosphate cement (SRS); Norian XR added a radiopacifier; Norian Drillable is a fiber-reinforced CPC that can be drilled and accept screws.

regulatory.reference: K041842 and K060406 (Norian SRS Fast Set Putty), K060408 (Norian SRS Bone Void Filler, 2006-03-21), K060443/K060445 (Norian CRS, 2006-04-13), K073303 (Norian Drillable, 2008-07-02), K102018 (Norian Reinforced, 2010-09-23), K102722 (Norian Drillable Inject / Fast Set Putty, 2011-01-27); applicant Synthes (USA) / Synthes USA Products LLC
on_label_indications: Bony voids or defects of the extremities and pelvis that are not intrinsic to the stability of the bony structure, surgically created or from traumatic injury
Adjunct to rigid hardware fixation; not intended to provide structural support during healing
regulatory.challenge: Norian Corporation was acquired by Synthes in 1999 and pleaded guilty in 2009 to off-label promotion of Norian XR for vertebroplasty (the spine product, not CRS). Whether every CRS SKU is still in the DePuy Synthes US catalog in 2026 was not verified; the pass-2 log found a Norian Putty leaflet dated September 2026, which supports continued sale of the family.

challenge: Status changed from off-market to established on the strength of DePuy Synthes/J&J MedTech documents dated through September 2026; the US J&J MedTech product page is behind Cloudflare and was not read, so confirm US availability and the Norian XR (spinal) labeling with a DePuy Synthes rep.

applications.evidence_summary: Two Swedish RCTs (Mattsson 2004 RSA study n=26; Mattsson 2005 n=112) showed less fracture motion and modest early pain/QoL benefit with Norian SRS augmentation of sliding hip screws, no radiographic difference.
applications.caveats: Industry-supported; outcomes modest; technique not adopted in US practice, superseded by PMMA augmentation of nails.

applications.evidence_summary: Small Scandinavian studies of CPC-augmented femoral neck screws; no adoption.
applications.caveats: Historical only.

applications.evidence_summary: Norian SRS is the cement used in the Russell & Leighton 2008 RCT that showed less subsidence than ICBG; it is the evidentiary anchor for the whole CPC class in plateau fractures.
applications.caveats: Product line's current US availability could not be confirmed (marked unverified); the brand is inseparable from the Synthes criminal case, which a hiring manager will raise.
applications.challenge: Whether any Norian SKU remains on the DePuy Synthes US catalog in 2026 was not verifiable from public sources.

applications.evidence_summary: Largest biologic RCT ever run in the wrist: 323 patients randomized to closed reduction with or without Norian SRS; better grip, motion and function at 6-8 weeks, no clinical difference at one year, more extraosseous cement deposits and slightly greater ulnar variance change (Cassidy 2003, PMID:14630841). Cochrane (Handoll 2008, PMID:18425972) pooled this with smaller trials and found short-term anatomic gains but no durable functional benefit.
applications.caveats: Pre-dates volar locking plates; industry-era trial; product line effectively ended by the 2009-2010 DOJ case. Historical reference only.

applications.evidence_summary: Calcium phosphate cement class evidence (Egol 2012) was largely generated with Norian-era cements.
applications.caveats: Brand attribution in the published series is inconsistent.

applications.evidence_summary: Gilardino 2009 long-term series of 46 Norian cranioplasties (mean 44 months): 26 percent complications, 9 infections, mean onset 20 months; complications tracked with the amount of cement and with onlay use in contaminated fields, and full-thickness defects over 25 cm2 trended worse.
applications.caveats: Single institution, no comparator; complications appeared years after implantation.

applications.evidence_summary: Secondary forehead contouring in 20 children with Norian: 10 of 17 followed (59 percent) developed infection at mean 17 months, 9 needing removal; infected patients had received more cement (32.5 vs 14.3 mL).
applications.caveats: Worst published outcome for any HA cement; large onlay volumes in a growing skull.

applications.evidence_summary: Labeled for craniofacial contour augmentation (fronto-orbital, malar, mental); used for secondary malar and frontal contour after trauma, no comparative data.
applications.caveats: Not for acute fracture fixation.

evidence.title: Resorbable cement for the augmentation of internally-fixed unstable trochanteric fractures. A prospective, randomised multicentre study.
evidence.finding: Norian SRS augmentation of a sliding hip screw reduced pain at 6 weeks and improved SF-36 at 6 weeks and 6 months; no other differences.

evidence.title: Unstable trochanteric fractures augmented with calcium phosphate cement. A prospective randomized study using radiostereometry.
evidence.finding: Augmented fractures moved 1.9 mm versus 4.0 mm at 1 week and 7.8 versus 13.2 mm by 6 months (RSA).

evidence.title: Comparison of autogenous bone graft and endothermic calcium phosphate cement for defect augmentation in tibial plateau fractures
evidence.finding: CPC (Norian SRS) matched ICBG on union and had significantly less articular subsidence.

evidence.title: Norian SRS cement compared with conventional fixation in distal radial fractures. A randomized study
evidence.finding: Early (6-8 week) functional advantage that disappeared by one year; extraosseous deposits were the main complication.

evidence.title: Injectable calcium phosphate bone cement Norian SRS for intra-articular compression fractures of the distal radius in osteoporotic women
evidence.finding: Cement plus pinning allowed 3 weeks of casting vs 6 weeks, with maintained reduction in osteoporotic women.

evidence.title: Bone grafts and bone substitutes for treating distal radial fractures in adults (Cochrane)
evidence.finding: Ten heterogeneous trials; scaffolding improved anatomical outcomes vs cast alone in four trials, but Norian SRS vs cast/external fixation showed no functional or anatomic difference at one year.

evidence.title: Long-term follow-up experience with carbonated calcium phosphate cement (Norian) for cranioplasty in children and adults
evidence.finding: Overall complication rate 26 percent (9 infections, 1 seroma, 2 draining sinuses) at mean 44 months; risk rose with cement volume and contaminated onlay use; defects over 25 cm2 trended worse.

evidence.title: Complications of hydroxyapatite bone cement in secondary pediatric craniofacial reconstruction
evidence.finding: 59 percent infectious complications after secondary forehead cranioplasty with Norian in children, mean onset 17.3 months, 9 of 10 requiring removal.

evidence.title: Utilization of carbonated calcium phosphate cement for contouring cranioplasty in syndromic craniosynostosis
evidence.finding: Forehead contouring (mean area 135 cm2, 17 g cement) improved Whitaker scores and held at over one year; two infections (9.5 percent) needed removal.

evidence.title: Comparison of calcium phosphate cement with patient-specific implants for cranial reconstruction: randomized controlled trial (AZ Sint-Jan, Belgium)
evidence.finding: Completed 2018; results not located on PubMed as of 2026-10-22.

bd.reimbursement: Bundled in inpatient MS-DRG; no separate payment.
bd.notes: The Norian case is the cautionary tale every trauma biologics rep is trained on: a labeled contraindication (vertebral use) was promoted through surgeon 'test markets' without an IDE; the result was a felony plea, a forced divestiture and prison time for executives under the responsible-corporate-officer doctrine. Do not call Norian 'divested and gone': DePuy Synthes still publishes Norian Drillable/Putty documents in 2026.

name: OsteoVation CMF, OsteoVation Impact and Callos CMF Bone Void Filler
composition: Self-setting calcium phosphate cement (apatitic) in putty and impact-resistant formulations

regulatory.reference: K042072 (Callos CMF, 2004-09-16), K051784 (OsteoVation CMF, 2005-07-20), K162864 (OsteoVation Impact, 2017-01-13); all product code GXP
on_label_indications: Repair of neurosurgical burr holes, craniotomy cuts and other cranial defects and restoration of craniofacial contour (per GXP class labeling; exact text not retrieved)

challenge: Included to show the long tail of GXP cements; current distribution and any clinical publication were not found, so grade V and unverified status.

applications.evidence_summary: No published clinical data located.
applications.caveats: Commodity cement, private company.

bd.reimbursement: Bundled.
bd.notes: Skeletal Kinetics also supplies calcium phosphate cement OEM to orthopedic companies (Callos); the CMF line's channel is unverified.

name: chronOS Inject (and chronOS beta-TCP granules/blocks)
ownership_history: Synthes/Mathys heritage product; Synthes acquired by J&J 2012. J&J announced on October 14, 2025 its intent to separate the DePuy Synthes orthopaedics business into a standalone company within 18-24 months.
composition: chronOS Inject: injectable, resorbable calcium phosphate cement (brushite-based, containing beta-TCP granules) that hardens in situ. chronOS granules/blocks: pure beta-tricalcium phosphate with interconnected porosity.

regulatory.reference: No US 510(k) under 'chronOS Inject'. openFDA device_name CHRONOS returns only Synthes records for the chronOS beta-TCP family (K013072 2002, K041350 2004, K043045 2005, K053022 2006, K071046 chronOS Composite 2007). DePuy Synthes EMEA IFU documents for other chronOS products carry 'not intended for distribution in the USA' language; no chronOS Inject IFU was retrieved.
on_label_indications: Not marketed in the US (no clearance found under this name); the US chronOS line is beta-TCP granules, preforms/blocks/wedges, strips

challenge: Treat chronOS Inject as ex-US/investigational for the US; the US entry belongs under the chronOS beta-TCP family (see chronos).

applications.evidence_summary: beta-TCP granules are a routine metaphyseal void filler; no femur-specific comparative trial found.
applications.caveats: Class-level use; no product-specific trauma RCT.

applications.evidence_summary: Used as an autograft extender in Masquelet reconstructions in case series.
applications.caveats: Extender only; no stand-alone efficacy evidence.

bd.reimbursement: Bundled in inpatient MS-DRG; packaged in outpatient APC.
bd.notes: Pulled through by the DePuy Synthes trauma bag (TFN-Advanced, LCP plates). Ownership of this franchise will change hands in the planned 2026-2027 DePuy Synthes separation.

name: OSTEOSET (calcium sulfate pellets; OSTEOSET DBM pellets)
company: Stryker (via Wright Medical Technology, acquired November 11, 2020)
ownership_history: Wright Medical Technology product since the late 1990s; Wright acquired by Stryker for ~$4.1 billion (closed November 11, 2020). Wright Medical Technology, Inc. remains the 510(k) applicant of record as a Stryker subsidiary.
composition: Medical-grade calcium sulfate hemihydrate pellets (OSTEOSET), or calcium sulfate pellets with demineralized bone matrix (OSTEOSET DBM).

regulatory.reference: OSTEOSET DBM Pellets K022828 (2004-04-02) and K053642 (2006-01-26); OSTEOSET BVF Kit K010532 (2001-10-26); applicant Wright Medical Technology. The original 1990s calcium sulfate pellet clearance does not appear under the OSTEOSET name in openFDA (K number not retrieved).
on_label_indications: Bone void filler for voids or gaps that are not intrinsic to the stability of the bony structure, extremities, spine and pelvis

challenge: OsteoSet is still listed on Stryker's bone grafting catalog page (2026-10-22) alongside Pro-Dense; the catalog-status concern is resolved.

applications.evidence_summary: Historical antibiotic-carrier and dead-space filler (OSTEOSET T, tobramycin-loaded, was ex-US); case series only.
applications.caveats: Rapid resorption; largely superseded by Stimulan and Cerament G.

applications.evidence_summary: Ferguson 2023 (PMID 37400090): preformed tobramycin calcium-sulfate pellets (n=179) vs gentamicin calcium-sulfate/hydroxyapatite (Cerament G, n=180) in single-stage long-bone osteomyelitis; recurrence 11.2% vs 4.4%, wound leakage 18.4% vs 10.0%, subsequent fracture 6.1% vs 1.7%, all favoring the biphasic carrier.
applications.caveats: UK study with OsteoSet T (not US-available); antibiotic-loaded use of plain OsteoSet in the US is off-label; long-bone, not diabetic foot.

evidence.title: A comparison of clinical and radiological outcomes between two different biodegradable local antibiotic carriers used in the single-stage surgical management of long bone osteomyelitis
evidence.finding: Preformed calcium-sulfate pellets had 2.9-fold higher odds of recurrence, leakage or fracture than the biphasic gentamicin carrier.

bd.reimbursement: Bundled in inpatient MS-DRG.
bd.notes: Legacy brand; Stryker's trauma biologics emphasis is Vitoss, Pro-Dense and Allomatrix.

catalog_status_2026: Stryker's US trauma-and-extremities bone grafting catalog page (read 2026-10-22) lists AlloFiber, AlloMatrix, Augment, BIO4, DBM, FusionFlex, HydroSet XT, Ignite, OsteoSet, Pro-Dense, Pro-Dense LoVisc, Pro-Stim, Tensix, Vitoss, Vitoss BA, Vitoss BA2X and Vitoss BBTrauma as current products.

name: OSTEOSET T (tobramycin-impregnated calcium sulfate pellets)
ownership_history: Wright Medical product (OSTEOSET calcium sulfate pellets cleared in the US; OSTEOSET T with 4% tobramycin CE-marked); Wright acquired by Stryker 2020. A planned US military open-fracture study was announced while 'awaiting FDA clearance' (Becker's, undated); no US clearance found.
composition: Medical-grade calcium sulfate pellets impregnated with 4% tobramycin sulfate

regulatory.reference: No OSTEOSET T (tobramycin) record in the openFDA 510(k) database (the only OSTEOSET device_name hits are the BVF kit and DBM pellets); Stryker's US catalog lists only 'OsteoSet resorbable beads'.
on_label_indications: Not marketed in the US; CE-marked ex-US as an antibiotic-impregnated bone void filler

applications.evidence_summary: UK series (n=21, chronic post-traumatic tibial osteomyelitis) reported eradication in 20 of 21 at 15-16 months with 33% early wound discharge; Lausanne pharmacokinetic study (NCT01938417) found no toxicity concern at 10-20 g doses without renal failure.
applications.caveats: Ex-US evidence; small retrospective series; not available to US surgeons.

evidence.title: Adjuvant treatment of chronic osteomyelitis of the tibia following exogenous trauma using OSTEOSET-T: a review of 21 patients in a regional trauma centre
evidence.finding: Infection eradicated in 20/21; early wound discharge 7/21 (33%), overall wound complications 52%; no industry funding.

bd.reimbursement: Not applicable in the US.
bd.notes: Illustrates the pre-CERAMENT G regulatory gap: FDA treated antibiotic-loaded calcium sulfate as a drug-device combination requiring more than a 510(k), which kept OSTEOSET T, PerOssal with antibiotics and Herafill out of the US for two decades.

catalog_status_2026: Plain OsteoSet is listed on Stryker's US bone grafting catalog page (2026-10-22); no tobramycin (OsteoSet T) listing appears, consistent with ex-US-only status.

name: PerOssal (nanocrystalline HA / calcium sulfate pellets)
ownership_history: Developed by Coripharm/aap Implantate; now OSARTIS GmbH (Münster). Heraeus Medical distributes in some markets. No US clearance found.
composition: 51.5% nanocrystalline hydroxyapatite and 48.5% calcium sulfate pellets, intended to be soaked in antibiotic solution before implantation

regulatory.reference: No FDA 510(k) found under PerOssal; openFDA applicant OSARTIS returns only BonOs bone cements (K192394, K202458, K210120, K210125) and spacer molds (K240856)
on_label_indications: Not marketed in the US; CE-marked as a resorbable bone substitute that can be loaded with antibiotics

applications.evidence_summary: German series in non-weight-bearing cancellous defects and osteomyelitis; no US data.
applications.caveats: Ex-US only; small series.

evidence.title: PerOssal in cancellous bone defects (Unfallchirurg 2007)
evidence.finding: Adequate support of cancellous defects in non-weight-bearing areas or with osteosynthesis.

bd.reimbursement: Not applicable in the US.
bd.notes: Included because US trauma surgeons trained in Europe ask for it; a US entry would now have a predicate pathway via 888.3046 only if preloaded with an aminoglycoside.

name: STIMULAN (Rapid Cure, Kit, Bullet Mat)
ownership_history: Privately held; TA Associates majority since 2017; March 2025 recapitalization brought Novo Holdings in as a co-controlling investor. Acquired Artoss (NanoBone) in June 2023.
composition: Pharmaceutical-grade synthetic calcium sulfate hemihydrate that sets into beads or paste; surgeons commonly mix antibiotics into it at the point of care (an off-label practice in the US).

regulatory.reference: K141830 (Stimulan Kit / Stimulan Rapid Cure, January 2015); earlier K001724, K003954, K021551
on_label_indications: Bone void filler for voids or gaps that are not intrinsic to the stability of the bony structure, in the extremities, pelvis and posterolateral spine, from surgery, cyst, tumor, osteomyelitis or traumatic injury; may be used at an infected site
Beads resorb in roughly 30-60 days when used per labeling

challenge: The US label does not cover antibiotic loading. STIMULAN VG (vancomycin/gentamicin premix) has no US marketing authorization as of 2026-10-22: it is a drug-device combination under IND (NCT06283979, randomized Phase II vs standard of care, n=60 planned, recruiting, est. primary completion 2026-12; NCT05539963 feasibility trial active, not recruiting) with an expanded-access program listed as available (NCT06808568).

applications.evidence_summary: Widely used as a dead-space filler and (off-label) antibiotic carrier in infected femoral nonunion and Masquelet stage one; evidence is case series and registry data, no RCT in the femur.
applications.caveats: Antibiotic loading is off-label in the US; calcium sulfate drainage/wound leakage is a known complication.

applications.evidence_summary: Pure calcium sulfate resorbs faster than bone forms, so it is a poor choice for load-adjacent metaphyseal voids; little published use.
applications.caveats: Class limitation (rapid resorption).

applications.evidence_summary: Antibiotic-loaded calcium sulfate is the most used dead-space carrier worldwide: 2022 meta-analysis of 16 studies (917 patients) pooled eradication 92%, reoperation 9%, delayed wound healing 20%, aseptic leakage 12%; a 2026 review of 41 studies found no RCTs. US surgeons mix antibiotics into STIMULAN off-label.
applications.caveats: 'May be used at an infected site' is not an antibiotic-delivery claim; US antibiotic mixing is off-label and the company cannot promote it. Wound leakage from calcium sulfate is a known trade-off.
applications.challenge: A hiring manager will probe whether the rep knows the exact line between 'infected site' labeling and off-label antibiotic loading in the US.

applications.evidence_summary: Single-stage tibial osteomyelitis series (n=42, 88.4% remission at 42.8 months) and 163-patient Chinese cohort with autograft (15.3% recurrence) used antibiotic-loaded calcium sulfate; bone-transport docking-site series report new bone around resorbing beads.
applications.caveats: Retrospective, non-comparative.

applications.evidence_summary: Alkayali 2024 (PMID 38371037): 45 US diabetic-foot-osteomyelitis cases with surgeon-mixed calcium-sulfate antibiotic beads; only 20% ulcer-free at 3 months, 29% at 6 months, 42% osteomyelitis recurrence at 12 months, 62% wound drainage, 9% acute kidney injury. Chatzipapas 2020 (PMID 33295248): 25 patients, no benefit of local carriers over debridement plus systemic antibiotics.
applications.caveats: Antibiotic loading is off-label (surgeon-compounded); 'may be used at an infected site' is the only infection language on the label. Diabetic-foot evidence is small and unfavorable; the favorable long-bone data use other carriers.

applications.evidence_summary: Widely used in infected Charcot reconstruction and after partial calcanectomy; no Charcot series found.
applications.caveats: Expert practice; wound drainage from calcium sulfate is the recurring complaint.

applications.evidence_summary: Antibiotic-loaded calcium sulfate beads are the most common US dead-space filler in bone infection, but the evidence is retrospective series dominated by the lower limb and diabetic foot; no upper-extremity-specific comparative study was found. Biocomposites is now running FDA-pathway trials of a premixed vancomycin-gentamicin version, STIMULAN VG, in diabetic foot osteomyelitis (NCT05539963, n=61) and pressure-ulcer osteomyelitis (NCT06283979, phase II, n=60), with an expanded-access program (NCT06808568).
applications.caveats: Off-label antibiotic mixing in the US; hypercalcemia and wound drainage are the known class complications.

evidence.title: Antibiotic-loaded calcium sulfate in clinical treatment of chronic osteomyelitis: systematic review and meta-analysis
evidence.finding: Overall eradication 92%; reoperation 9%, refracture 2%, delayed wound healing 20%, aseptic leakage 12%; tobramycin vs vancomycin+gentamicin loading did not change eradication.

evidence.title: Single-stage treatment of chronic localized tibial osteomyelitis with local debridement and antibiotic-loaded calcium sulfate implantation: 42 patients
evidence.finding: 88.4% infection remission without recurrence at mean 42.8 months; prolonged aseptic drainage in 30%.

evidence.title: Multi-center, single-arm, historically controlled pivotal trial of genex G in surgical treatment of osteomyelitis of the extremities
evidence.finding: Recruiting; Biocomposites' gentamicin-preloaded calcium sulfate aimed at the 888.3046 regulation created by CERAMENT G; primary completion October 2027.

evidence.title: Are biodegradable calcium sulfate antibiotic beads effective and safe adjuvants for diabetic foot osteomyelitis?
evidence.finding: 42% osteomyelitis recurrence at 12 months and 62% wound drainage; authors advise caution pending an RCT.

evidence.title: Local antibiotic delivery systems in the surgical treatment of diabetic foot osteomyelitis: again, no benefit?
evidence.finding: Healing 87.5% systemic only vs 100% PMMA beads vs 87.5% calcium sulfate/hydroxyapatite beads; no difference.

evidence.title: A scoping review on the use of antibiotic-impregnated beads and applications to vascular surgery
evidence.finding: 275 publications on antibiotic beads; only 11 RCTs, all but one at high risk of bias; 94% of papers positive, suggesting publication bias.

evidence.title: Randomized phase II trial of STIMULAN VG with debridement and systemic antibiotics vs standard of care for osteomyelitis in stage IV pressure ulcers
evidence.finding: Recruiting; primary completion December 2026.

evidence.title: Randomized feasibility trial of STIMULAN VG with abbreviated vs full systemic antibiotics for diabetic foot osteomyelitis
evidence.finding: Active, not recruiting; primary completion June 2025; results not yet posted.

bd.reimbursement: Bundled in inpatient MS-DRG; in outpatient settings packaged into the procedure APC.
bd.notes: Biocomposites sells direct in the US (Wilmington, NC subsidiary) and via distributors elsewhere; Stimulan is the value alternative to Cerament G in infection cases, with surgeon-mixed antibiotic as the differentiator and the liability.

pipeline.expected_milestone: STIMULAN VG would be the first premixed antibiotic calcium sulfate with a US label; timing unknown

name: BIO4 viable bone matrix
company: Stryker (manufactured by Osiris Therapeutics, a Smith+Nephew company)
ownership_history: Osiris Therapeutics developed the viable bone matrix (marketed earlier as OvationOS). Osiris announced an exclusive worldwide commercialization agreement with Stryker in December 2014 (Osiris manufactures and does research; Stryker markets); Stryker launched BIO4 at AAOS in March 2015. Smith+Nephew completed its acquisition of Osiris on 2019-04-17, so a Stryker competitor's subsidiary manufactures BIO4. Stryker's US spine and trauma/foot-and-ankle BIO4 pages, checked 2026-10-22, still state 'BIO4 is manufactured by Osiris Therapeutics, Inc.'; Smith+Nephew's FY2025 Form 20-F does not discuss BIO4 or the Stryker agreement, and the agreement's current term and renewal terms are not public.
composition: Viable bone matrix containing endogenous bone-forming cells, cancellous bone and demineralized bone; 1-10 cc sizes

regulatory.reference: Section 361 HCT/P (21 CFR 1271)
on_label_indications: Bone void filler for voids or gaps not intrinsic to the stability of the bony structure (361 homologous use)

applications.evidence_summary: Single-center 1-2 level ACDF study with BIO4 in an allograft spacer (NCT03077204, Seton Healthcare, n=20) completed 2020; publication not retrieved. A 2021 systematic review listed one ongoing BIO4 trial and no published BIO4 spine series.
applications.caveats: Weakest published evidence among the major cellular allografts.

applications.evidence_summary: Stryker's Trauma & Extremities page links a 'BIO4: high-energy pilon fractures' case resource; no peer-reviewed foot/ankle study was found.
applications.caveats: Marketing case material only.

applications.evidence_summary: No published foot/ankle series found in PubMed searches for this sweep.
applications.caveats: Evidence gap.

evidence.title: Clinical and radiographic outcomes of BIO4 bone matrix in 1 or 2-level ACDF
evidence.finding: Completed January 2020; no results posted.

bd.reimbursement: Bundled in fusion MS-DRGs.
bd.notes: Stryker direct spine and trauma reps; supply dependency on a Smith+Nephew subsidiary is a structural oddity worth asking about in any Stryker biologics conversation. Confirmed 2026-10-22: Stryker still lists BIO4 on its US spine and trauma pages with Osiris named as manufacturer; terms of the Stryker-Osiris agreement after the Smith+Nephew deal are not in any public filing found.

challenge: BIO4 is listed as a current Stryker bone grafting product on stryker.com (2026-10-22), which supports the Stryker-Osiris arrangement continuing; the contract itself was not seen.
catalog_status_2026: Stryker's US trauma-and-extremities bone grafting catalog page (read 2026-10-22) lists AlloFiber, AlloMatrix, Augment, BIO4, DBM, FusionFlex, HydroSet XT, Ignite, OsteoSet, Pro-Dense, Pro-Dense LoVisc, Pro-Stim, Tensix, Vitoss, Vitoss BA, Vitoss BA2X and Vitoss BBTrauma as current products.

name: OSTEOAMP / OSTEOAMP SELECT Fibers / OSTEOAMP Flowable
ownership_history: Developed by Advanced Biologics LLC; Bioventus acquired the OsteoAMP product line, IP and commercial business in October 2014. Still a Bioventus Surgical Solutions product in the FY2024 10-K (no divestiture).
composition: Allograft bone processed to retain endogenous growth factors (BMP-2, BMP-7, VEGF, TGF-beta per company claims) in fibers, putty, sponge, granule and flowable (cannula-delivered, 2024) formats; donor bone from AATB-accredited, FDA-registered US tissue banks

regulatory.reference: No 510(k) for OsteoAMP in openFDA (device_name OSTEOAMP: no matches). The only Bioventus 510(k) tied to it is K233368 'Allograft Delivery Device (OFAC-C)' (2024-06-25, product code FMF), which clears the cannula for delivering hydrated allograft, not the allograft itself. Bioventus FY2025 10-K: allograft from AATB-certified, FDA-registered US tissue banks; sold only in the US.
on_label_indications: Bone void filler for voids or gaps not intrinsic to the stability of the bony structure (361 homologous use)

applications.evidence_summary: Bioventus registered an intra-patient RCT of OSTEOAMP SELECT Fibers vs Infuse in lumbar fusion (NCT05405374, n=101, 9 sites, started 2022, status unknown as of this review); no peer-reviewed spine fusion outcome paper retrieved.
applications.caveats: Evidence gap; the Infuse-comparator design, if completed, would be the strongest cellular/allograft dataset.

applications.evidence_summary: No foot/ankle clinical data found; published comparison is TLIF/PLIF vs rhBMP-2 (PMID 38759243). A 2026 rat muscle-pouch study found OsteoAMP failed to form bone histologically (PMID 42774656, from a competitor-affiliated group).
applications.caveats: Classification as 'cellular-allograft' is for atlas grouping; it is a growth-factor-retaining allograft without viable cells. The growth-factor claim is contested in the independent preclinical literature.

evidence.title: OSTEOAMP SELECT Fibers vs Infuse as autograft substitute in lumbar fusion: prospective randomized intra-patient controlled multicenter investigation
evidence.finding: Status unknown; primary completion was planned October 2024.

evidence.title: Comparison of TLIF and PLIF outcomes in patients receiving a novel allograft versus rhBMP-2
evidence.finding: Spine interbody comparison of OsteoAMP vs rhBMP-2; not foot/ankle.

evidence.title: A novel growth factor bioavailability-enhanced allograft for use in craniomaxillofacial bone regeneration
evidence.finding: Athymic rat muscle pouch: OsteoAMP, OsteoFactor and i-FACTOR failed to form bone; cellular allografts formed bone inconsistently.

bd.reimbursement: Bundled in fusion MS-DRGs.
bd.notes: Bioventus direct Surgical Solutions reps plus an indirect team; two issued US patents expire 2029. K233368 (2024-06-25) clears only the cannula-based Allograft Delivery Device used with OsteoAMP Flowable; do not describe OsteoAMP as 510(k)-cleared.

challenge: OsteoAMP itself is a 361 HCT/P with no premarket review; Bioventus's 2024 'FDA approval' of the cannula delivery system is the K233368 510(k) for the delivery device only.

name: OsteoVive Plus viable bone allograft
ownership_history: Xtant Medical (Belgrade, MT; formerly Bacterin); Xtant acquired Surgalign's biologics assets (2023) and the nanOss production line from RTI, and sells OsteoSponge, OsteoSelect DBM, 3Demin fibers and OsteoVive Plus.
composition: Viable cell-containing cancellous bone with demineralized bone (Xtant describes OsteoVive Plus as a viable bone allograft)

regulatory.reference: No 510(k) for OsteoVive in openFDA (device_name OSTEOVIVE: no matches). Xtant FY2025 10-K (filed 2026-03-31) describes OsteoVive Plus as a viable bone allograft introduced in 2024 and carries a disease-transmission risk factor for it; 361 HCT/P status is inferred from the 10-K's statement that Xtant's products are HCT/Ps, 510(k)-cleared, or both
on_label_indications: Bone void filler for voids or gaps not intrinsic to the stability of the bony structure (361 homologous use)

applications.evidence_summary: No clinical study retrieved.
applications.caveats: Evidence gap.

bd.reimbursement: Bundled in fusion MS-DRGs; Xtant holds biologics contracts with Vizient, Premier and HealthTrust.
bd.notes: Over 670 independent commissioned sales agents and stocking distributors (10-K FY2024); growing private-label/OEM business, including supplying SimpliGraft and SimpliMax under distributor brands. Representative of the small-cap tissue-based spine biologics tier.

name: Osteocel Plus / Osteocel Pro cellular allograft
ownership_history: Developed by Osiris Therapeutics (Osteocel, 2005); NuVasive acquired the Osteocel business from Osiris in 2008 and launched Osteocel Plus (2009) and Osteocel Pro; Globus Medical completed its merger with NuVasive on 2023-09-01. Globus's FY2025 10-K names Osteocel Plus and Osteocel Pro as its allograft cellular lines, processed in San Antonio, TX and Audubon, PA.
composition: Cancellous bone with retained viable mesenchymal stem and osteoprogenitor cells combined with demineralized bone matrix; Pro is a next-generation formulation with higher cell viability claims

regulatory.reference: Section 361 HCT/P (21 CFR 1271); Globus is FDA-registered and state-licensed as a tissue processor; No Osteocel 510(k)/PMA in openFDA (device_name OSTEOCEL: no matches); Globus FY2025 10-K treats Osteocel Plus and Pro as allograft tissue implants supplied by tissue banks (361 HCT/P status inferred)
on_label_indications: Bone void filler for voids or gaps that are not intrinsic to the stability of the bony structure (361 homologous use)

applications.evidence_summary: NuVasive-sponsored prospective multicenter cohort (Eastlack 2014, NCT00942045, n=182, 249 levels): 92% of single-level and 87% of combined 1-2 level segments showed solid bridging at 24 months; no revision for pseudarthrosis.
applications.caveats: Nonrandomized, sponsor-funded; largest cellular allograft dataset in ACDF.

applications.evidence_summary: Retrospective MIS-TLIF series (Ammerman 2012, n=23): 91.3% fusion at 12 months; NuVasive TLIF (NCT00947583, n=19) and PLIF (NCT00941980, n=28) cohorts completed 2012.
applications.caveats: Small, single-surgeon.

applications.evidence_summary: Osteocel Plus was NuVasive's house biologic for XLIF; a 104-patient multicenter XLIF cohort (NCT00948532) completed 2012 and a 51-patient ALIF cohort (NCT00948831).
applications.caveats: Publications for the XLIF/ALIF cohorts not retrieved here.

applications.evidence_summary: No trauma data; all published evidence is spinal fusion.
applications.caveats: Same FDA constraints as Trinity.

applications.evidence_summary: No foot or ankle clinical study found; the product's published evidence is spine (single-level ACDF multi-institutional pseudarthrosis analysis, PMID 34062497).
applications.caveats: Spine-focused franchise; foot/ankle use is extrapolation.

applications.evidence_summary: Spine-positioned product; included only because Globus/NuVasive trauma reps can access it. No upper-extremity data.
applications.caveats: No evidence.

applications.evidence_summary: Single-site blinded RCT (Whitt 2020, 11 subjects, 18 sinuses): Osteocel Plus gave a higher vital bone percentage than conventional corticocancellous allograft at posterior sinus sites at 14 weeks; no difference anteriorly.
applications.caveats: Tiny split-mouth trial, histologic surrogate; 361 tissue used in dentistry on homologous-use grounds; CMS and commercial payers call cellular allografts investigational in spine, and dental use is private pay.

evidence.title: Osteocel Plus cellular allograft in ACDF: clinical and radiographic outcomes from a prospective multicenter study
evidence.finding: Solid bridging in 92% of single-level and 87% of all levels at 24 months; 93% patient satisfaction.

evidence.title: The role of Osteocel Plus as a fusion substrate in minimally invasive instrumented TLIF
evidence.finding: 91.3% of patients and 92.3% of levels fused by 12 months.

evidence.title: Osteocel Plus in XLIF: evaluation of radiographic and patient outcomes
evidence.finding: Completed 2012; 13 sites.

evidence.title: Pseudarthrosis rate following anterior cervical discectomy with fusion using an allograft cellular bone matrix: a multi-institutional analysis
evidence.finding: Multi-institutional ACDF series with Osteocel; spine only.

evidence.title: Efficacy of stem cell allograft in maxillary sinus bone regeneration: randomized controlled clinical and blinded histomorphometric study
evidence.finding: Osteocel Plus produced significantly more vital bone than alloOss allograft at posterior grafted sites (p=0.03) in 18 sinuses; no anterior difference.

bd.reimbursement: Bundled in fusion MS-DRGs; payer policies list Osteocel as investigational for spine fusion.
bd.notes: Globus sells primarily through an exclusive global sales force, with some US reps employed by exclusive independent distributors; Globus relies on several tissue banks for allograft supply and processes Osteocel in-house (former NuVasive facilities).

name: Trinity ELITE / Trinity Evolution viable cellular bone allograft
ownership_history: Trinity Evolution launched 2009 (Orthofix/MTF); Trinity ELITE (moldable) 2014; Orthofix holds exclusive worldwide marketing rights and MTF processes, holds inventory and invoices customers, paying Orthofix a marketing service fee ($51.7 million in 2024, ~31% of Orthofix Biologics revenue). The May 2022 renewal runs through 2032. Orthofix and SeaSpine completed their all-stock merger effective 2023-01-05 (SeaSpine survives as an Orthofix subsidiary).
composition: Cryopreserved cancellous bone containing viable mesenchymal stem/osteoprogenitor cells, combined with demineralized cortical bone (ELITE adds demineralized fibers for moldability)

regulatory.reference: Regulated solely under Section 361 PHS Act / 21 CFR 1271 (no premarket review); homologous use as a bone void filler
on_label_indications: Bone void filler for voids or gaps that are not intrinsic to the stability of the bony structure (361 HCT/P homologous-use statement)

applications.evidence_summary: Prospective multicenter single-arm studies (NCT00951938): single-level ACDF with Trinity Evolution in a PEEK cage fused 93.5% at 12 months (Vanichkachorn 2016, n=31); two-level ACDF fused 89.4% per subject at 12 months (Peppers 2017, n=40).
applications.caveats: Orthofix-funded, single-arm with historical comparison; a 2021 systematic review found no comparative multicenter trial of any cellular bone matrix free of industry conflicts.

applications.evidence_summary: Orthofix PLIF/TLIF cohort (NCT00965380, n=207) completed 2014; a 300-patient Trinity ELITE lumbar post-market study (NCT02969616) has unknown status. Trinity ELITE is the comparator in Kuros's MagnetOs Flex Matrix PLF RCT (NCT05037968).
applications.caveats: Lumbar results not retrieved as a publication in this sweep.

applications.evidence_summary: Rat PLF model ranked Trinity ELITE highest among cellular matrices (8/15 fused vs 0/15 Osteocel Pro, 2/15 ViviGen; Lin 2020); human PLF comparative data pending NCT05037968.
applications.caveats: Animal data; payer policies (e.g., Blue Cross FEP 8.01.52) list Trinity, Osteocel and ViviGen as investigational for spine fusion.

applications.evidence_summary: PubMed search for Trinity/ViviGen/Osteocel in fracture, nonunion or trauma returned no relevant clinical studies; the evidence base is spine (and some foot-and-ankle fusion). FDA position: a 361 HCT/P may not be marketed with osteoinductive or cell-potency claims, and nonunion use is a homologous-use argument at best.
applications.caveats: Price per cc is the highest in the trauma graft set with no trauma data; the 'viable cells' claim is unproven in fracture healing. Treated as investigational for trauma per the atlas rules.
applications.challenge: A trauma biologics manager will ask for one nonunion study; there is none.

applications.evidence_summary: Jones 2015 (FAI; PMID 25976919; NCT00988338): prospective, multicenter, open-label, single-arm trial of Trinity Evolution in 92 patients (153 joints) with foot and/or ankle arthrodesis; fusion at 12 months 71.1% of patients and 86.8% of joints, with no CBA-attributed adverse events.
applications.caveats: Orthofix-funded with Orthofix employees as authors; predecessor product; no control arm, so the 'comparable to autograft' claim is against historical rates; 16 of 92 patients lost by 12 months.

applications.evidence_summary: Same single-arm trial (PMID 25976919) included subtalar, talonavicular, calcaneocuboid, double and triple fusions.
applications.caveats: As above.

applications.evidence_summary: Donaghue 2024 (PMID 38562146): single-site retrospective series of 22 patients (29 joints) with at least one nonunion risk factor fused with Trinity ELITE; 95% fusion at 12 months.
applications.caveats: Single author, single site, 22 patients, no comparator; cited by Orthofix marketing.

applications.evidence_summary: Marketed into nonunion revision as an autograft replacement; the company's cited studies are all spine (cervical and lumbar fusion). No upper-extremity clinical data found.
applications.caveats: FDA position: a 361 HCT/P may not be labeled or promoted with osteoinductive/osteogenic claims that imply more than minimal manipulation and homologous use; the cell-count claims are manufacturer specifications, not clinical outcomes.

applications.evidence_summary: No evidence; usage anecdotal.
applications.caveats: As above.

applications.evidence_summary: No dental or maxillofacial clinical study of Trinity Elite located on PubMed as of 2026-10-22; Orthofix positions it for general bone grafting and does not market a dental program.
applications.caveats: Listed for completeness; the cellular allograft dental evidence is the Osteocel Plus pilot RCT.

evidence.title: Prospective 12-month outcome study of single-level ACDF using Trinity Evolution with comparison to historical controls
evidence.finding: Fusion 78.6% at 6 months, 93.5% at 12 months; no graft-related serious AEs.

evidence.title: Prospective evaluation of Trinity Evolution in two-level ACDF
evidence.finding: Per-subject fusion 89.4%, per-level 93.4% at 12 months; no revisions.

evidence.title: Existing clinical evidence on the use of cellular bone matrix grafts in spinal fusion: updated systematic review
evidence.finding: 12 studies of 6 products (Osteocel n=354, Trinity n=114, ViviGen n=171, map3 n=41, VIA Graft n=75) all reported 87-100% fusion but were single-center/noncomparative; 7 disclosed industry COI; insufficient evidence to recommend CBMs over cheaper materials.

evidence.title: Prospective, multicenter evaluation of allogeneic bone matrix containing viable osteogenic cells in foot and/or ankle arthrodesis
evidence.finding: 12-month fusion 71.1% per patient and 86.8% per joint with Trinity Evolution; high-risk subgroups fused at similar rates.

evidence.title: Trinity Evolution Matrix in subjects undergoing foot and ankle fusion
evidence.finding: Registry record for the Jones 2015 study; completed January 2013, 10 sites.

evidence.title: Radiographical outcomes of a cellular based allograft following foot/ankle arthrodesis in patients with risk for non-union
evidence.finding: 21 of 22 patients fused by 12 months with Trinity ELITE as the primary graft.

bd.reimbursement: Bundled in fusion MS-DRGs; +20930 bundled; many commercial payers deem cellular allografts for spine fusion investigational, which can trigger denials when itemized.
bd.notes: Orthofix books marketing-service fees rather than product revenue; MTF is single-source for Trinity and FiberFuse (10-K risk factor). Orthofix distributes biologics globally through distributors and sales representatives; the 2025 Trinity ELITE 'full market release' refers to a relaunch of updated formulations.

name: ViviGen / ViviGen Formable / ViviGen MIS cellular bone matrix
company: LifeNet Health (processor/owner); DePuy Synthes (exclusive worldwide marketer)
ownership_history: Processed and owned by LifeNet Health (Virginia Beach, VA nonprofit tissue bank); LifeNet's own page calls it 'a 361 Human Cells, Tissues, and Cellular-based Product'. DePuy Synthes holds an exclusive worldwide agreement to market and promote ViviGen (launched late 2014, full US release January 2015) and ViviGen Formable (2017), per OrthoWorld/Becker's; J&J MedTech still lists 'ViviGen Cellular Bone Matrix' as a DePuy Synthes product in 2026 (the page carries no IFU or processor statement). Terms of the agreement are not public.
composition: Cryopreserved viable lineage-committed bone cells within corticocancellous bone matrix plus demineralized bone; Formable adds a moldable DBM fiber component

regulatory.reference: No premarket number; LifeNet states ViviGen is a 361 HCT/P (21 CFR 1271)
on_label_indications: Bone void filler / repair or reconstruction of musculoskeletal defects (361 homologous use; voids not intrinsic to the stability of the bony structure)

applications.evidence_summary: Matched retrospective cohort (Zakko 2023, n=68): no difference in fusion or PROMs between ViviGen and DBM in 1-4 level ACDF; DePuy's 100-patient 2-3 level ACDF cohort (NCT02814825) completed 2021 (publication not retrieved).
applications.caveats: Only comparative data show equivalence to a much cheaper DBM.

applications.evidence_summary: Investigator-initiated RCT vs local autograft in PLF (NCT03733626, Corewell Health, n=46) completed 2024, results not yet published; an Ohio State single-arm PLF study (NCT04007094) was terminated; a Swiss RCT vs rhBMP-2 in ALIF/XLIF (NCT05238740, n=168) is recruiting to 2032.
applications.caveats: Rat PLF model: ViviGen 2/15 fused vs Trinity ELITE 8/15 (Lin 2020).

applications.evidence_summary: No trauma or nonunion clinical evidence found; spine case series only.
applications.caveats: Same FDA constraints as Trinity.

applications.evidence_summary: LifeNet cites Moran, Sequeira and Park (Foot Ankle Specialist 2020), a retrospective review of foot and ankle arthrodesis and ORIF augmented with ViviGen, and Roukis 2020 comparing ViviGen with Trinity in foot/ankle arthrodesis; neither was retrieved with a PMID in this sweep.
applications.caveats: Small retrospective series from authors featured on the manufacturer's site; the strongest independent data are in spine (prospective 20-patient intrapatient PLF comparison, PMID 39667224, and ACDF series).

applications.evidence_summary: Case series only (Roukis and Samsell 2018 ankle/hindfoot arthrodesis; salvage of failed ankle arthroplasty case report).
applications.caveats: No comparator; no foot/ankle prospective trial found.

applications.evidence_summary: LifeNet is running a 250-patient prospective registry of ViviGen in fracture care including nonunion and arm fractures (NCT04299022, primary endpoint reintervention, completion 2028). Published data are spine fusion (96-patient and multilevel series) and foot/ankle; the company page itself says further study vs autograft is needed.
applications.caveats: No upper-extremity outcomes published; registry is sponsor-run.

evidence.title: ACDFs supplemented with cellular or noncellular allografts have similar radiographic fusion and clinical outcomes
evidence.finding: No difference in fusion at any time point; no revisions for pseudarthrosis in either group.

evidence.title: Clinical outcomes with ViviGen in conjunction with posterolateral fusion for lumbar DDD (vs local autograft)
evidence.finding: Completed June 2024; results pending.

evidence.title: ALIF and XLIF with rhBMP-2 vs ViviGen: prospective randomised assessor-blind monocentric trial (Lindenhofgruppe)
evidence.finding: Recruiting; primary completion 2032.

evidence.title: A prospective evaluation of cellular bone matrix for posterolateral lumbar fusion
evidence.finding: Intrapatient ViviGen vs autograft in PLF: grade A fusion 62% vs 44% (p=0.056) at 12 months; spine, not foot/ankle.

evidence.title: Characterization of an advanced viable bone allograft with preserved native bone-forming cells
evidence.finding: Bench characterization of lineage-committed cell content; industry-authored.

evidence.title: Safety, efficacy and use of ViviGen cellular bone matrix allograft in orthopaedic fracture care: multi-center prospective registry
evidence.finding: Recruiting; conditions include nonunion, open fractures and arm fractures; primary completion July 2028.

evidence.title: Lumbar spine fusion outcomes using a cellular bone allograft with lineage-committed bone-forming cells in 96 patients
evidence.finding: Spine reference series cited by the company; not upper extremity.

bd.reimbursement: Bundled in fusion MS-DRGs; listed as investigational by several payers.
bd.notes: LifeNet Health processes and owns the tissue; DePuy Synthes markets through its direct spine force. LifeNet also sells its own branded grafts (e.g., Optium DBM), so the OEM supplier competes with its distributor in some accounts. LifeNet (processor, also sells its own Optium DBM) and DePuy Synthes (exclusive marketer) are separate companies; Optium is not part of the DePuy channel.

name: Autologous bone flap banking (cryopreservation or subcutaneous abdominal pocket): the cranioplasty benchmark, not a product
company: n/a (hospital tissue storage; some centers use AATB-accredited tissue banks for flap storage)
composition: The patient's own craniectomy flap stored at minus 20 to minus 80 C or in a subcutaneous abdominal pocket and reimplanted weeks to months later

regulatory.reference: Not a regulated product; FDA 361 tissue rules do not apply to autologous use within the same institution

applications.evidence_summary: Meta-analysis of 1 RCT and 11 cohorts (1,586 implants): autologous flaps had 1.91 times the reoperation odds of synthetic implants, driven by resorption (20 percent pooled) and infection, with no difference in infection alone; network meta-analysis of 30 studies found resorption only in autologous bone (15.1 percent) and no other complication difference once resorption is excluded. Storage method does not matter: 48 studies and 5,346 patients show infection 7.3 versus 7.1 percent and resorption 9.7 versus 7.7 percent for cryopreserved versus subcutaneous flaps; a 2026 meta-analysis of 7 comparative studies (811 patients) agrees.
applications.caveats: Pediatric banked flaps resorb in about 40 percent and fail in 40 percent, which is why children get fresh bone or custom implants. The economic case for custom implants rests on avoiding the 15 to 20 percent resorption reoperation.

evidence.title: Autologous cranioplasty is associated with increased reoperation rate: systematic review and meta-analysis
evidence.finding: Autologous implants had more reoperations than synthetic (OR 1.91, 95 percent CI 1.40 to 2.61); 54 percent of reoperations for resorption, 41 percent for infection; pooled resorption 20 percent; no difference in infection (OR 1.24).

evidence.title: Complications and cosmetic outcomes of materials used in cranioplasty following decompressive craniectomy: network meta-analysis
evidence.finding: 30 studies: overall complications higher for autologous bone than alloplasts (RR 1.56), hydroxyapatite (RR 2.60), PMMA (RR 1.50) and titanium (RR 1.56); resorption 15.1 percent in autologous bone and 0 in alloplasts; no difference once resorption excluded.

evidence.title: Complications after in vivo and ex vivo autologous bone flap storage for cranioplasty
evidence.finding: 48 studies: cryopreserved versus subcutaneous flaps showed infection 7.3 versus 7.1 percent, revision 15.9 versus 7.6 percent and resorption 9.7 versus 7.7 percent, none significant.

evidence.title: Biological and clinical implications of autologous bone flap preservation strategies after decompressive craniectomy: systematic review and meta-analysis
evidence.finding: Seven studies (337 subcutaneous, 474 cryogenic) with GRADE-rated outcomes for infection, revision and resorption and a UK NHS cost analysis built on randomized revision rates.

evidence.title: Optimal timing of cranioplasty after craniectomy: systematic review and meta-analysis
evidence.finding: 55 studies: cranioplasty within 100 days improved Barthel and FIM scores versus delayed cranioplasty; ultra-early (30 to 45 days) reduced bone flap resorption; no increase in complications; material did not change the effect.

evidence.title: Outcomes and complications of pediatric cranioplasty: systematic review
evidence.finding: Banked bone flaps in children had 51 percent overall complications, 39.7 percent resorption and 40.2 percent failure; fresh bone and titanium had the lowest infection (0.4 and 3.3 percent); PEEK had the highest infection (16.1 percent).

evidence.title: The role of autologous bone in cranioplasty: systematic review of complications and risk factors by using stored bone
evidence.finding: 132 studies, 13,592 patients and 14,960 implants; a third of studies had under three months of follow-up and 19 to 30 percent did not report complication management, so published rates understate failure.

bd.reimbursement: CPT 62143 (replacement of bone flap or prosthetic plate) and 62140, 62141; MS-DRG 025 to 027; the cost of flap storage is hospital overhead.
bd.notes: Benchmark for every cranial biologic and implant claim; the 15 to 20 percent resorption reoperation is the number custom-implant makers sell against.

name: EXOGEN (LIPUS) and PEMF bone growth stimulators (adjacent, not biologics)
company: Bioventus (EXOGEN); Orthofix (AccelStim LIPUS, PhysioStim PEMF); Zimmer Biomet (EBI/OrthoPak); DJO/Enovis (CMF)
ownership_history: EXOGEN: Exogen Inc (1994 PMA) acquired by Smith & Nephew (1999), spun into Bioventus (2012); Bioventus IPO 2021. AccelStim: Orthofix 2023. PEMF devices date to the 1979 EBI PMA.
composition: Non-invasive external devices: low-intensity pulsed ultrasound (1.5 MHz, 30 mW/cm2, 20 min/day) or pulsed electromagnetic fields; no implant, no biologic

regulatory.reference: EXOGEN P900009 (approved 1994-10-05, 'Sonic Accelerated Fracture Healing System', 44 supplements; 2020 labeling update added adjunct use in nonunion with hardware, infection or poor bone quality)
on_label_indications: EXOGEN: non-invasive treatment of established nonunions excluding skull and vertebra

EXOGEN: accelerating healing of fresh, closed, posteriorly displaced distal radius fractures and fresh, closed or Grade I open tibial diaphysis fractures managed by closed reduction and cast immobilization in skeletally mature individuals

applications.evidence_summary: One-paragraph adjacent note. The TRUST trial (BMJ 2016, n=501, 43 North American centers, sham-controlled) found LIPUS did not accelerate radiographic healing or functional recovery after IM nailing of tibial fractures; a 2014 meta-analysis of 13 RCTs (737 patients) found no reduction in nonunion with PEMF or LIPUS in acute fractures. The PMA fresh-fracture indication is limited to cast-managed fractures and predates TRUST. Stimulators are not biologics and do not compete for the surgeon's graft decision, but they do compete for the nonunion-prevention budget and are the only nonunion product class with a dedicated HCPCS/DME payment.
applications.caveats: Negative Level I data for the operatively treated tibia; nonunion indication rests on older uncontrolled PMA data; industry-funded registries dominate the rest.
applications.challenge: TRUST is the trial a hiring manager will cite; the rep must know it and the 2020 label change.

applications.evidence_summary: Nonunion indication (established nonunion, excluding skull and vertebra) is based on self-controlled PMA series; no RCT against surgery.
applications.caveats: Uncontrolled evidence.

evidence.title: Re-evaluation of low intensity pulsed ultrasound in treatment of tibial fractures (TRUST): randomized clinical trial
evidence.finding: Sham-controlled, blinded, 43 centers; LIPUS did not improve radiographic healing or SF-36 physical component after operatively managed tibial fractures.

evidence.title: Effects of LIPUS and PEMF bone growth stimulation in acute fractures: systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs
evidence.finding: 13 trials; no significant difference in proportion of nonunion between PEMF/LIPUS and control.

bd.reimbursement: Durable medical equipment: HCPCS E0760 (ultrasound osteogenesis stimulator) and E0747 (electrical, non-spinal); Medicare NCD 150.2 covers LIPUS for nonunion with documented failure to progress on serial radiographs over at least 3 months (criteria to be re-verified); Orthofix 10-K notes bone growth therapy devices are exempt from DMEPOS competitive bidding and that CMS has considered prior authorization.
bd.notes: Adjacent-only record per the atlas brief. Sales model is DME prescription and prior-authorization support, a different channel from the operating room.
