evidence.finding: Wharton's jelly products fail minimal manipulation and homologous use; marketed for orthopedic procedures, bone spurs and non-union fractures.

evidence.title: FDA Warning Letter to Dynamic Stem Cell Therapy (CBER 25-712579)
evidence.finding: Umbilical-cord product marketed for sports injuries, arthritis and joint pain; misbranded drug, unlicensed biologic, fails 1271.10(a).

pipeline.expected_milestone: None; legitimate allogeneic cord-derived MSC products (e.g., Korean Cartistem for cartilage) have not entered US pivotal trials for bone.

bd.reimbursement: None; cash-pay.
bd.notes: Compliance red flag for any orthopedic distributor; FDA treats the distributor as a manufacturer when it labels or approves product (R3 letter: Regen Suppliers subject to CGMP under 21 CFR 210.3(b)(12)).

name: Amniotic and placental tissue products (dHACM injectables, amnion sheets and tendon wraps; e.g., MiMedx AmnioFix/EpiFix, Organogenesis, Integra and others)
company: Multiple (MiMedx, Organogenesis, Integra, Smith+Nephew, BioTissue and many tissue banks)
ownership_history: Fragmented; MiMedx is the largest US amnion processor.
composition: Dehydrated or cryopreserved human amnion/chorion membrane, as sheets (wraps/barriers) or micronized powder reconstituted for injection; some products are flowable amniotic fluid or umbilical-cord derived

regulatory.reference: Sheet forms used as a covering or barrier are regulated as 361 HCT/Ps when minimally manipulated and homologous. Micronized or injectable forms used to treat tendinopathy, fasciitis or arthritis do not meet the 361 criteria and require a BLA; FDA's enforcement-discretion period for such products ended 2021-05-31, and MiMedx stated that AmnioFix Injectable, EpiFix Micronized and AmnioFill were affected while its sheet products were not.
on_label_indications: Sheet products: homologous use as a wound covering or barrier (no FDA-reviewed therapeutic indication)
Injectable/micronized products for plantar fasciitis or tendinopathy: no FDA approval; investigational (IND/BLA) only after 2021

applications.evidence_summary: Plantar fasciitis injection, not bone healing: Cazzell 2018 (PMID 30058377) 14-site RCT, 145 patients, single micronized dHACM injection vs saline; VAS fell 76% vs 45% at 3 months (p<0.0001). Zelen 2013 (PMID 23945520) 45-patient RCT positive at 8 weeks; Hanselman 2014 (PMID 25249320) cryopreserved amnion vs corticosteroid, 23 patients, mostly no difference. Network meta-analysis of 22 injection RCTs (PMID 27143138) found dHACM superior to corticosteroid only in the short term with no data beyond 2 months.
applications.caveats: MiMedx-funded trials with company authors; the injectable products studied are no longer lawfully marketed without a BLA; no evidence for bone healing in the foot. Tendon-wrap use (Achilles, peroneal) rests on case series. Tiered investigational per FDA position.

applications.evidence_summary: No controlled trial of any amniotic product for bone healing, fracture or fusion; orthopedic marketing is for osteoarthritis, tendinopathy, plantar fasciitis and 'inflammation', which FDA treats as non-homologous.
applications.caveats: The wound-care evidence base for 361 amniotic sheets (DFU/VLU) does not transfer to injection or bone indications.

evidence.title: Randomized controlled trial of micronized dehydrated human amnion/chorion membrane (dHACM) injection compared to placebo for the treatment of plantar fasciitis
evidence.finding: 76% VAS reduction vs 45% placebo at 3 months; FFI-R improved 60% vs 40%.

evidence.title: Prospective, randomized, blinded, comparative study of injectable micronized dehydrated amniotic/chorionic membrane allograft for plantar fasciitis
evidence.finding: AOFAS hindfoot score improved 51-53 points with mDHACM vs 13 points with saline at 8 weeks.

evidence.title: Cryopreserved human amniotic membrane injection for plantar fasciitis: a randomized, controlled, double-blind pilot study
evidence.finding: Mostly no difference vs corticosteroid; pilot.

evidence.title: Injection therapies for plantar fasciopathy: a systematic review and network meta-analysis of 22 randomised controlled trials
evidence.finding: Dehydrated amniotic membrane superior to corticosteroid at 0-2 months; no data beyond 2 months.

evidence.title: FDA Warning Letter to Frontier Biologics LLC (CBER 25-686059)
evidence.finding: Amniotic-fluid injectable marketed for osteoarthritis, joint pain and soft-tissue injury is not an HCT/P; amniotic membrane marketed for healing/anti-inflammation fails homologous use; CGMP violations.

evidence.title: FDA Warning Letter to Celularity Inc. (CBER 25-681480)
evidence.finding: Interfyl decellularized placental matrix marketed (via Arthrex) for orthopedic soft-tissue healing fails homologous use; unapproved drug and unlicensed biologic; 483 responses found inadequate.

evidence.title: FDA Warning Letter to BioXtek LLC (CBER 26-715478)
evidence.finding: Amniotic membrane products marketed for wound healing and orthopedic tendon repair fail homologous use (1271.10(a)(2)).

bd.reimbursement: Facility use (wraps in surgery) is packaged with no separate payment. Office injections billed under product-specific Q-codes have been targeted by Medicare contractors with overpayment demands since 2022; Medicare treats non-wound orthopedic amniotic injections as not reasonable and necessary, and CMS's CY2026 physician fee schedule overhauled skin-substitute payment (details not verified in this sweep). Commercial payers largely exclude amniotic injections as experimental.
bd.notes: Sold by wound-care and podiatry reps; the post-2021 market is sheet products for wounds and surgical wraps. Any BD plan treating injectable amnion as an orthopedic product must assume BLA-level development; MiMedx has pursued IND-based trials for its injectable.

pipeline.expected_milestone: None for bone. Adjacent context: CMS CY2026 PFS final rule (Oct 31, 2025) set skin-substitute payment at $127.28/cm2 from Jan 1, 2026, exempting 351-licensed products, after a ~40-fold rise in Medicare spending over five years; this reprices the Q-code economy that funds many amniotic tissue banks.

name: Exosome / extracellular-vesicle / 'secretome' products marketed to orthopedic and pain clinics
company: Numerous; public FDA letters name Kimera Labs (XoGlo, XoGlo Pro), New Life Medical Services (Rexo), R3 Medical / Regen Suppliers (ReBellaXO, ReBellaXOL), Dynamic Stem Cell Therapy (exosome marketing); Invitrx (2022), Evolutionary Biologics (2024) and Chara Biologics (2025) are reported in secondary sources
ownership_history: Not applicable (class record).
composition: Vesicle-containing conditioned media or lyophilized fractions derived from cultured MSCs, amniotic fluid or umbilical cord tissue; FDA has found in at least one case (R3, 2026) that the process 'does not appear to isolate exosomes' at all

regulatory.reference: No FDA-approved exosome product for any indication (FDA Public Safety Notification Dec 6, 2019; Consumer Alert July 22, 2020, updated Apr 9, 2024; Approved CGT Products list as of Sept 17, 2026). Exosomes intended to treat disease are drugs and biologics requiring an IND and BLA; they are not HCT/Ps (no cells or tissue) so the 361 lane is unavailable. Kimera Labs held an IND (26535) but was cited for commercial distribution under it (21 CFR 312.7(b)).

applications.evidence_summary: No human trial of an exosome product for bone healing, fusion or fracture has been published; the field is preclinical (MSC-derived EVs loaded on scaffolds in rodent calvarial and femoral defect models) and reviews through 2026 identify manufacturing standardization, potency assays and dosing as unsolved prerequisites for an IND.
applications.caveats: Commercial 'exosome' injections for joints, discs and tendons are sold without any controlled data; FDA documented serious adverse events (Nebraska, 2019) and sterility failures (Kimera lot with positive sterility test fully distributed).

evidence.title: FDA Public Safety Notification on Exosome Products
evidence.finding: Serious adverse events in Nebraska patients treated with unapproved products marketed as exosomes; 'there are currently no FDA-approved exosome products'.

evidence.title: FDA Warning Letter to Kimera Labs, Inc. (CBER 23-649343)
evidence.finding: XoGlo/XoGlo Pro/Amnio2X are unapproved drugs and unlicensed biologics; ~37,000 vials made under deficient CGMP; closeout June 12, 2026 after the company ceased the products.

evidence.title: FDA Warning Letter to R3 Medical Companies (CBER 26-726330)
evidence.finding: Products marketed as exosomes (ReBellaXO/XOL) made by a process that does not appear to isolate exosomes; umbilical-cord products fail homologous use; CGMP failures; orthopedic claims (arthritis, cartilage repair, tendonitis).

pipeline.expected_milestone: No orthopedic exosome IND with public efficacy data as of Oct 2026.

bd.reimbursement: None; cash-pay. Billing Medicare for these injections has been the basis of fraud prosecutions (secondary reports; not verified here).
bd.notes: A legitimate company cannot touch this category in the US without an IND; any distributor relationship with an exosome supplier is a compliance liability (see Arthrex named as distributor in the Celularity letter for the analogous amniotic case).

name: Gene therapy for bone regeneration (BMP-2/BMP-7/VEGF via adenoviral, AAV or non-viral vectors) - preclinical only
company: Academic groups (e.g., Mayo, UCLA, Pittsburgh, Jerusalem; Kolon TissueGene for cartilage)
ownership_history: Not applicable.
composition: Regional gene therapy: osteogenic transgenes delivered by viral vectors or transduced cells on scaffolds to critical-size defects, fractures or fusion beds

regulatory.reference: No US IND for a bone-healing gene therapy identified; no gene therapy on FDA's approved CGT list is for bone (list current Sept 17, 2026).

applications.evidence_summary: Rodent and large-animal models show adenoviral or cell-based BMP-2 delivery can heal critical-size defects; immunogenicity, dose control and ectopic bone have kept the field preclinical for 25 years.
applications.caveats: One-line record by design; no clinical data.

evidence.title: Constructing Gene-Enhanced Tissue Engineering for Regeneration and Repair of Osteochondral Defects (Adv Biosyst 2019; DOI 10.1002/adbi.201900004)
evidence.finding: Example of adenovirus-vector growth-factor gene delivery combined with scaffolds achieving osteochondral repair in an animal model.

pipeline.expected_milestone: None.

bd.reimbursement: Not applicable.
bd.notes: Placeholder so the app can state plainly that no gene therapy for bone is in US clinical testing.

name: NB1 (rhNELL-1 with DBM)
ownership_history: Bone Biologics Corp (NASDAQ: BBLG), Burlington, MA; exclusive worldwide license from UCLA for NELL-1 in spine fusion, trauma and osteoporosis; historically MTF Biologics was a major shareholder and the DBM carrier partner (not confirmed in sources fetched here).
composition: Recombinant human NEL-like molecule-1 (NELL-1) osteoinductive protein combined with demineralized bone matrix; proposed as a more bone-specific signal than BMP-2 with less ectopic bone and inflammation

regulatory.reference: No US IDE yet; pilot study design reviewed by FDA Division of Orthopedic Devices in a Pre-Submission; pilot run under Australian HREC approval

applications.evidence_summary: NCT03810573: multicenter randomized pilot in up to 30 adults with single-level DDD (L2-S1, up to Grade 1 listhesis) undergoing TLIF in Australia; first two patients treated June 2024; expanded to six Australian sites September 2026 with enrollment targeted to finish by end of 2026; primary endpoints fusion at 12 and 24 months and ODI change; 12-month data expected Q4 2027. Only preclinical efficacy data exist.
applications.caveats: Comparator not specified in public materials; company reports cash runway only through Q2 2027.

evidence.title: Multi-center, prospective, parallel group, randomized pilot study of NB1 bone graft device in DDD patients undergoing TLIF
evidence.finding: Recruiting (Australia); primary completion December 2026.

evidence.title: Nell-1 protein promotes bone formation in a sheep spinal fusion model (Tissue Eng Part A 2011; DOI 10.1089/ten.TEA.2010.0486)
evidence.finding: NELL-1 at 0.3 or 0.6 mg/mL with DBM (n=8/group) or heat-inactivated DBM (n=4/group) increased interbody bone formation vs DBM alone in sheep.

pipeline.expected_milestone: Pilot 12-month data Q4 2027, then US IDE pivotal and PMA (company statements, Sept 2026)

bd.reimbursement: Not applicable.
bd.notes: Micro-cap with a single asset; the 'hard healers' (smokers, diabetics, obese) positioning overlaps directly with PearlMatrix's high-risk subgroup claims.

name: Osteogrow (rhBMP6 in autologous blood coagulum) / Osteogrow-C
ownership_history: Genera Research Ltd (Zagreb, Croatia; Slobodan Vukicevic), EU FP7-funded OSTEOGROW project; a related rhBMP6 product (AGA111, Angitia Biopharmaceuticals) was tested in a US/China TLIF RCT, relationship to Genera unverified.
composition: Recombinant human BMP-6 delivered in an autologous blood coagulum carrier, mixed with cancellous allograft (Osteogrow-A) or synthetic calcium phosphate ceramics (Osteogrow-C)

regulatory.reference: EU clinical trials only: EudraCT 2017-000860-14 (Osteogrow-A, PLIF, 143 randomized in Austria, ended 13 Mar 2023, results posted 11 Feb 2026) and a TLIF trial; no US IDE/IND found
on_label_indications: Investigational: fracture nonunion, HTO gap healing, distal radius fracture, dental (company list)

applications.evidence_summary: Osteogrow-A phase II (EudraCT 2017-000860-14): randomized, double-blind, n=143 at three Austrian centers (62 ICBG standard of care, 61 high-dose 2 mg rhBMP6, 20 low-dose 1 mg) in PLIF for L3-S1 DDD; 20-month composite 'overall clinical success' was very low in every arm, bilateral bridging was observed in only 4-6% of subjects in any arm, and the sponsor concluded the success definition was overly strict; fewer serious AEs with Osteogrow (31.1% HD vs 54.1% SoC); results posted February 2026. A separate 63-patient placebo-controlled rhBMP6 (AGA111) TLIF RCT was presented at AAOS 2025. Earlier Genera trials were in distal radius fracture and high tibial osteotomy.
applications.caveats: The posted PLIF fusion numbers are implausibly low for any arm and should be read from the EU register directly before being quoted; no peer-reviewed spine publication retrieved.

applications.evidence_summary: Preclinical only: rabbit and sheep posterolateral fusion with rhBMP6/ABC plus ceramics (PMID 38086987).
applications.caveats: No human PLF data.

applications.evidence_summary: EU-funded phase I/II in HTO distraction-gap healing and distal radius fractures (CORDIS project page describes plans; peer-reviewed phase II results were not retrieved in this sweep). ClinicalTrials.gov search for OSTEOGROW/rhBMP6 returned nothing.
applications.caveats: Company-reported status only; no registry or FDA footprint found.
applications.challenge: Verify any trial claim against EU CTIS before citing.

applications.evidence_summary: Phase III in nonunion is a stated plan, not a registered trial.
applications.caveats: Unverified.

applications.evidence_summary: Randomized, double-blind Phase 1 (n=32) in closed distal radius fractures treated with K-wires: 250 ug rhBMP6/mL coagulum injected at the fracture accelerated CT/radiographic healing vs placebo coagulum and standard of care at 5 and 9 weeks (p=0.027), with no difference by 13 weeks; no anti-BMP6 antibodies; no serious adverse reactions (Bone 2020).
applications.caveats: Tiny n, short-term radiographic surrogate, sponsor-affiliated authors; effect disappeared by 13 weeks.

evidence.title: Patient- and evaluator-blinded non-inferiority study of Osteogrow in adults undergoing PLIF for degenerative disc disease (Osteogrow-A)
evidence.finding: Non-inferiority claimed on a composite endpoint with very low success in all arms; fewer SAEs with rhBMP6; trial ended March 2023, results posted February 2026.

evidence.title: Calcium phosphate ceramics combined with rhBMP6 within autologous blood coagulum promote posterolateral lumbar fusion in sheep
evidence.finding: Osteogrow-C produced radiographic fusion with complete integration to transverse processes in sheep.

evidence.title: A novel autologous bone graft substitute comprised of rhBMP6 blood coagulum as carrier tested in a randomized and controlled Phase I trial in patients with distal radial fractures (Bone 2020; DOI 10.1016/j.bone.2020.115551)
evidence.finding: Accelerated trabecular healing at 5 and 9 weeks vs placebo and standard of care; equivalent by 13 weeks; good tolerability.

evidence.title: Recombinant Human BMP6 Applied Within Autologous Blood Coagulum Accelerates Bone Healing: Randomized Controlled Trial in High Tibial Osteotomy Patients (J Bone Miner Res 2020; DOI 10.1002/jbmr.4107)
evidence.finding: First placebo-controlled BMP trial on a trabecular bone surface; CT BMD in the wedge defect roughly doubled vs placebo at 9 and 14 weeks.

pipeline.expected_milestone: No US filing announced; next step unclear (company website undated)

bd.reimbursement: Not applicable.
bd.notes: Academic-origin program; the autologous-blood-carrier concept avoids collagen sponge and is pitched as lower-dose, lower-inflammation BMP.

challenge: EU CTR results page read directly on 2026-10-22. As posted: arms Standard of Care n=62 (55 mITT), HD Osteogrow n=61 (56 mITT), LD Osteogrow n=20 (19 mITT); primary 'overall clinical success' at 20 months 1.9% SoC vs 0.2% HD (LD none), difference -1.7 points, one-sided 95% lower limit -5.2 against a -10 margin, reported as non-inferior; radiographic fusion 3.8/5.6% at 6 months, 4.4/6.0% at 12 months, 6.2% SoC vs 4.2% HD at 20 months (difference -2, lower limit -9.5); serious TEAEs 54.1% SoC, 31.1% HD, 25.0% LD; 3 deaths in SoC. These success and fusion proportions are implausibly low for PLIF and almost certainly reflect a unit or data-entry error in the register posting (e.g. fractions mislabeled as percent); the extraction is verified but the numbers should not be quoted as fusion rates without the sponsor's publication.

name: TETRANITE regenerative bone adhesive (cranial flap fixation)
composition: Synthetic, injectable, self-setting calcium phosphate and phosphoserine-based bone adhesive that resorbs and is replaced by bone; derived from sandcastle-worm chemistry (LaunchPad Medical origin)

regulatory.reference: FDA IDE approval December 2023 for a 20-patient pilot of stand-alone cranial flap fixation; NIH NINDS Phase II SBIR $2.4M September 2024; sites Semmes Murphey (Memphis) and Brigham and Women's (Boston)

applications.evidence_summary: First five patients enrolled by September 2024 with company-reported radiographic adhesion and no complications at over three months in the first patient; no peer-reviewed results or NCT number located as of 2026-10-22.
applications.caveats: Company statements only; would replace plates and screws rather than a biologic; a De Novo or PMA is the likely path.

evidence.title: RevBio receives $2.4 million NIH grant for first-in-human trial of regenerative bone adhesive for cranial flap fixation and enrolls first five patients
evidence.finding: 20-patient pilot under an FDA-approved IDE; five enrolled; early radiographs reported as showing continued adhesion of the flap with no complications.

pipeline.expected_milestone: Completion of the 20-patient pilot and a pivotal design; no date published (RevBio press releases 2023 and 2024).

bd.reimbursement: n/a
bd.notes: If it works, it competes with cranial fixation plates (hardware) and with Montage Flowable's registered flap-fixation study, not with void fillers.

name: TG-C (TissueGene-C; Invossa) - adjacent, knee osteoarthritis
company: Kolon TissueGene, Inc. (US subsidiary of Kolon Life Science, Korea)
ownership_history: Invossa-K was approved by Korea's MFDS in 2017 and the license was revoked in 2019 after the second cell component proved to be kidney-derived (GP2-293) rather than chondrocyte-derived; FDA placed the US Phase 3 on clinical hold in May 2019 and lifted it in April 2020, with broader recruitment resuming November 2021 (CGTLive 2026-07-23).
composition: Allogeneic human chondrocytes mixed 3:1 with irradiated, TGF-beta1-transduced cells (GP2-293 derived), single intra-articular injection; a cell-mediated gene therapy

regulatory.reference: US IND; two Phase 3 trials (ACTiVION-I NCT03203330, n=535; ACTiVION-II NCT03291470). Not approved anywhere after the Korean revocation.

challenge: Adjacent (cartilage/OA, not bone); kept as a live example of cell-therapy risk: ACTiVION-II missed its co-primary endpoints on 2026-07-20 (between-group VAS difference 0.5 points, p=0.83).

evidence.title: ACTiVION-II: randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled Phase 3 of TG-C in knee OA
evidence.finding: Missed co-primary endpoints (company release, July 2026, via CGTLive).

evidence.title: ACTiVION-I: Phase 3 of TG-C in KL grade 2-3 knee OA
evidence.finding: Active, not recruiting; 44 sites; primary completion July 2024; topline expected Oct 2026.

pipeline.expected_milestone: ACTiVION-II (NCT03291470) read out 2026-07-20 and missed both co-primary endpoints (VAS and WOMAC at month 12; placebo response high); ACTiVION-I (NCT03203330, n=535) topline was guided for October 2026 and had not been found as of 2026-10-22. A Phase 1 in discogenic back pain (NCT06144970) is registered as not yet recruiting.

bd.reimbursement: None.
bd.notes: Benchmark for the cost of a two-trial US Phase 3 program in a cell therapy; parent company exposure to Korean regulatory and legal history.

name: VIA Disc NP (nucleus pulposus allograft)
ownership_history: VIVEX Biologics (Miami; formerly VIVEX Biomedical). Product earlier marketed as VIA Disc Matrix.
composition: Micronized, processed human nucleus pulposus allograft (with cells, viability not claimed as mechanism) reconstituted with saline and injected intradiscally

regulatory.reference: Marketed on the manufacturer's determination that supplementation of nucleus pulposus tissue is a minimally manipulated, homologous use; no FDA premarket review. ClinicalTrials.gov: ASCEND NCT06615505 (Vivex; n=121 actual; active not recruiting; primary completion 2026-02-06) and a sham-controlled pivotal-size trial NCT06778447 (n=325 estimated; recruiting; primary completion est. 2027-10); the sponsor's regulatory intent (361 versus BLA) is still not public.
on_label_indications: Supplementation of degenerated nucleus pulposus tissue (361 homologous-use positioning; not an FDA-approved indication)

challenge: Trial records re-checked on ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT06615505 active not recruiting, NCT06778447 recruiting). No FDA letter, RFD or BLA statement about VIA Disc NP was found in FDA letters or web search, so the 361-versus-BLA tension remains an open question; the 2018 market year is still secondary-source.

applications.evidence_summary: VAST trial (NCT03709901; 218 enrolled, 13 US sites) randomized 3.5:1:1 to allograft, saline, or nonsurgical management; the published interim report (Beall 2020, n=24) was descriptive and not powered; sponsor-reported 12-month data in the larger cohort showed VAS improvement with no separation from saline until after 3 months. A 2:1 sham-controlled 325-patient trial began Feb 2025.
applications.caveats: Sponsor-funded; published data are a 24-subject interim with 4 placebo patients; full VAST results not peer-reviewed in PubMed at review; VA Office of Community Care review notes conflicts of interest not disclosed in the journal article.

evidence.title: VAST Clinical Trial: Safely Supplementing Tissue Lost to Degenerative Disc Disease (Int J Spine Surg 2020; DOI 10.14444/7033)
evidence.finding: Interim analysis of the first 24 subjects (16 allograft, 4 saline, 4 NSM crossover): VAS fell from 54.8 to 12.3 (allograft) and 55.3 to 19.7 (saline) at 12 months; adverse events transient; not powered for significance.

evidence.title: Randomized, sham-controlled, double-blind trial of nucleus pulposus allograft in lumbar discogenic pain
evidence.finding: Recruiting at 19 sites; started Feb 17, 2025; 2:1 randomization vs sham; primary completion Oct 2027.

evidence.title: ASCEND: randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled Phase I/II of VIA Disc NP
evidence.finding: Active, not recruiting; 5 sites; primary completion Feb 2026; results not posted.

evidence.title: VIA Disc NP Registry 3.0
evidence.finding: Observational registry at 24 sites; primary completion Jan 2027. Prior registry (NCT04652687, n=83) terminated.

pipeline.expected_milestone: Pivotal sham-controlled trial primary completion Oct 2027 (ClinicalTrials.gov); regulatory intent (361 vs BLA) not publicly stated.

bd.reimbursement: Sold today as a 361 tissue through pain-management and spine practices; CPT 0627T-0630T (intradiscal allogeneic disc tissue injection) exist as Category III codes; most commercial payers deem it investigational (e.g., VA review cites non-coverage).
bd.notes: Commercial exposure: if FDA concluded the product fails homologous use, current sales would be of an unlicensed biologic. Regenexx (a competitor) publicly critiques the VAST data.

name: AMPLEX (B2A peptide on HA/beta-TCP granules)
company: Ferring Pharmaceuticals (sponsor of pivotal); originally BioSET Inc
ownership_history: BioSET (Texas) developed the B2A synthetic BMP-2 receptor-targeting peptide; Ferring sponsored the hindfoot/ankle pivotal (NCT03028415) after licensing; commercial status after 2020 completion not public.
composition: Synthetic peptide B2A that augments BMP-2 receptor signaling, coated on hydroxyapatite/beta-TCP ceramic granules

regulatory.reference: Pivotal IDE study NCT03028415 (Ferring; ankle fusion and hindfoot; n=56; completed, primary completion 2020-01-09); no PMA exists: openFDA PMA search for trade name AMPLEX returns nothing and Ferring's only PMAs are Euflexxa (P010029) and Nuxflexxa
on_label_indications: Investigational: supplemental graft in single, double or triple hindfoot or ankle arthrodesis (not trauma)

applications.evidence_summary: Included because the brief asked; AMPLEX has no trauma program. The pivotal (n=56 randomized vs autograft, 38 US/Canada sites, completed July 2020) has results posted on ClinicalTrials.gov but the outcome was not retrieved and no PMA has been announced, which suggests the program stalled.
applications.caveats: No trauma relevance; elective fusion only.

applications.evidence_summary: NCT03028415: multicenter randomized pivotal study of AMPLEX vs autogenous bone graft in hindfoot or ankle arthrodesis, 36 sites, listed enrollment 56, completed January 2020; no results posted and no FDA decision or publication found. Pilot NCT01224119 (24 patients, 2011-2012).
applications.caveats: A 56-patient enrollment at 36 sites suggests the pivotal trial was stopped or under-enrolled; program status unknown.

evidence.title: Multi-center randomized pivotal study evaluating AMPLEX compared to autogenous bone graft in hindfoot or ankle arthrodesis
evidence.finding: Completed; primary endpoint a 5-part composite at 52 weeks; results posted; no publication or PMA found.

evidence.title: Multi-center randomized pilot study evaluating Amplex compared to autograft bone in foot and ankle fusion surgery
evidence.finding: Pilot; status unknown.

pipeline.expected_milestone: Unknown; no public update since 2020.

bd.reimbursement: None.
bd.notes: Peptide-on-ceramic is the same construct class as i-Factor (P-15); that is the comparator a hiring manager will raise.

name: KUR-113 / Fibrin-PTH (TGplPTH1-34 in fibrin)
ownership_history: Originated at Kuros Biosurgery AG (Zurich); Kuros merged with Xpand Biotechnology (2016), later acquired by... (no; Kuros remains independent, SIX: KURN) and now markets MagnetOs synthetic bone graft; Fibrin-PTH was discontinued per the company's FY2023 report (March 13, 2024).
composition: Engineered PTH(1-34) fragment with a transglutaminase substrate and plasmin-cleavable linker, covalently bound into a fibrin matrix applied at the fracture or fusion site

regulatory.reference: US IND for the STRUCTURE Phase 2 TLIF trial NCT04294004 (Kuros Biosurgery AG; n=50 actual; start 2020-08-27; ClinicalTrials.gov status UNKNOWN, last updated 2023-08-09; flagged FDA-regulated drug). Discontinuation after Phase 2 is reported only in the Synapse summary of Kuros releases; no Kuros primary document was retrieved.

applications.evidence_summary: Phase 2 randomized, open-label (dose-blinded) trial in 200 open tibial shaft fractures (NCT00533793; JBJS 2022): 6-month healing 76%, 80% and 69% for low, mid and high dose plus standard of care vs 65% for standard of care alone; the mid-dose met the prespecified primary endpoint.
applications.caveats: Sponsor-funded; open-label; non-monotonic dose response; no Phase 3 followed in fracture.

applications.evidence_summary: STRUCTURE Phase 2 (NCT04294004, n=50, two dose levels vs local autograft in single-level TLIF) completed enrollment July 2023; results were not published and the company elected not to proceed to Phase 3.
applications.caveats: Registry status 'unknown' (last verified Aug 2023); the only public efficacy signal is the company's decision to stop.

evidence.title: Novel Parathyroid Hormone-Based Bone Graft, KUR-113, in Treatment of Acute Open Tibial Shaft Fracture: A Phase-2 Randomized Controlled Trial (J Bone Joint Surg Am 2022; DOI 10.2106/JBJS.20.02109; erratum PMID 35442252)
evidence.finding: Four arms (SoC; SoC + 4 mL KUR-113 at 0.133, 0.4 or 1.0 mg/mL); mid-dose met the primary healing endpoint at 6 months (80% vs 65%).

evidence.title: STRUCTURE: KUR-113 bone graft vs local autograft in single-level TLIF (Phase 2)
evidence.finding: Enrollment completed July 2023 (company); results not posted; program discontinued Dec 2023.

pipeline.expected_milestone: None; discontinued (company FY2023 results, March 2024, as summarized by Synapse; primary Kuros document not retrieved).

bd.reimbursement: Not applicable.
bd.notes: Kuros redeployed capital to MagnetOs (510(k) synthetic), which is now running RCTs vs Trinity Elite (NCT05037968) and vs DBM (NCT04679844). A PTH-in-fibrin asset could be licensed.

challenge: Registry record confirms the Phase 2 (NCT04294004, n=50, status UNKNOWN since 2023). The discontinuation decision still rests on a secondary summary; Kuros IR pages return 403, so the primary document was not read.

name: LDGraft (low-dose encapsulated rhBMP-2)
ownership_history: Locate Bio Ltd (Nottingham, UK), private; raised GBP 9.2 million in April 2024 to fund the RESTORE study; US subsidiary Locate Bio Pty/Inc.
composition: rhBMP-2 pre-encapsulated in a resorbable polymer (dose-shielding microparticles) within a bone graft substitute carrier, designed for sustained 28-day release at doses well below Infuse

regulatory.reference: Breakthrough Device designation May 2023 (single-level ALIF, L3-S1, DDD); FDA IDE approval announced 2025-09-08. ClinicalTrials.gov has two LDGraft records: NCT06462729 (Locate Bio Pty Ltd; Phase 1/2, ALIF, n=40 estimated; IDE-flagged unapproved device; recruiting since 2024-11-12; sites in Newcastle, Australia and Fort Wayne, Nashville and Pinehurst, US; last update 2026-08-26) and NCT07858643 (Locate Bio Ltd; 'AMBITION', n=25, sites in Tbilisi, Georgia; started 2026-04-08). NCT06462729 is the registration that matches the Australia-plus-US IDE study.
on_label_indications: Investigational: single-level ALIF for degenerative disc disease (spine); no trauma indication proposed

applications.evidence_summary: RESTORE (NCT06462729): first-in-human, randomized 3:3:2 dose-finding, single-blind, two LDGraft doses vs 100% allograft in single-level ALIF (L3-S1) with cage and plate; n=40; sites in Australia (Newcastle) and US (Fort Wayne, Pinehurst, Nashville); started November 2024, primary completion December 2027. Preclinical: 120-sheep study reported all three doses equivalent to ICBG at 6 months.
applications.caveats: No human efficacy data; the brief's description of a TLIF/PLF trial was wrong, the trial is ALIF only.

applications.evidence_summary: No trauma program announced; included because a controlled-release BMP-2 would be the natural successor to Infuse in open fractures and nonunion if the spine study succeeds.
applications.caveats: Spine-only development; no trauma data.

evidence.title: A randomized study of LDGraft in single-level ALIF (RESTORE)
evidence.finding: Recruiting; primary endpoints CT fusion, no secondary surgery, ODI 15-point improvement, neuro status and no device-related SAE at 12 and 24 months.

evidence.title: AMBITION: a study of LDGraft in single-level lumbar interbody fusion (Phase 1/2, single group)
evidence.finding: Recruiting; start April 8, 2026; primary completion Oct 2027; two sites in Tbilisi, Georgia; excludes smokers, BMI > 40, osteoporosis.

pipeline.expected_milestone: RESTORE primary completion December 2027; pivotal IDE would follow (company statements)

bd.reimbursement: Not applicable; would be bundled like Infuse if approved.
bd.notes: Positioned as 'Infuse efficacy at a fraction of the dose' to neutralize the YODA safety narrative; small company likely to need a commercial partner.

challenge: Two separate registrations exist; the Australia-plus-US IDE study is NCT06462729. The sponsor's 'RESTORE' name was not seen on either record.

name: Novosis / Novosis Putty (rhBMP-2 bone graft, Korea) - not US-marketed
company: CGBio (Korea); rhBMP-2 manufactured by Daewoong Pharmaceutical
ownership_history: Approved by Korea's MFDS as the country's first rhBMP-2 bone graft (year not confirmed); second-generation Novosis Putty received FDA Breakthrough Device designation in January 2024 (trade press). J&J and CGBIO signed an exclusive Asia-Pacific distribution and promotion deal in February 2025 (Korea, Taiwan, Thailand, India, Hong Kong, Macau; later expanded). On 2026-05-26 DePuy Synthes announced an exclusive distribution agreement with CGBIO for the US, Canada and Australia covering spine, CMF and trauma, with rights of first negotiation for other markets; CGBIO's release (2026-05-27) adds joint clinical development and regulatory steps including FDA IDE and PMA and a steering committee. No financial terms disclosed.
composition: E. coli-derived rhBMP-2 on a hydroxyapatite/calcium phosphate carrier (Novosis) or putty formulation (Novosis Putty)

regulatory.reference: Not cleared or approved in the US; FDA Breakthrough Device designation (Jan 2024, trade press). J&J MedTech's 2026-05-26 release says a US IDE study for spine procedures is approved and 'actively enrolling'; CGBIO's 2026-05-27 release says the IDE study is being prepared with a target start in the second half of 2026. The two statements conflict; no NCT number located.

applications.evidence_summary: Korean clinical data exist (e.g., Korea University publications on efficacy and safety of rhBMP-2) but no US trial; Breakthrough designation does not imply efficacy.
applications.caveats: Non-US product; included as the most credible 'second rhBMP-2' attempt and as a reminder that no rhBMP-2 generic or biosimilar pathway exists for a PMA combination product (Infuse is a device, so the biosimilar statute does not apply).

pipeline.expected_milestone: US spine IDE study (type not stated): J&J says approved and enrolling; CGBIO says start targeted for H2 2026. No PMA submission announced.

bd.reimbursement: Not applicable in US.
bd.notes: A Chinese rhBMP-2 bone repair material (Hangzhou Jiuyuan) is listed as an implanted device registered in China; NMPA details not verified. Neither product can be imported for US clinical use outside an IDE.

challenge: The two companies' releases disagree on whether the US IDE has started enrolling; treat enrollment as unconfirmed until an NCT/IDE listing appears.

name: CERAMENT V (vancomycin-eluting)
composition: Cerament biphasic ceramic premixed with vancomycin; CE-marked in Europe.

regulatory.reference: No US authorization as of 2026-10-22. The submission was moved from 510(k) to the De Novo process on 2025-12-02 (company release); BONESUPPORT's Q3 2026 interim report (2026-10-22) says it submitted the supplemental data package FDA requested under De Novo and the dialogue is 'constructive'. FDA granted Breakthrough Device designation (bone infection). CMS's FY2027 final rule creates a code for vancomycin-eluting bone void fillers effective 2026-10-01 and would assign CERAMENT V to it only if FDA grants De Novo classification. BONESUPPORT's US portfolio page lists only CERAMENT G and CERAMENT Bone Void Filler.
on_label_indications: Proposed: adjunct to systemic antibiotics and debridement in the treatment of bone infection in extremity defects (vancomycin for gram-positive/MRSA coverage); not yet authorized in the US

challenge: Ex-US only today (CE-marked); US De Novo still under review as of 2026-10-22.

applications.evidence_summary: European use in infected nonunion and Masquelet reconstructions (e.g., Lyon cohort NCT03970941, n=8); no US data.
applications.caveats: Not available in the US.

applications.evidence_summary: European use in osteomyelitis, PJI and diabetic foot; UK post-market study of CERAMENT V/G in foot osteomyelitis (NCT06628115, n=25) and Italian revision-arthroplasty study (NCT03389646); no US data.
applications.caveats: Not authorized in the US as of this review; evidence is observational.

evidence.title: Post-market study of CERAMENT V/G in foot osteomyelitis (Mid and South Essex NHS)
evidence.finding: Completed August 2026; results not yet public.

bd.reimbursement: Not applicable in the US.
bd.notes: Relevant only as pipeline for the US; its vancomycin loading targets MRSA where gentamicin resistance limits Cerament G.

pipeline.expected_milestone: FDA De Novo decision pending (no date given; supplemental data package submitted per the 2026-10-22 Q3 report).

ownership_history: CE-marked 2015; FDA Breakthrough Device designation for bone infection; US submission planned as 510(k) with CERAMENT G as predicate (July 2024 announcement), transferred to De Novo in December 2025; complete additional data package submitted 2026-09-21.

name: ALLOB (allogeneic osteoblastic cell therapy) - failed
ownership_history: Bone Therapeutics (Gosselies) developed ALLOB and PREOB; reverse merger with Medsenic created BioSenic (2022); ALLOB Phase IIb in tibial fracture failed (June 2023); company pivoted to oral arsenic trioxide and later licensed/returned ALLOB rights amid a terminated Pregene license (2023).
composition: Allogeneic bone-marrow MSCs differentiated to osteoblastic lineage, cryopreserved, injected percutaneously

regulatory.reference: EU ATMP trials (EudraCT 2018-001054-96); no US IND found
on_label_indications: None; development discontinued

applications.evidence_summary: Phase IIb (n=57 treated) in acute tibial fractures at risk of delayed union gave ALLOB days after injury; it failed to accelerate healing and BioSenic suspended the program (June 2023), concluding MSCs should not be given in the acute inflammatory window. An earlier mid-phase delayed-union study had been positive.
applications.caveats: Negative RCT; informative for anyone proposing early cell therapy in acute fracture.
applications.challenge: Cited as the reason cell therapy in acute trauma is out of favor.

applications.evidence_summary: Phase 2b randomized 1:1 placebo-controlled trial in high-risk tibial fractures (NCT04432389, n=57) showed no acceleration of fracture healing on the primary efficacy endpoint; no treatment-related serious adverse events (BioSenic, June 2023).
applications.caveats: Underpowered after restructuring; endpoint reclassified during the trial (July 2022); results not located in a peer-reviewed journal during this review.

evidence.title: Bone Therapeutics' final asset buried after failure in phase 2 fracture study (Fierce Biotech)
evidence.finding: ALLOB did not accelerate fracture healing in the Phase IIb; safety acceptable; program suspended.

evidence.title: Phase 2b of ALLOB in patients with high-risk tibial fractures
evidence.finding: Negative on the primary efficacy endpoint; sponsor paused development and redirected resources (CGTLive, June 19, 2023).

bd.reimbursement: None.
bd.notes: Case study for diligence: a cell therapy with positive delayed-union signal that failed when moved to acute fracture.

challenge: The assignment brief described this as a failed Phase 3; the trial was a Phase 2b (n=57 analyzed after a mid-study amendment reduced the target from 178 to 132 evaluable). It is the clearest randomized negative result for an allogeneic MSC product in fracture healing and belongs in the atlas as a cautionary comparator.

pipeline.expected_milestone: None announced; development paused June 2023, company has stated it would consider later-timepoint dosing but has no active trial.

name: BoneSource Hydroxyapatite Cement (HAC), Fast Setting and Rapid Setting
company: Stryker (originally Osteogenics; Leibinger; Howmedica Osteonics / Stryker Instruments)
ownership_history: Developed at the American Dental Association Paffenbarger Research Center (Chow and Takagi); cleared to Osteogenics in 1996 and 1997 (K953339, K964537), then Stryker Leibinger (K991398, 1999), Stryker Instruments (K021440 2002, K032366 Fast Setting 2003, K043334 Rapid Setting 2005) and a BoneSource BVF orthopedic version to Howmedica Osteonics (K031435, MQV, 2003). Stryker's current US CMF catalog does not list BoneSource; HydroSet (2006) and DirectInject (2015) appear to have replaced it.
composition: Tetracalcium phosphate and dicalcium phosphate powder mixed with a sodium phosphate solution, setting to carbonated hydroxyapatite

on_label_indications: Self-setting calcium phosphate cement intended for repairing neurosurgical burr holes and cranial defects and for restoring bony contour in the craniofacial skeleton (per the 2002 to 2005 510(k) summaries; no clinical data provided, bench testing only)

challenge: Current US availability could not be confirmed either way: no discontinuation notice was found, but BoneSource is absent from Stryker's CMF product pages and no 510(k) activity since 2005. Treat as legacy; the clinical literature (Friedman, Costantino, Kveton) is the origin of the HA cement evidence base now claimed by HydroSet.

applications.evidence_summary: Friedman 2000 three-center controlled cohort of 40 patients with frontal sinus and frontofacial defects up to 25 cm2: 82 percent successful reconstruction at 24 months and about 5 percent infection-related removal versus historical methyl methacrylate controls; Costantino 2001 sealed 21 of 21 sphenoethmoid CSF leaks.
applications.caveats: Nonrandomized, historical controls, investigator-developed material (ADA Paffenbarger and NIST patents).

applications.evidence_summary: Reinforced BoneSource with tantalum mesh for nine cranioplasties over 25 cm2 (mean 128 cm2): two constructs removed for infection within three months; pediatric series of 78 children (Mimix or BoneSource) with 7 complications and 6 removals.
applications.caveats: Off-label when reinforced above 25 cm2; infection when contiguous with sinus mucosa.

applications.evidence_summary: Secondary contour cranioplasty in 48 patients with fast-setting HAC: five complications including two infections, 38 good results (Magee 2004).
applications.caveats: Single surgeon, no comparator.

evidence.title: Reconstruction of the frontal sinus and frontofacial skeleton with hydroxyapatite cement
evidence.finding: 82 percent successful reconstruction of frontal-cranial defects up to 25 cm2 at 24 months; two implants (about 5 percent) removed for infection; osseointegration confirmed on explant biopsy.

evidence.title: Sphenoethmoid cerebrospinal fluid leak repair with hydroxyapatite cement
evidence.finding: All 21 sphenoethmoid CSF leaks sealed on first application with no recurrence at mean 36 months; extrusion when placed transnasally in the ethmoid region.

evidence.title: Correction of large (over 25 cm2) cranial defects with reinforced hydroxyapatite cement
evidence.finding: Nine cranioplasties of 40 to 196 cm2 using HAC over tantalum mesh and titanium bars; two constructs removed for infection at one and three months.

evidence.title: Use of fast-setting hydroxyapatite cement for secondary craniofacial contouring
evidence.finding: Five complications (two infections, one seroma, one persistent swelling, one retained drain); 38 good and 7 acceptable results, 3 reoperations for contour.

evidence.title: Use of hydroxyapatite cement in pediatric craniofacial reconstructive surgery: strategies for avoiding complications
evidence.finding: 78 children reconstructed with Mimix or BoneSource (mean 57 g): 7 complications (trauma, infection, exposure), 6 requiring removal; every complication followed a traumatic event.

evidence.title: BoneSource hydroxyapatite cement: a novel biomaterial for craniofacial skeletal tissue engineering and reconstruction
evidence.finding: Review of material chemistry and clinical use guidelines by the developers; sets the 25 cm2 and no-sinus-contact rules later written into labels.

bd.reimbursement: Bundled (see hydroset).
bd.notes: Legacy brand; evidence base inherited by HydroSet in Stryker marketing.

name: map3 Cellular Allogeneic Bone Graft
ownership_history: Launched by RTI Surgical in 2014 using multipotent adult progenitor cell (MAPC) technology licensed from Athersys. FDA issued RTI a Warning Letter on 2017-11-08 (OBPO-1 18-01) holding that map3 could not be regulated solely as a 361 HCT/P. RTI ceased manufacturing and distributing map3 and incinerated its remaining inventory on 2018-12-19 under FDA observation; FDA's closeout letter is dated 2019-04-12 (MARCS-CMS 525318). RTI's spine business became Surgalign in 2020 (Surgalign went bankrupt in 2023; Xtant bought its assets), and RTI Surgical's OEM business was sold to Montagu Private Equity (announced 2020). Neither Xtant's FY2025 10-K nor RTI's current site lists map3: the product has been off the market since 2018.
composition: Cortical cancellous allograft chips, demineralized bone and cryopreserved multipotent adult progenitor cells (MAPC)

regulatory.reference: Section 361 HCT/P as claimed by RTI; FDA Warning Letter 2017-11-08 disputed this (map3 also subject to drug and biological product requirements); closeout letter 2019-04-12 after RTI stopped manufacture and distribution
on_label_indications: Bone void filler for voids or gaps not intrinsic to the stability of the bony structure (361 homologous use)

applications.evidence_summary: One retrospective ALIF series (n=41) reported fusion equivalent to rhBMP-2 at 1 year (cited in the 2021 CBM systematic review); RTI's 30-patient ALIF/LLIF cohort (NCT02628210) completed 2020.
applications.caveats: Product may no longer be sold; a 2014 foot/ankle study was terminated after one patient.

evidence.title: Interbody spacers with map3 cellular allogeneic bone graft in ALIF or LLIF
evidence.finding: Completed June 2020; no results posted.

bd.reimbursement: Bundled in fusion MS-DRGs.
bd.notes: Illustrates the OEM-tissue-bank problem: when the distributor (Surgalign) failed, the brand effectively disappeared even though the processor (RTI) survived.

challenge: Discontinued 2018 (not merely absent from Xtant's list): FDA closeout letter 2019-04-12.

name: Kryptonite Bone Cement
composition: Calcified triglyceride (castor-oil-derived polyurethane with calcium carbonate) expanding adhesive cement; not a calcium phosphate

regulatory.reference: K091382 (2009-11-16, product code GXP, Methyl Methacrylate for Cranioplasty); FDA recall Z-1496-2012, event 61709
on_label_indications: Repair of cranial defects (cranioplasty)

applications.evidence_summary: Marketed 2010 to 2012 as an adhesive, expanding cranioplasty cement; a bench study found unpredictable expansion (mean 49 percent, SD 22) and a single-center cohort reported post-craniotomy infection of 17.8 percent in exposed versus 0.42 percent in unexposed patients (RR 42). The firm initiated a Class 2 recall of all lots (3,100 kits) on 2012-04-06 because strength and stiffness fell below specification at body temperature; the recall was terminated 2015-07-14 and the product has not reappeared.
applications.caveats: The FDA record is a voluntary recall, not a formal withdrawal; no relaunch, sale of the asset or new 510(k) was found.

evidence.title: The expansile properties of Kryptonite relating to cranioplasty
evidence.finding: Ten reconstituted samples expanded a mean 49 percent (SD 22) in saline, most within two hours, explaining the contour irregularities seen clinically.

evidence.title: FDA recall record Z-1496-2012, Kryptonite Bone Cement 5cc and 10cc kits
evidence.finding: Class 2 recall of 3,100 kits distributed January 2010 to April 2012 because bone cement strength and stiffness fall below specification at body temperature; terminated 2015-07-14.

evidence.title: Single-hospital retrospective cohort of post-craniotomy infection with Kryptonite exposure (Cureus, 2014)
evidence.finding: Infection 17.8 percent in Kryptonite-exposed craniotomies versus 0.42 percent unexposed, relative risk 42.1 (95 percent CI 5.1 to 348).

bd.reimbursement: n/a
bd.notes: Cautionary case for the GXP product code: cleared on bench data as substantially equivalent to PMMA, failed in the field within two years.

name: OP-1 Implant / OP-1 Putty (rhBMP-7, eptotermin alfa)
company: Withdrawn from the US; last held by Olympus Biotech Corporation (rights later passed to Ember Therapeutics and reportedly Viscogliosi Brothers)
ownership_history: Creative BioMolecules developed OP-1; Stryker Biotech (Hopkinton, MA) commercialized it, receiving HDE H010002 on October 17, 2001 for long-bone nonunion and HDE H020008 (2004) for revision posterolateral lumbar fusion. An FDA advisory panel voted against a PMA for OP-1 Putty in uninstrumented posterolateral fusion in 2009. Stryker agreed on 2010-12-06 to sell the OP-1 family to Olympus Corporation for $60 million and closed the sale on 2011-02-01 (Olympus Biotech). Olympus closed Olympus Biotech's US operations and discontinued US sales in 2014. Ember Therapeutics later held the asset and announced a divestiture to Viscogliosi Brothers in 2018; the FDA HDE record still lists Olympus Biotech as applicant.
composition: Recombinant human osteogenic protein-1 (BMP-7) 3.5 mg with 1 g bovine type I collagen carrier (Implant); Putty adds carboxymethylcellulose.

regulatory.reference: H010002 (OP-1 Implant; HDE original received 2001-05-29, approved 2001-10-17; product code OKD); H020008 (OP-1 Putty; received 2002-12-23, approved 2004-04-07; product code OJZ; revision posterolateral lumbar fusion); both combination products with supplements through S033/S022
on_label_indications: Alternative to autograft in recalcitrant long bone nonunions where use of autograft is unfeasible and alternative treatments have failed (HDE; use limited to 4,000 patients per year with IRB oversight)

applications.evidence_summary: Pivotal IDE RCT in tibial nonunion (Friedlaender 2001, 122 patients/124 nonunions): OP-1 plus IM nail was statistically indistinguishable from autograft (clinical success 81% versus 85%; radiographic 75% versus 84%), with no donor-site pain. Equivalence was not demonstrated to PMA standard, hence the HDE.
applications.caveats: Tibial data; non-inferiority not formally shown; sponsor-funded; product no longer available in the US.

applications.evidence_summary: Friedlaender 2001 (n=122 patients, 124 tibial nonunions) randomized OP-1 vs autograft with IM nailing; OP-1 reached clinical and radiographic success comparable to autograft without donor-site morbidity. This remains the only RCT of a BMP against autograft in tibial nonunion.
applications.caveats: HDE, not PMA: FDA did not require demonstrated effectiveness; partially blinded; product withdrawn 2014 so the evidence has no commercial vehicle in the US.
applications.challenge: A hiring manager will ask why the best nonunion RCT in the field belongs to a dead product and whether rhBMP-2 can borrow it (it cannot, legally).

applications.evidence_summary: Diamond-concept series (Giannoudis group) used rhBMP-7 with RIA graft and BMAC in femoral and tibial nonunions (n=64; n=14 subtrochanteric) with high union rates; the 2025 network meta-analysis pools these BMP-7 era trials.
applications.caveats: Series are European and used BMP-7 that is no longer sold; cannot be reproduced in the US.

applications.evidence_summary: The HDE long-bone nonunion indication covered the humerus; comparative data (Hackl 2017, PMID:28784168) showed no benefit of adding rhBMP-7 to properly revised humeral, femoral and tibial nonunions.
applications.caveats: Product withdrawn; included for history and because surgeons still cite OP-1 data when arguing for BMP in the upper extremity.

applications.evidence_summary: Bilic 2006 RCT (n=17) is the only randomized BMP evidence in the carpus.
applications.caveats: Tiny trial; not reproducible with any marketed product.

evidence.title: Osteogenic protein-1 (bone morphogenetic protein-7) in the treatment of tibial nonunions.
evidence.finding: OP-1 with IM nailing matched fresh autograft on clinical and radiographic success at 9 months without donor-site morbidity.

evidence.title: Long bone non-unions treated with the diamond concept: a case series of 64 patients
evidence.finding: Revision fixation plus RIA graft, BMP-7 and concentrated marrow aspirate in femoral (55%) and tibial (34%) nonunions; high union with painless weight bearing as the clinical definition.

evidence.title: Osteogenic protein-1 (BMP-7) accelerates healing of scaphoid non-union with proximal pole sclerosis
evidence.finding: Faster radiographic healing with OP-1; allograft plus OP-1 equaled autograft.

evidence.title: Long-term outcome following additional rhBMP-7 application in revision surgery of aseptic humeral, femoral, and tibial shaft nonunion
evidence.finding: No difference in healing or function with rhBMP-7.

bd.reimbursement: Not applicable (withdrawn).
bd.notes: The lesson for BD: an HDE caps volume at 4,000 units a year and requires IRB approval at every site, which kept OP-1 a sub-scale product; failure to convert to a PMA (2009 panel) and the Stryker Biotech off-label promotion case (Stryker Biotech pleaded guilty to a misdemeanor in 2012 over OP-1 Putty/Calstrux promotion; not re-verified here) ended the franchise.
